Scarlatti D.Sonata in G major K 180.YT_description:
Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in G major K. 180.
00:10 Introduction
01:45 Sonata
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
La Sonata in in Sol maggiore K. 180 di Domenico Scarlatti che presenteremo oggi consiste in circa un minuto e mezzo di magia tastieristica, una parentesi di spudorato buonumore musicale con un tocco di genio. La Sonata è un piccolo capriccio, molto brillante e difficile da eseguire, con stravaganti figure veloci alla mano destra e arditi salti alla sinistra, ma il miracolo avviene nel mezzo del pezzo: Domenico vuole un episodio di contrasto, e allora dispiega una delle sue “vamp”. Comincia con una nota sola, alla mano sinistra, che la ripete mentre la destra intona una piccolissima melodia di due note. Intanto, la nota singola alla sinistra cresce: prima diventa un bicordo, poi un tricordo, accarezzando anche armonie avventurosamente dissonanti, e genera l'impressione di una inarrestabile inflazione sonora che è addirittura scioccante perché, alla fine, questa piccola, singola nota si trasforma in un accordone quasi cacofonico di cinque note, sempre contrapposto alla medesima, piccola melodia alla destra. L'effettò è spettacolare. Un vero colpo di genio! Dopo un passo così intenso, la musica torna alla baraonda degli esordi per chiudere la Sonata con il botto. Tutto ciò, come dicevo, in un minuto e mezzo di grande musica.
Buon ascolto.

Scarlatti D.Sonata in C major K. 339.YT_description:
Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in C major K. 339
00:10 Introduction
02:29 Sonata 
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
La Sonata in Do maggiore K. 339 di Domenico Scarlatti che presenteremo oggi è gfra le meno frequentate dell'intera collezione, e forse a cagion di buon motivo: è una Sonata complessa, punto amichevole verso il suonatore, e confesso candidamente d'aver avuto io stesso i miei bei problemi nell'interpretarla; vedevo troppe idee, che a me parevano scollate, e non riuscivo a venirne a capo. Ovviamente, però, una delle belle cose di questo programma è che riusciamo a comunicare, e qualche volta non è difficile imparare l'una dall'altro. Qualche mese fa il Signor Giacobbe Nevio Zanivan lasciò un commento, a proposito d'una altra Sonata, che menzionava le doti imrovvisatorie di Domenico. Mi dette da pensare. Allora andai a consultare il bel libro che il Maestro Baiano ha scritto sulle Sonate di Scarlatti, e vi trovai un bel brano in cui l'estemporaneità delle improvvisazioni di Scarlatti erano sottolineate. Dopo un po' più di studio, mi convinsi che questa Sonata altro non è che la trascrizione di un'improvvisazione. Comincia in modo contrappuntistico, come un Canone, con un tema piuttosto innocente. Poi la musica si ferma, e quando riparte Domenico scrive un episodio di tragico lirismo il quale, però, pare non andare da nessuna parte. Dopo qualche fioritura, fa capolino un motivo di scale il quale chiude la prima parte del pezzo; quando si fa il ritornello, si suona un pochino più spediti perché ora Domenico sa perfettamente dove andrà a parare con la sua improvvisazione. La seconda parte si apre con una espansione del motivo lirico, molto bella, ma ben presto ricompare il tema di scale, stavolta carico di significati reconditi: siccome Domenico è un virtuoso, saltabecca su e giù per la tastiera e scrive una foresta di scale da par suo, le quali porteranno a termine la Sonata. Interessante notare che questa è una delle poche Sonate per le quali Domenico scrive un paio di battute per tornare “a capo” anche nella seconda parte del pezzo: non vi è dubbio che vuole risentire anche quella! Dev'essere stato parecchio fiero del suo pezzo! Spero vi piaccia.
Buon ascolto.

Scarlatti D.Sonata in C minor K 56.YT_description:
Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in c minor K. 56.
00:10 Introduction
02:44 Sonata
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
Quando ci capita fra le mani un pezzo di musica come la Sonata in do minore K. 56 di Domenico Scarlatti che presenteremo oggi, è quasi impossibile non pensare a Thomas Roseingrave ed alla usa famosa reazione quando per la prima volta udì Domenico suonare. Al povero Thomas parve che “mille diavoli” sedessero alla tastiera del clavicembalo! La Sonata in questione è una tarantella, ma non è una tarantella qualsiasi. Questa è di quelle infernali.  Ci è pervenuta in una copia manoscritta datata 1742, ossia in un momento storico perfettamente a cavallo fra l'era barocca e quella classica. All'epoca, la musica era un affare piuttosto educato, galante, garbato. Non è punto difficile immaginare la reazione degli ascoltatori dell'epoca ad una cosa di questo genere: sgomento, terrore, incredulità. La Sonata comincia con grandi gesti, piccanti dissonanze, e l'intera prima pagina serve a preparare la scena per quello che ha da venire: Domenico è Belzebub, che chiama a raccolta i suoi diavoletti e piano piano li incita alla danza. Quando la tarantella vera e proprio comincia, Domenico infesta la partitura con ogni tipo di diavoleria: incroci di mano pazzeschi, un irresistibile ritmo folle, e poi, nella seconda parte, alcune scale fulminanti che segnalano la fine del pezzo, ma quando finalmente raggiungiamo la fine del pezzo, la mano destra vola fino ad un Do acuto, praticamente la fine della tastiera a disposizione di Domenico, e per finire il pezzo il fellone ci chiede di volare, con la stessa mano ed a tempo, sul do grave, quattro ottave più in basso. Ovviamente, è una trovata da spacconi, di quelle che si fanno per mettersi in mostra. Ma, in fondo, questo è un pezzo da sfoggio per eccellenza, ed è un grande privilegio, per me, potervelo presentare.
Buon ascolto.

【譜めくり日めくり#126】I. モシェレス／12の性格的練習曲　作品95　第4-7番

4. ユーノー(Juno), Allegro maestoso, A-dur 0:00
5. おとぎ話(A Child's Fable), Allegretto grazioso, Es-dur 3:58
6. バッカナール(Bacchanale), Allegro con spirito, C-dur 8:12
7. 優しさ(Tenderness), Andante molto espressivo, G-dur 12:32

モシェレスの続きをアップします。
この曲集は、曲間にブリッジというか、数小節の小さい間奏が挟まっている箇所があって、今回の第4番と第5番の間がそうです。その繋ぎの関係もあり、今回は第7番まで弾きました。

だんだん開き直ってきまして、モンタージュをあまり厭わないことにしました。各部分が少しでもマシな方がやっぱりいいかな、と。
通してバシッと弾ければ、それに越したことはないのですが、無理です^_^;;

The comprehensive programme is set to delight pianophiles and new audiences alike with concerts on DG Stage, a heritage project on YouTube featuring video clips of great performers past and present, and a specially curated collection of piano albums on sale at DG Store.
 
“Music crosses all boundaries to touch people from so many places and backgrounds,” comments Dr Clemens Trautmann, President Deutsche Grammophon. “We’re delighted to be an integral part of World Piano Day for a third year running. Our inaugural online festival in March 2020 and its successor last year both reached global audiences of well over a million piano lovers. This year’s festival, which includes brand-new productions, exclusive premieres and a fantastic selection of archive recordings, celebrates the limitless beauty of great pianism. I would like to thank all pianists and partners involved in this wonderfully uniting project.”

Liszt F.Gretchen (from A Faust Symphony).YT_description:
Franz Liszt - "Gretchen" from Faust Symphony 
Tatiana Primak Khoury
Live from Balamand University
the Faust Symphony has always been recognized as one of Liszt's pinnacles of achievement. Although Liszt produced the whole symphony (and all of the Dante Symphony) for two pianos, Gretchen, the second movement of the Faust Symphony, is the only movement that he published in a version for solo piano: a pity, because he has done the job so beautifully, in exactly the same spirit in which he approached the transcriptions of the Beethoven Symphonies. The piece is a character portrait of Goethe's heroine, cast in a simple ternary form. The main material is woven around two of Liszt's finest themes, one a delicate melody with a single line of more florid accompaniment, and the other a theme whose opening chords reveal some splendid part-writing in the imitations of the inner voices. The music of the central section is effective enough without the need to have observed its origins in the first movement. Those who wish to follow all of the extra-musical possibilities would need to hear the whole Symphony, but as a single movement piano piece, the work does not stand in need of further gloss.

Moscheles I.Etude in Bb minor No 12 from.YT_description:
I. Moscheles - Etude op.70 n.12
Fausto Bongelli, piano
Ignaz Moscheles, (born May 23, 1794, Prague, Bohemia, Austrian Habsburg domain [now in Czech Republic]—died March 10, 1870, Leipzig [Germany]), Czech pianist, one of the outstanding virtuosos of his era.
Moscheles studied at the Prague Conservatory and later at Vienna under Johann Georg Albrechtsberger and Antonio Salieri. In 1814, commissioned by Artaria & Co., publishers, he made the first piano arrangement of Ludwig van Beethoven’s opera Fidelio, under the composer’s supervision. After giving piano recitals in Germany and France, he settled in London in 1821. In 1829 he took part in the first London performance of the Concerto for Two Pianos by Felix Mendelssohn, who had been his pupil. He conducted the first English performance of Beethoven’s Missa Solemnis and later conducted Beethoven’s Ninth Symphony at the Philharmonic Society, of which he was a regular conductor from 1845. From 1846 he was principal professor of piano at the Leipzig Conservatory, and his reputation and skill as a teacher were important factors in the continued success of that institution.
Moscheles belonged to a conservative school of piano playing that did not lend itself to the works of Frédéric Chopin and Franz Liszt; of the younger composers of his day, he leaned more toward Mendelssohn and Robert Schumann. Nevertheless, his explorations of the gradations of tone colour influenced Liszt as well as Schumann. He was also admired for his brilliant extempore performances. His own compositions include eight piano concerti, studies, and chamber works.

Scarlatti D.Sonata in G minor K 108.YT_description:
Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in g minor K. 108.
00:10 Introduction
01:21 Sonata
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
La Sonata in sol minor K. 108 che presenteremo oggi è una delle più estreme dell'intera collezione. Sin dalle prime mosse, le pretese tecniche si avvicinano al feroce: ottave, note doppie, modulazioni astruse e folli incroci di mano, mentre tutto il tempo la musica è portata avanti da un ritmo apparentemente inarrestabile. La cosa più importante, però, è l'impressione che questa musica genera nell'ascoltatore: un'impressione di paurosa minaccia, quasi come un grande stregone il quale, intento a mescolare il suo elisir nel crogiolo, non voglia essere disturbato. Ascoltando un pezzo come questa Sonata non è punto difficile immaginare quello che intendeva Thomas Roseingrave quando, dopo aver ascoltato Domenico suonare il clavicembalo, disse d'aver avuto l'impressione che mille diavoli sedessero allo strumento. Beh, in questa occasione i diavoli sono in giro, alla grande.
Buon ascolto.

A fascinating set of pieces, Visions Fugitives was created out of the spontaneous compositional style of Prokofiev, who would usually write down musical ideas as they occurred to him, to put them together later on. In 1915, five of these short pieces were born, and composed six more a year later. In 1917 he added the remaining nine, shaping a set of 20 miniatures that comprised different moods and characters individually and showed a logical sequence when performed as a whole.

Domenico Scarlatti
Sonata in C major K. 271
Sandro Ivo Bartoli
piano

Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in C major K. 271.
00:10 Introduction
02:15 Sonata
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
Siamo a Madrid, in una caldissima domenica di luglio nell'anno 1750. Domenico ha avuto i figli a pranzo, si è divertito, e si è goduto sia la sangria che il Rioja, ma è vecchiotto e sicché, quando i familiari sono andati via, è corso a schiacciare un pisolino. Purtroppo, non è giornata: si presenta un messo reale per dirgli che è desiderato da Sua Maestà, e Domenico non ha scampo. Si veste in fretta e si precipita a palazzo. La Regina gli intima di improvvisare un minuetto, e Domenico farfuglia qualche scusa: “Maestà, sono stanco; è caldo, e o anche mangiato troppo...” ma la ragale allieva insiste, e non è possibile evadere il regio comando. Allora Domenico si siede al clavicembalo, e comincia a improvvisare qualche passaggio lesto ma la Regina, dal suo trono, gli urla “Ho detto un Minuetto”. Allora Domenico mette assieme qualche battuta che pare un minuetto, ma proprio non ha punta voglia di fare un minuetto. Riappaiono i passi brillanti, dai quali Domenico si lascia trasportare fino a quando la Regina interrompe di nuovo: “Minuetto! Ho detto Minuetto!”. E la storia di ripete: Domenico accenna qualche battuta nello stile di un minuetto, ma poi non ce la fa più: i passi brillanti si susseguono, e perfino la Regina, alla fine, è ben lieta d'aver ascoltato una brillantissima toccata. Ora, se una storiella come questa fosse davvero accaduta, il risultato musicale potrebbe essere qualcosa di molto simile alla Sonata in Do maggiore K. 271 di Domenico Scarlatti che presenteremo oggi. 
Buon ascolto.

Scarlatti D.Sonata in D major K 299.YT_description:
Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in D major K. 299.
00:10 Introduction
01:10 Sonata
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
Nonostante sia un bellissimo, piccolo fandango, la Sonata in Re maggiore K. 299 di Domenico Scarlatti che presenteremo oggi è fra le meno frequentate dell'intera collezione. Stavolta, però, il motivo è evidente: le difficoltà tecniche che questa piccola Sonata pone all'interprete sono feroci sin dall'esordio. La Sonata mostra una scrittura molto densa, con note doppie ovunque, ma quel che la rende un incubo per i tastieristi è la profusione di folli salti, equamente divisi fra le due mani, che trasformano anche i passi più lirici in qualcosa di altamente avventuroso da suonare.
Buon ascolto.

Scarlatti D.Sonata in F major K 44.YT_description:
Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in F major K. 44.

00:10 Introduction
01:21 Sonata
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
La Sonata in Fa maggiore K. 44 di Domenico Scarlatti che presenteremo oggi è un lavoro giovanile molto importante, un'opera che cerca di rendere omaggio alla tradizione pur essendo già un compendio di meraviglie tecniche e trucchi mirabolanti. La Sonata comincia come un innocuo pezzettino galante, e questo è l'omaggio alla tradizione: già dal secondo rigo Domenico scrive floride ornamentazioni (per esteso), qualche salto birichino, poi si lancia in un episodio di melismo napoletano che è pieno di pathos, al quale fa seguito un esteso passo a mani incrociate. A questo punto non ci sono più limiti, e allora Domenico scrive un passaggio reboante e fragoroso, con ottave alla mano sinistra e note doppie alla mano destra, che eventualmente chiuderà la Sonata con splendore. Questo, secondo me, è un piccolo capolavoro.
Buon ascolto.

Recorded in the Belle Shenkman Studio, 18 July 2018, Royal College of Music London

Clara Wieck-Schumann [1819 – 1896]
Sonata in G minor (1841-42)
0:00 i. Allegro 
08:20 ii. Adagio 
11:20 iii. Scherzo
14:00 iv. Rondo

For more of Clara Schumann: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLLu4HogDGXKGccu-kGSfFdqlS6B8ZmvYg 

#ClaraSchumann #womencomposers #sonata
Considered one of the most distinguished pianists of the Romantic era, Wieck-Schumann’s qualities as a composer are often overlooked. This Sonata was her sole attempt at writing a piano sonata and marked a turning point in her artistic and personal life. Throughout the Sonata’s genesis, she experienced emancipation from her controlling father, an acclaimed transition from prodigy virtuoso to mature artist, and the joys and power imbalances in marriage. In terms of form and sound aesthetic, the Sonata reflects the Schumanns’ changing views on virtuosity and their joint studies of Bach’s counterpoint, songs and literature, Mozart’s and Beethoven’s symphonies and chamber works. However, it was never premiered or published till 1989 and 1991 respectively. She had also left the final movement unannotated; a meaningful challenge and opportunity for the interpreter. 

Wieck-Schumann’s music exhibits a unique personality compared to her husband’s freneticism. Through her mastery of sonata form and pianistic texture, she maintains a flowing continuum between fiery passion and poised restraint. Wieck-Schumann quoted her own theme from 'Er ist gekommen in Sturm und Regen' (He Came in Storm and Rain), a lieder she contributed to the Schumanns' collective Liebesfrühling [1840]. In the original song accompaniment, the turbulent piano figuration swirls urgently beneath an anxiously beseeching soprano line, in a masterful soundpainting of Friedrich Rückert's text. In this Sonata's Allegro, the theme is often in the tenor voice, perhaps representing the enigmatic 'He' of Rückert's text. Wieck-Schumann appeared to be preoccupied with this ‘storm’ imagery, for the quotation was also present in her Scherzo No. 2. The Adagio is beautifully succinct and features a quotation of Robert Schumann’s Schlummerlied (Lullaby). The Schlummerlied had been his gift for her upon the birth of their first child, Marie. The sprightly Scherzo movement alternates youthful levity with the elegiac tone of Trio. Finally, the Rondo bears thematic references to the Allegro, demonstrating Wieck-Schumann’s grasp of cyclicism and coherence. Its main theme shares a melodic outline with her ‘Sie liebten sich beide’ (They Loved Each Other) from her Sechs Lieder Op. 13 No. 2 (1844). The musical character shifts between yearning lyricism and restlessness, before coming to an assertive conclusion. Wieck-Schumann’s Sonata, eclipsed for 150 years, is now reborn into the 21st century, offering listeners a window into imagining her world.

Bonds M.Troubled Water.YT_description:
SUBSCRIBE: https://www.youtube.com/mbaczewska88

6:10 Margaret Bonds: Troubled Water
Magdalena Baczewska, piano

In this episode of Bach@Home pianist Magdalena Baczewska celebrates Margaret Bonds: a pianist, composer, pedagogue, and a lifetime supporter of the creativity of African-American artists and musicians. Despite the racial discrimination she faced in college Bonds became the first African-American woman to ever perform with a renowned American orchestra, the Chicago Symphony. In this episode, you will learn about the spirituals and their function in the lives of enslaved African-Americans. As always, you will hear a live performance, Margaret Bonds' piano fantasy "Troubled Water." The piece is based on a popular spiritual "Wade in the Water," a melody that is said to have been strategically used by Harriet Tubman, who brought as many as 70 slaves to freedom. Following the performance you will hear a short analysis of the techniques and influences Bonds used in her composition. 

Magdalena Baczewska is the Director of the Music Performance Program and member of Faculty of Arts and Sciences at Columbia University. For more info, visit MagdalenaNYC.com

Mikrokosmos, progressive pieces for piano in 6 volumes, Sz. 107, BB 105 (1926-1939)

145. 0:00 
146. 3:36
147. 5:42

Claude Helffer, piano
Haakon Austbö, second piano

Mikrokosmos was originally designed as a collection of pieces for the beginning pianist, but over time it took on grander proportions, comprising 153 individual pieces that spanned the range of technical difficulty. Dividing into six volumes, it begins with pieces for beginners and progresses to those that challenge even the most accomplished pianist. That Mikrokosmos has become a viable progressive method is demonstrated by its ubiquity in the repertories of modern piano students, but its reputation rests on more than its technical and pedagogical applications; Bartók's work represents a varied and finely crafted catalog of twentieth century musical idioms. In Bartók's own words, it "appears as a synthesis of all the musical and technical problems which were treated and in some case only partially solved in the previous piano works." Perhaps chief among these musical problems was Bartók's attempted synthesis of Eastern and Western European musical traditions, particularly Eastern folk music with the Germanic tradition (as represented by Bach and Beethoven) and with the progressive harmonies of Claude Debussy. 

The first 66 pieces in Mikrokosmos (Vols. 1 and 2) are dedicated to Bartók's son, Peter, for whose use they were originally intended. Many of these pieces are technical exercises, useful for developing finger and hand independence, as well as hand span; however, they are also of interest for their musical language. Hungarian folk tunes, pentatonic, whole-tone and modal harmonies, as well as more adventurous octatonic chromatic scales all form the basis for these short pieces. 

Volumes 3 and 4 make up numbers 67 through 121. These pieces display increased harmonic complexity and technical demands. Bartók employs more polymodes (the use of different modes, or keys, simultaneously), along with octatonic and diatonic scale fragments to construct these pieces. The compositions in the third and fourth volumes are also important because they betray the influence of Franz Liszt, particularly in terms of tone color; Bartók wrote of his desire, in these pieces, to "poetically color the piano tone." 

The final volumes (5 and 6) of the Mikrokosmos were intended as concert pieces for professional pianists. They differ from the preceding pieces in many respects: their contrapuntal texture is more dense (four parts), the melodic and harmonic material is more characteristic of Bartók's non-pedagogical works, and rhythmic structures are much more complicated and include vigorous syncopations and Bulgarian dance rhythms. 

While Bartók's intention to synthesize Bach, Beethoven, and Debussy was perhaps not fully realized, Mikrokosmos nonetheless compares well with some of Bach and Debussy's ostensibly pedagogical keyboard works. Like Bach's Inventions or Debussy's Études, for example, Mikrokosmos is not merely a work of practical value, but also a work of art with much purely musical substance. [Allmusic.com]

In the sonata's four movements, you hear the music tearing at the seams of classical and serial structure, as the 23-year-old Boulez tries to find a language that will exorcise the ghosts of classical music, from Bach to Schoenberg. Like all exorcisms, this one is defined by physical paroxysms and emotional extremes: the blasted soundscape of the start of the slow second movement, the exploded, eruptive sonata form of the first movement, or the fucked-up fugue of the final movement..... The ambiguous, desolate coda sounds like a lament, not just in terms of the trajectory of the piece, but also for the possibility of musical discourse in post-war Europe. (Adapted from Tom Service)

Feldman M.Piano.YT_description:
"Piano" written in 1977 is a transitional work in Feldman's output, between the miniature Webernesque pieces of the 50's and 60's, and the vast cathedrals of sound of the 80's.

One characteristic of this transitional period are the loud outbursts (marked fff) against a global ppp dynamic (at 14:14, 15:03 and 16:32). This could be characterized as a violent red slash in one of the canvases of his buds. Rather than characterize this as whisper soft and deafeningly loud, I've tried to scale the dynamics in a "musical" manner.

One of the remarkable things in this score are the segments where the standard 2 staff system is expanded to 4 (6:23, 15:00, 16:11 and 20:40) and 6 (10:02, 16:23 and 20:53) staves. At the final appearance, Feldman further maxes the counting difficulties by superposing different time signatures. This kind of composing verges on irrational rhythms, i.e. no direct relationship. What he appears to be doing is take a 2 or 3 piano work, and direct a single performer to realize it.

Another innovative touch is how he splits a triplet group (for example in bar 3); the first part of the triplet offsets the attack, and is made up for at the end of the measure.

For the performer, the slow pace is deceptive; the carefully noted rhythmic markings are precise and demand that the performer "count like crazy." Take your best shot.

In this realization, I've observed the slur markings as a pedal down. In the 2 and 3 piano sections, I've panned left right and center.

I've become quite fond of this piece and can only recommend that you the listener take this opportunity to get to know this masterpiece.

I found the score (which is still under copyright) at some Russian website, so this is a disclaimer. This video is intended for educational purposes only.

Body J.Totentanz from Sarajevo.YT_description:
Jack BODY Sarajevo - Jeffrey Grice, piano  
1) Remembering imperfectly
2) Totentanz 
3) Lacrymae

Jack Body wrote Sarajevo in 1996 in evocation of the terrible Balkan conflict. This score is published by Waiteata Music Press, Wellington, New Zealand, and played here by Jeffrey Grice in the concert Between two worlds at the Salle Gaveau in Paris in 2007.

Les œuvres de Jack Body sont jouées dans le monde entier (Kronos Quartet, BBC Scottish Orchestra...) Professeur de composition à l'université de Victoria à Wellington, il a créé le Asia Pacific Music Festival et mène de front un combat aussi bien pour la musique contemporaine que pour la découverte des musiques du monde. « Bien que je sache que mon chez-moi, « l'endroit auquel j'appartiens », ne peut être que la Nouvelle-Zélande, je suis un voyageur invétéré, particulièrement à des pays dont les cultures sont très différentes de la mienne...J'ai appris que toutes les valeurs sont relatives, qu'il n'y a pas d'absolus. Bien entendu, le vrai sens de ce que je vois, entends et éprouve, reste impénétrable. Mais à travers ces rencontres, mes propres idées et perceptions sont bouleversées, transformées et enrichies. »

Sarajevo évoque le conflit terrible qui a déchiré les Balkans dans les années 90. En se souvenant....imparfaitement. Totentanz... la danse macabre d'une mitraillette qui tire à l'aveuglette. Suivi par la complainte Lachrymae, les larmes en Latin...

http://www.marktaratushkin.com

The premiere of the piano cycle “Sarcasms” op. 17 took place on November 27, 1916 in the St. Petersburg Conservatory with the personal performance of the musician. G.G. Neuhaus recollected of one of the first performances of “Sarcasms”: “Pince-nez placed on his nose, F.M. Blumenfeld cast his glance over Prokofiev’s head at the score. Sergei Sergeyevich was already prepared to begin, when he turned around suddenly and said: ‘Felix Mikhailovich! I’d rather you’d step to the side. I’m afraid you’ll hit me in the head with your fist.’ Everyone laughed. F.M. blew it off, but nevertheless stepped slightly to the side. Sergei Sergeyevich played through all the ‘Sarcasms.’ The impression he made was absolutely extraordinary. Some of the audience, among whom more than a few socially respectable people were to be found, were delighted; others were, however, scandalized.”

The grotesque elements of Prokofiev’s compositional style were received by the public as well as the critics with deep equivocation. The composer wrote the following in a letter to his friend and mentor Myaskovsky about the first performances of the Cycle: “People take their head in their hands, some of whom in order to plug their ears, the others—to express their excitement, and still more out of pity for the poor, once promising composer.”

To the admirers of “Sarcasms” belonged members of the popular St. Petersburg circle “Contemporary,” which guaranteed Prokofiev a good reception in the progressive cultural intelligentsia at the beginning of the 20th century. Karatygin, the music critic and one of the most significant ideological representatives of the circle, aptly characterized the Prokofiev-ish slap in the face to public sensibility:

“The daemons of Prokofiev’s boundless imagination abandon themselves to an orgiastic dance over the graves of every single fundament of musical beauty…”
(W. Karatygin – speech from November 30, 1916)

The “Sarcasms” themselves were an expression of the young composer’s bitter smile, the scornful irony he felt towards his culture and the art of his time, which remained alien to him. “The Sarcasms, compared to the verse of the early Myaskovsky, were more harshly and painfully barbed. The fearful shock that they unleashed coursed through consciousness with an awful power…” B. Asafjew – “Thoughts and Ideas,” Ch. VII.

Although the fifth piece, with its logical construction and flawlessly honed style, belongs to the early works of the composer, one can already discern the true Prokofiev and his singular talent.

“I still have the program for one of the ‘Sarcasms’ (the fifth piece): sometimes we laugh malevolently at someone or something, but when we look more closely at what we’re laughing about, we see just how wretched and miserable it is. Then we begin to feel uneasy. Although the laughter resounds in our ears, it is now laughing at us.”
(from the Autobiography)

Mikrokosmos, progressive pieces for piano in 6 volumes, Sz. 107, BB 105 (1926-1939)

140. 00:00
141. 01:35

Claude Helffer, piano
Haakon Austbö, second piano

Mikrokosmos was originally designed as a collection of pieces for the beginning pianist, but over time it took on grander proportions, comprising 153 individual pieces that spanned the range of technical difficulty. Dividing into six volumes, it begins with pieces for beginners and progresses to those that challenge even the most accomplished pianist. That Mikrokosmos has become a viable progressive method is demonstrated by its ubiquity in the repertories of modern piano students, but its reputation rests on more than its technical and pedagogical applications; Bartók's work represents a varied and finely crafted catalog of twentieth century musical idioms. In Bartók's own words, it "appears as a synthesis of all the musical and technical problems which were treated and in some case only partially solved in the previous piano works." Perhaps chief among these musical problems was Bartók's attempted synthesis of Eastern and Western European musical traditions, particularly Eastern folk music with the Germanic tradition (as represented by Bach and Beethoven) and with the progressive harmonies of Claude Debussy. 

The first 66 pieces in Mikrokosmos (Vols. 1 and 2) are dedicated to Bartók's son, Peter, for whose use they were originally intended. Many of these pieces are technical exercises, useful for developing finger and hand independence, as well as hand span; however, they are also of interest for their musical language. Hungarian folk tunes, pentatonic, whole-tone and modal harmonies, as well as more adventurous octatonic chromatic scales all form the basis for these short pieces. 

Volumes 3 and 4 make up numbers 67 through 121. These pieces display increased harmonic complexity and technical demands. Bartók employs more polymodes (the use of different modes, or keys, simultaneously), along with octatonic and diatonic scale fragments to construct these pieces. The compositions in the third and fourth volumes are also important because they betray the influence of Franz Liszt, particularly in terms of tone color; Bartók wrote of his desire, in these pieces, to "poetically color the piano tone." 

The final volumes (5 and 6) of the Mikrokosmos were intended as concert pieces for professional pianists. They differ from the preceding pieces in many respects: their contrapuntal texture is more dense (four parts), the melodic and harmonic material is more characteristic of Bartók's non-pedagogical works, and rhythmic structures are much more complicated and include vigorous syncopations and Bulgarian dance rhythms. 

While Bartók's intention to synthesize Bach, Beethoven, and Debussy was perhaps not fully realized, Mikrokosmos nonetheless compares well with some of Bach and Debussy's ostensibly pedagogical keyboard works. Like Bach's Inventions or Debussy's Études, for example, Mikrokosmos is not merely a work of practical value, but also a work of art with much purely musical substance. [Allmusic.com]

Art by Jean Dubuffet

After Chopin’s death many composers tried to master the artistic form of mazurka. His beloved miniature found a true continuator only almost a century later as Karol Szymanowski. This great Polish composer of the XXth century wrote altogether 22 mazurkas in years 1924-26 (20 Mazurkas op.50) and 1933-34 (2 Mazurkas op.62). Szymanowski very often expressed how difficult he felt it was to undertake the historical dialogue with Chopin’s tradition of the mazurka genre. Although he kept the rhythmical structure and the ABA construction of the piece, he changed the function of the melody making the rich, varied and colourful harmony the core of his compositions. Unlike the later Mazurkas op.62, the 20 Mazurkas op.50 represent a strong connection to the folklore of southern Poland - very characteristic of Szymanowski’s compositions written at the end of his life. The whole cycle consists of contrasting pieces with slower and faster dances following each other alternately. Different miniatures were written for composer’s family and fellows - the first four mazurkas being dedicated to Arthur Rubinstein, Szymanowski’s closest friends and one of the greatest interpreters of his works.

Piano music spanning three decades by the foremost living Minimalist composer of our time. 

John Adams has won listeners from far beyond the traditional classical world thanks to his energy over the course of more than half a century in writing music that speaks directly to hearts and minds with undiminished energy, reflecting contemporary concerns and technologies while also crafted with traditional finesse. 

As well as a composer he has been an active promoter and performer – not only of his own music but of his contemporaries and those who exercised a decisive influence on him as a student in California, including Debussy and Stravinsky. His parents were both jazz musicians and he grew up in a household where, as he says, ‘Benny Goodman and Mozart were not separated’. There is a corresponding harmony between traditional and modern idioms in his own music.

The eight Études Op 42 bring us to 1903. Scriabin was by now an established composer with two symphonies to his credit, and as a pianist was a respected interpreter of his own music. Much was changing personally, philosophically and musically. In 1897 he had married the pianist Vera Ivanovna, but in 1902 Tatyana Schloezer became his pupil; a romance developed and in 1904 Scriabin and Tatyana travelled to Paris together. They married later despite Russian legal complications. Significantly, the Op 42 Études were the last of Scriabin’s piano music that Vera worked on with him.

Around 1900 Scriabin joined the circle around the Moscow philosopher Prince Trubetskoy; the climate in this group tended towards the mystical and apocalyptic. Scriabin also read Nietzsche and later became involved with theosophy. These trends of thought, together with a pampered early upbringing by a devoted aunt, led to an increasingly solipsistic world-view,summed up later in Scriabin’s exclamation to the composer Liadov: ‘I am the creator of new worlds. I am God!’

The Etudes of Op 42 are firmly rooted in tonality but frequently carry chromaticism and metrical complexity to extremes. No 1 is written in a restless cross-rhythm of nine against five; further, the right hand’s melodic groupings go across the bar lines in carefully asymmetrical units of 3, 4, 5 and 6 (later, 5 and 4). Speed, lightness, mobility and ceaseless fluid motion again create the sensation of exhilarating flight.

No 2 exploits Scriabin’s favourite five against three, but here the left-hand figures are shifted across the beats as in Op 8 No 7, giving a feeling of underlying disquiet. This surfaces in the final bars where both hands, as Chopin said of the finale of his B flat minor Sonata which this passage seems to recall, ‘chatter in unison’.

No 3 is a superlative trill study; its ethereal register and chromatic fleetness have earned it the apt Russian nickame of ‘The Mosquito’. Its F sharp major tonality is shared by No 4, an idyllic love song (for Tatyana?).

In violent contrast is No 5, eloquently marked ‘Affanato’—breathless and anxious. This atmosphere is created by a restless, dense texture and a harmonic language in which nearly every chord is darkened and destabilized by the addition of a seventh. An aspiring second subject, one of Scriabin’s finest melodic inspirations, affords some relief from the grip of nightmare.

‘Esaltato’—‘elated’—is the marking of No 6, hinting perhaps at Scriabin’s Nietzschean aspirations; the melodic gestures are imperious, and underlying exhilaration is conveyed not only by constantly swirling cross-rhythms but also by delaying the arrival of the tonic harmony for sixteen bars. This signals an increasing tendency in Scriabin’s music: in its final phase, from 1911 on, tonality became a background element, obliquely referred to but rarely overtly stated. Liszt had hinted at this possibility in the Bagatelle sans tonalité back in 1885, but Scriabin could not have known the piece; it remained unpublished until 1956.

The Brahmsian sixths and rhythmic devices of No 7 are comparatively conservative; this may be the Étude mentioned in a letter of 1899 from the composer to his publisher Belaiev. No 8 shares the first study’s aerial quality, but here the shifting of both hands’ figures across the beat (again in cross-rhythms) creates a weightless, wind-borne impression. By contrast, the central section is solidly grandiose, like that of Op 8 No 7, but its much more advanced harmonic language has a strong foretaste of Scriabin’s next major work, The Divine Poem.

Cari amici buongiorno,
La Sonata in Mi bemolle maggiore K. 370 di Domenico Scarlatti che presenteremo oggi è in piccolo capolavoro di equilibrismo musicale. Il pezzo comincia con due voci alla mano destra, subito riprese dalla mano sinistra, poi la Sonata vera e propria prende il suo abbrivio e la musica pare fluire dalla penna di Domenico senza il minimo sforzo. Quando raggiunge la fine, Domenico ha asserito il tono di Mi bemolle maggiore in tutta la sua gloria, in un piccola gemma musicale.

Composer Note: The titles for these pieces were taken from lines of a poem by John Ashbery called "No Longer Very Clear." (However, as with Debussy's Preludes, the music came first.)

Vast Antique Cubes/Throbbing Still (2000) was commissioned by Franklin and Marshall College for the pianist John Browning who premiered both works at The Ann and Richard Barshinger Center for Musical Arts in Hensel Hall at Franklin & Marshall College on September 16, 2000. In Vast Antique Cubes, I wanted to create a sense of a very large space that moved quite slowly from low to high and higher still. Within this reaching upwards, are suggestions of Debussy and Chopin–two composers whom I played frequently as a pianist. By contrast, in the much more energetic and faster Throbbing Still, the music of Stravinsky and the Latin Inca rhythms that I grew up with in South America continue to play a powerful role–to "throb still" in my music.

Mikrokosmos, progressive pieces for piano in 6 volumes, Sz. 107, BB 105 (1926-1939)

140. 00:00

144. 06:41

Claude Helffer, piano
Haakon Austbö, second piano

Mikrokosmos was originally designed as a collection of pieces for the beginning pianist, but over time it took on grander proportions, comprising 153 individual pieces that spanned the range of technical difficulty. Dividing into six volumes, it begins with pieces for beginners and progresses to those that challenge even the most accomplished pianist. That Mikrokosmos has become a viable progressive method is demonstrated by its ubiquity in the repertories of modern piano students, but its reputation rests on more than its technical and pedagogical applications; Bartók's work represents a varied and finely crafted catalog of twentieth century musical idioms. In Bartók's own words, it "appears as a synthesis of all the musical and technical problems which were treated and in some case only partially solved in the previous piano works." Perhaps chief among these musical problems was Bartók's attempted synthesis of Eastern and Western European musical traditions, particularly Eastern folk music with the Germanic tradition (as represented by Bach and Beethoven) and with the progressive harmonies of Claude Debussy. 

The first 66 pieces in Mikrokosmos (Vols. 1 and 2) are dedicated to Bartók's son, Peter, for whose use they were originally intended. Many of these pieces are technical exercises, useful for developing finger and hand independence, as well as hand span; however, they are also of interest for their musical language. Hungarian folk tunes, pentatonic, whole-tone and modal harmonies, as well as more adventurous octatonic chromatic scales all form the basis for these short pieces. 

Volumes 3 and 4 make up numbers 67 through 121. These pieces display increased harmonic complexity and technical demands. Bartók employs more polymodes (the use of different modes, or keys, simultaneously), along with octatonic and diatonic scale fragments to construct these pieces. The compositions in the third and fourth volumes are also important because they betray the influence of Franz Liszt, particularly in terms of tone color; Bartók wrote of his desire, in these pieces, to "poetically color the piano tone." 

The final volumes (5 and 6) of the Mikrokosmos were intended as concert pieces for professional pianists. They differ from the preceding pieces in many respects: their contrapuntal texture is more dense (four parts), the melodic and harmonic material is more characteristic of Bartók's non-pedagogical works, and rhythmic structures are much more complicated and include vigorous syncopations and Bulgarian dance rhythms. 

While Bartók's intention to synthesize Bach, Beethoven, and Debussy was perhaps not fully realized, Mikrokosmos nonetheless compares well with some of Bach and Debussy's ostensibly pedagogical keyboard works. Like Bach's Inventions or Debussy's Études, for example, Mikrokosmos is not merely a work of practical value, but also a work of art with much purely musical substance. [Allmusic.com]

Falla M. deMontanesa No 3 from 4 Piezas.YT_description:
I have many favorite Spanish composers, but Manuel de Falla is one of my most favorite. And among his piano oeuvre, the Quatre Pieces Espagnoles, dating from 1908, are among my most favorite, second only to the Fantasia Baetica. These works show Falla being under the spell of Albeniz, and they have something of the grandeur and exuberant pianism of Iberia, albeit on a smaller scale. These rather difficult pieces have been taunting me for many years, and I believe I finally got the better of them.

I would like to dedicate these humble amateur recordings to the memory of Alicia de Larrocha, who will forever reign supreme in this repertoire.

Bartok B.Allegretto No 3 from For Childr.YT_description:
Here is my new recording, made last weekend, of  Bartók's educational set For Children. The colorful Hungarian title "A Gyermekeknek" somehow always amuses me. The pieces were penned down in 1908/09, but Bartók revised the set in 1945, towards the end of his life, leaving out 6 pieces and slightly altering others. It is this final version that I play here.

The two books are quite different in character. I marginally prefer 
Book I, based on Hungarian Folk Tunes. These are more ebullient, the colors brighter, than those in Book II, based on Slovak Folk Tunes, which are generally darker and more introspective, at times 
reminiscent of Janacek (as they ought to be, being Slovak). 

Both books contain a wealth of great music, and certainly not all of the pieces seen suitable for children - unless they have advanced technique and musicality. I hope my cycle can be enjoyed despite a couple of small read errors (which, obviously and  irritatingly, I only noticed during video preparation).

Bartok B.Andante (No 2 from For Children.YT_description:
Here is my new recording, made last weekend, of  Bartók's educational set For Children. The colorful Hungarian title "A Gyermekeknek" somehow always amuses me. The pieces were penned down in 1908/09, but Bartók revised the set in 1945, towards the end of his life, leaving out 6 pieces and slightly altering others. It is this final version that I play here.

The two books are quite different in character. I marginally prefer 
Book I, based on Hungarian Folk Tunes. These are more ebullient, the colors brighter, than those in Book II, based on Slovak Folk Tunes, which are generally darker and more introspective, at times 
reminiscent of Janacek (as they ought to be, being Slovak). 

Both books contain a wealth of great music, and certainly not all of the pieces seen suitable for children - unless they have advanced technique and musicality. I hope my cycle can be enjoyed despite a couple of small read errors (which, obviously and  irritatingly, I only noticed during video preparation).

Bailey K.Triadic Excursion.YT_description:
https://kerinbailey.com.au/music-shop/jazzin-around-2-piano/#.YnhbAehByUk

Level: Early Intermediate - about grade 3-4

Triadic Excursion - from Jazzin' Around 2 - is a study in RH triads and LH bass line in a Latin style. Every melody note has the other two chord tones tucked underneath. Try to bring out the melody note and shape the phrases. The slurs are for the phrasing, so the 1st chord in each measure may be a bit detached. The pedal is marked for clarity: depress on beats 2 and 4 and release on beats 3 and 1. So it is down for 1/4 note length only.

The key to the RH is 2nd finger for 1st inversion, 3rd finger 2nd inversion. In measure 2, smaller hands may prefer 5th on the Gm 1st inversion. 
The LH is a typical Latin/rock rhythmic pattern. Try to have this down independently of the RH. The RH rhythm is repetitive to enable mastery of the triads.

Form: 3 sections - A 1-8, B 9-12, C (A2) 13-end; Key: F major

Bartok B.Lost Cat from For Children BB 5.YT_description:
Here is my new recording, made last weekend, of  Bartók's educational set For Children. The colorful Hungarian title "A Gyermekeknek" somehow always amuses me. The pieces were penned down in 1908/09, but Bartók revised the set in 1945, towards the end of his life, leaving out 6 pieces and slightly altering others. It is this final version that I play here.

The two books are quite different in character. I marginally prefer 
Book I, based on Hungarian Folk Tunes. These are more ebullient, the colors brighter, than those in Book II, based on Slovak Folk Tunes, which are generally darker and more introspective, at times 
reminiscent of Janacek (as they ought to be, being Slovak). 

Both books contain a wealth of great music, and certainly not all of the pieces seen suitable for children - unless they have advanced technique and musicality. I hope my cycle can be enjoyed despite a couple of small read errors (which, obviously and  irritatingly, I only noticed during video preparation).

Bach J.S.French Suite No 3 in B minor BW.YT_description:
www.szaluckapiano.com

00:00-03:28 Allemande
03:28-05:29 Courante
05:29-09:06 Sarabande
09:06-10:39 Anglaise
10:39-13:47 Menuet-Trio
13:47-15:38 Gigue

The form of Suite was very popular in baroque. It brings together dances from diferrent parts of Europe making it one integrated whole. There are four dances that originally form the core of the baroque suite: German Allemande, French Courante, Spanish Sarabande and Enligh Gigue. Additionally the Suite could be (and usually was) extended by other dances: Menuet, Passapied or even Polonaise. Bach wrote his six French Suites in year 1722-25 and they were originally designed to be played on a harpsichord. Bach himself considered the Suites as a bridge between the Inventions and Das Wohltemperierte Klavier. The title ‘French’ was not given by the composer but by the society to differentiate the French Suites from the previously written English Suites. Funny enough, they are, however, written in an Italian manner.
There is no surviving manuscript of these Suites, therefore the execution of the ornaments can be a very exciting and inspiring challenge for the performer. Scarlatti D.Sonata - K 527 C major.YT_description:
Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in C major K. 527.
00:10 Introduction
01:54 Sonata
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
Se vi dicessi che la Sonata in Do maggiore K. 527 di Domenico Scarlatti che presenteremo oggi è una seguidilla, ossia una danza veloce spagnola in tempo ternario, probabilmente non mentirei, ma neanche sarei completamente onesto. Indubbiamente vi è un importante elemento danzante in questa musica, ma mi pare incidentale, dato che credo questo pezzo essere uno studio di effetti speciali. L'esecuzione della musica folclorica, in tutto il mondo, si appoggia gravosamente sul contributo degli strumenti a percussione i quali generano, o quantomeno punteggiano, il ritmo della musica. In Spagna questi sono le nacchere, e più specificamente il tamburello basco. Occasionalmente, nei pezzi più sofisticati di musica popolare, gli strumenti a percussione non vengono usati in senso ritmico, ma coloristico: succede quando intervengono sul tempo debole della musica, ed aggiungono una nota di colore esotico. Avete indovinato: questo è precisamente ciò che accade qui! In quasi tutto il pezzo, è la mano sinistra a portare avanti il discorso musicale (e danzante) mentre la destra commenta con degli abbellimenti a note doppie sul tempo debole. Forse non la cosa più semplice da eseguire, ma di sicuro molto divertente e pittoresca. Come dicevo prima, un “effetto speciale”.
Buon ascolto.

Scarlatti D.Sonata - K 506 F major.YT_description:
Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in F major K. 506.
00:10 Introduction
01:32 Sonata
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
La Sonata in Fa maggiore K. 306 di Domenico Scarlatti che presenteremo oggi è un pezzo di musica fantastico, pieno di grandi idee. Di fatto, studiarlo è come aprire un piccolo scrigno ove troviamo una meraviglia dietro l'altra. La Sonata comincia con una bordata di scale nel tono di Fa maggiore, tre ottave discendenti alla mano destra e tre ottave ascendenti alla sinistra, poi la musica irrompe in un bellissimo passaggio colmo di lirismo e assai commovente; è come trovarsi nel Primo Concerto di Čajkovskij: questo è il tema più bello del pezzo, ma lo ascolteremo solo qui, perché non tornerà più. Dopo questa parentesi, infatti, la Sonata si rivela per quello che è, ossia una piccola toccata, e Domenico scrive una sventagliata di passi brillanti incluso uno che reca l'indicazione “Detto solo”, ossia “dito solo”: sono brevi scale veloci da eseguirsi con un solo dito, ancora una volta esempio primigenio di “glissando”. Nella seconda parte vi è un brevissimo episodio contrappuntistico, ma ben presto il movimento brillante s'impossessa della musica ancora una volta, e la Sonata finisce gioiosamente. Questo è proprio un bell'esempio di grande musica!
Buon ascolto.

Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in C major K. 548.
00:10 Introduction
01:27 Sonata
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
La Sonata in Do maggiore K. 548 che presenteremo oggi è una delle grandi Sonate della maturità di Domenico. Ormai è anziano, ma non ha perso nulla di quello smalto strumentale che lo ha reso, probabilmente, il più grande clavicembalista della storia. La Sonata è piena di trucchi virtuosistici: salti, note doppie, terze, seste, ottave; è una danza, per la precisione un fandango, che Domenico ci chiede di suonare “Allegretto”, non troppo velocemente (forse vuole che abbiamo il tempo di assaporare ogni nota che ha scritto). La propulsione ritmica è irresistibile, ed il contrasto è assicurato da due episodi di “cante Jondo”, dal carattere molto melancolico, i quali entrambe le volte si risolvono in vertiginosi passaggi di seste che riportano alla figura del fandango, la quale eventualmente chiude la Sonata trionfalmente. Questa è scrittura tastieristica ai massimi livelli.
Buon ascolto

The form of Suite was very popular in baroque. It brings together dances from diferrent parts of Europe making it one integrated whole. There are four dances that originally form the core of the baroque suite: German Allemande, French Courante, Spanish Sarabande and Enligh Gigue. Additionally the Suite could be (and usually was) extended by other dances: Menuet, Passapied or even Polonaise. Bach wrote his six French Suites in year 1722-25 and they were originally designed to be played on a harpsichord. Bach himself considered the Suites as a bridge between the Inventions and Das Wohltemperierte Klavier. The title ‘French’ was not given by the composer but by the society to differentiate the French Suites from the previously written English Suites. Funny enough, they are, however, written in an Italian manner.
There is no surviving manuscript of these Suites, therefore the execution of the ornaments can be a very exciting and inspiring challenge for the performer. The third Suite in B minor is one of the most frequently played ones. It consists of Allemande, Courante, Sarabande, Anglaise (previously named as Gavotte), Menuet, Trio and Gigue.

Liszt F.Abschied S251.YT_description:
Le pianiste Alexandre Kantorow joue Abschied, pièce composée en 1885 par Franz Liszt. Extrait de son récital donné le 26 mars 2022 à la Maison de la Radio et de la Musique



En 1835, Liszt quitte Paris avec sa maîtresse Marie d’Agoult pour se rendre en Suisse. À partir de 1837, il séjourne en Italie. Dans ses Années de pèlerinage, il regroupe des pièces qui font écho à cette période, mais dont la composition s’étend jusqu’au début des années 1880. Le cahier médian, « Deuxième année – Italie », comporte trois morceaux inspirés par des sonnets de Pétrarque : il s’agit en réalité de versions pianistiques de mélodies vocales écrites dans les années 1840, ce dont témoigne leur ligne héritée du bel canto. Après une introduction agitato assai, le Sonnet n° 104 « Pace non trovo » prend la forme d’un nocturne influencé par Chopin. Au centre, un épisode passionné et tumultueux traduit le sujet du poème : l’impossibilité pour l’amant d’accéder à une paix intérieure. Liszt, qui compose nombre de ses œuvres instrumentales à partir d’un substrat littéraire, ne pouvait qu’être fasciné par Dante.
Le poète, mis en musique par les madrigalistes de la fin de la Renaissance, était ensuite entré dans un purgatoire dont il sort seulement au début du XIXe siècle. Toutefois, seule une partie de son œuvre rencontre la sensibilité romantique : les musiciens choisissent presque toujours la Divine Comédie et privilégient L’Enfer, qui entre en résonance avec leur goût pour le fantastique et leurs interrogations sur le destin de l’homme. En outre, ils assimilent la trajectoire de l’enfer vers le paradis à la quête de l’idéal, Dante à l’artiste romantique.
Placée au cœur d’une réflexion sur la poétisation de la musique, la Divine Comédie suscite de nombreuses œuvres instrumentales, presque toutes oubliées de nos jours, à l’exception de celles de Liszt et Tchaïkovski (Francesca da Rimini, 1876). Après une lecture du Dante est esquissé en 1837. Liszt envisage un temps de l’intituler Paralipomènes à la Divina Commedia. Fantaisie symphonique : signe qu’il considère sa pièce pianistique comme un « supplément » à l’œuvre de Dante – non comme une « illustration » – et qu’il ambitionne de lui donner une ampleur orchestrale. La source littéraire motive l’élaboration d’une forme émancipée des schémas préétablis, même si subsistent quelques traces de forme sonate, comme le suggère le sous-titre « fantasia quasi sonata ». Elle encourage des audaces de langage sans équivalent à l’époque : dès les premières mesures, le triton (la-mi bémol), en détruisant tout sentiment tonal, évoque les puissances infernales (depuis le XIe siècle, l’intervalle est associé à Satan et surnommé « diabolus in musica »). Dante « trouvera peut-être un jour son expression musicale dans le Beethoven de l’avenir », suppute Liszt, en s’identifiant à cette figure de prophète.

Scarlatti D.Sonata - K 543 F major.YT_description:
Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in F major K. 543.
00:10 Introduction
01:16 Sonata
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
La Sonata in Fa maggiore K. 543 di Domenico Scarlatti che presenteremo oggi è una delle grandi Sonate della maturità di Domenico, uno di quei lavori nei quali il supremo dominio della tastiera è messo all'esclusivo servizio del messaggio musicale, che qui è intimo e semplice. A me pare che questa Sonata abbia quasi il sentimento di una ninnananna: si allontana di rado dal tono d'impianto di Fa maggiore, ma quel che stupisce è l'estrama raffinatezza con la quale è scritta questa musica. Tutta la Sonata, in pratica, è una successione di figurazioni l'una più bella e sorprendente dell'altra. L'ornamentazione è ricca, e per definizione lascia all'interprete una certa libertà di manovra nel realizzarla. Credo, tuttavia, che questo sia principalmente un pezzo semplice, e che vada apprezzato in tutta la sua semplicità e grande bellezza.
Buon ascolto.

Scarlatti D.Sonata - K 448 F minor.YT_description:
Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in f sharp minor K. 448
00:10 Introduction
01:30 Sonata
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
La Sonata in fa diesis minore K. 448 di Domenico Scarlatti che presenteremo oggi non è un pezzo molto ben conosciuto, ma a ma pare che dovrebbe esserlo in quanto è un miracolo di invenzione e di maestria. La Sonata è una piccola toccata che presenta due elementi contrastanti. Il primo lo sentiamo sin dall'inizio: grandi gesta plateali, con figurazioni discendenti che raggiungono il fondo della tastiera in modo assai drammatico. Poco dopo, però, fa capolino il secondo elemento: un piccolo passo di danza nel quale un orecchio esperto potrebbe forse riconoscere l'idea di un fandango. In apertura di seconda parte, questa “idea” di fandango viene esplorata più a fondo dal nostro Domenico: sentiamo senza dubbio un passo di danza, ma ricamato in una tecnica tastieristica fra le più sublimi immaginabili. Alla fine ritorneranno le grandi gesta degli esordi, e chiuderanno la Sonata con un'affermazione di orgogliosa determinazione. Un altro grande, piccolo pezzo di musica.
Buon ascolto.

Grieg E.Scherzo-Impromptu - op 73 no 2 B.YT_description:
This collection of piano pieces called Stimmungen ("Moods") was written in 1905 and is among the last things Grieg wrote towards the end of his career. His creative powers dwindling, he harked back to some older sketches and completely reworked them into a set that was meant to be like a new book of Lyric Pieces but a bit more ambitious. The difference in scope turned out to be not all that big.

I would not claim this is one of Grieg's best piano works but as always, there is much to enjoy. My recording was made on august 3, 2010. A couple of tiny imperfections are hopefully not distracting.

Scarlatti D.Sonata - K 536 A major.YT_description:
Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in A major K. 536.
00:10 Introduction
01:30 Sonata
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
La Sonata in La maggiore K. 536 di Domenico Scarlatti che presenteremo oggi reca l'indicazione di tempo “Cantabile”, un indizio verso la natura fondamentalmente lirica di questa musica. La Sonata è una delle grandi opere mature di Domenico, un capolavoro quasi di diritto, e si apre in modo molto melodioso con un tema sereno presentato prima dalla mano destra e poi ripreso dalla mano sinistra. Questa alternanza del materiale melodico fra le due mani sarà la colonna portante dell'intero pezzo, perché dopo la breve introduzione Domenico comincia a scrivere lunghe catene di terzine le quali rimbalzano da mano a mano, coprono tutta l'estensione della tastiera, e nel farlo attraversano un grande spettro armonico obbedendo ad una legge sola: la fantasia ed il capriccio di Domenico. Di fatto, questa Sonata mi pare la rappresentazione musicale della libertà più assoluta, e mi sono detto: perché non cominciare il nuovo anno con un inno alla libertà?
Buon ascolto.
Scarlatti D.Sonata - K 536 A major.YT_title: SCARLATTI / ALL SONATAS #265: Sonata in A major K. 536

Scarlatti D.Sonata - K 501 C major.YT_description:
Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in C major K. 501
00:10 Introduction
01:25
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
La Sonata in Do maggiore K. 501 di Domenico Scarlatti è giustamente annoverata fra i lavori più celebri del nostro caro Domenico, anche perché è una di quelle Sonate in cui egli pare guardare nella sua sfera di cristallo e predire il futuro della musica. In questo caso parliamo di forma: qui si trova l'embrione dello sviluppo tematico, ossia quello che diverrà un ingrediente fondamentale della “forma sonata”, in pratica il veicolo preponderante per esprimere la grande musica in epoca classica e romantica con Maestri come Haydn, Mozart, Beethoven e via discorrendo. Non solo. La Sonata si muove nell'ambito dello stile galante, ed è magnificamente scritta. Non mancano gli elementi di contrasto, con una prima parte piuttosto leggera alla quale segue una seconda parecchio più drammatica. Se aggiungiamo a tutto ciò il fatto che la Sonata non è particolarmente difficile da eseguire, e che è un gran bel pezzo di musica, avremo ampi motivi per giustificare la grande popolarità di questo splendido lavoro.
Buon ascolto.

Scarlatti D.Sonata - K 505 F major.YT_description:
Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in F major K. 505
00:10 Introduction
01:23 Sonata
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
Notoriamente, Domenico Scarlatti pubblicò un solo lavoro durante la sua vita, gli “Essercizi per gravicembalo”. Forse a cagione di ciò, molti pensano ancora che tutte le sue Sonate siano nulla più che “essercizi”, ma questo non è assolutamente vero. Bisogna dire, però, che in certe occasioni Domenico si concesse la licenza di scrivere – se non proprio “essercizi” - pezzi che avevano il carattere di banchi di prova, forse per misurare i progressi dei suoi allievi più dotati. La Sonata in Fa maggiore K. 505 che presenteremo oggi è di certo uno di questi. Sotto le mentite spoglie di una innocua invenzione, infatti, la Sonata racchiude una serie di difficoltà quali polifonia a mano sola, grandi salti, e di certi richiede agilità dal principio alla fine. Questi, ovviamente, sono solo dettagli tecnici: quando leggiamo la Sonata nella sua interezza ci accorgiamo che è un pezzo estremamente grazioso, ed è un gran piacere, per me, potervelo presentare.
Buon ascolto.

Tchaikovsky P.Countryside Echo - op 72 n.PS_title: Countryside Echo - op 72 no 13 Eb major
Tchaikovsky P.Countryside Echo - op 72 n.YT_description:
Five years ago, I performed a recital at midnight on November 6 - the day of Tchaikovsky's passing - in Izhevsk, my hometown, which is a mere 20 miles away from Tchaikovsky's birthplace. It was a significant and heartfelt concert for me, and very unusual - how often one gets to play a midnight recital? The hall was full of young people, and for some of them, it was their very first classical concert. But there also were regular concert-goers and even some kids.
I wore jeans on stage and made an edgy hairdo, many things seemed anew that night, but the main hero of the recital - Tchaikovsky's brilliant cycle of 18 pieces, op.72, - felt even more refreshing, like a discovery. 
This work is a one-piece organism, consisting of different parts-moods. It can be melancholic, striking, soothing, refreshing, mournful, inspiring, colorful, trembling, and at the end of the day, grandiose in its depiction of an enormous human soul. It is Tchaikovsky's last solo piano work.
Today, I am celebrating Tchaikovsky's 180-th Birthday with this performance.

Scarlatti D.Sonata in Bb minor K 131.YT_description:
Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in b flat minor K. 131
00:10 Introduction
01:53 Sonata
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
La Sonata in si bemolle minore K. 131 di Domenico Scarlatti che presenteremo oggi è un capolavoro pressoché sconosciuto. Questa è una delle due sole Sonate che Domenico ci ha lasciato in questo tono misterioso (l'altra è la Sonata in si bemolle minore K. 128, che abbiamo presentato nell'episodio numero 340; se non la ricordate andate a sentirla: è una bella tarantella). Con questa Sonata rimaniamo in ambito di danza: è un grande fandango che però non è punto amichevole quanto la sua compagna. Questa musica è quasi concettuale, e Domenico si produce in ogni sorta di stratagemma per imitale i passi e le mosse dei ballerini. Vicino all'inizio, ad esempio, vi è una sincope che mi pare proprio rappresentare lo sbattere dei tacchi dell'uomo, mentre poco più avanti si trovano passi a note ribattute che potrebbero rappresentare il suono delle nacchere della señorita. Più avanti ancora troviamo uno di quei celebri passaggi scarlattiani in cui si eseguono certe note a mani incrociate, ma prima con la destra sopra la sinistra e poi viceversa: qui mi pare un'evidente allusione agli ammiccamenti, agli inchini, ed alle effusioni che i danzatori si reciprocano. È un pezzo di musica molto bello, tuttavia come dicevo non è il più facile da ascoltare, né da suonare, della collezione; forse, queste due ragioni combinate offrono una spiegazione plausibile della sua quasi totale oscurità. Spero vi piaccia.
Buon ascolto.

Scarlatti D.Sonata in G major K 240.YT_description:
Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in G major K. 240.
00:10 Introduction
01:29 Sonata
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
La grande Sonata in Sol maggiore K. 240 di Domenico Scarlatti è fra le più importanti ed impressionanti dell'intera collezione, un pezzo ricchissimo di idee musicali, monumentale maestria e seria ispirazione. Per qualche oscura ragione i pianisti non tendono a frequentare questa meravigliosa Sonata, ma i clavicembali si, eccome! Qui su Youtube potrete trovare le letture di due giganti com Rafael Puyana ed Enrico Baiano, e di fatto il Maestro Baiano, in due separati video, la esegue sia sul clavicembalo che sul fortepiano: un'operazione interessante quanto coraggiosa! La Sonata è scritta sul modello di una grande fantasia, comincia im modo improvvisatorio e presenta una bella quantità di passaggi brillanti. Ma poi, la musica irrompe in un episodio drammatico e lirico che pare essere uscito da un'opera di Bellini o di Donizetti, e l'effetto è straordinario.
Questa è di certo una grande Sonata!
Buon ascolto.
Scarlatti D.Sonata in G major K 240.YT_title: SCARLATTI / ALL SONATAS #315: Sonata in G major K. 240

Scarlatti D.Sonata - K 533 A major.YT_description:
Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in A major K. 533.
00:10 Introduction
01:52 Sonata
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
La Sonata in La maggior K. 533 di Domenico Scarlatti che presenteremo oggi è una tipica Sonata scarlattiana per eccellenza: è brillante, veloce, e soprattutto divertente! Questa, però, è anche famosa perché era nel repertorio di Emil Gilels, uno dei grandissimi pianisti russi del secolo scorso, il quale (e per fortuna) ce ne ha lasciato diverse registrazioni; se ne avrete la voglia e la possibilità, ascoltatele: ne vale la pena... Qui troviamo Domenico in ottima e dispettosa forma: apre la Sonata con un tema ascendente che si muove a grandi intervalli, e questo si traduce nell'esigenza, per il suonatore, di estendere molto le dita vicine, la qual cosa è parecchio scomoda ed è anche tipicamente scarlattiana.  Domenico apre la Sonata con un ostacolo piuttosto arduo, e pare vole mettere alla prova il suonatore: “Vuoi suonare la mia musica? Allora prima devi sudare!”. Per fortuna questa minuta introduzione non dura più d'una manciata di battute, dopo le quali la Sonata vera e propria comincia e si rivela una brillante toccata piena di sorprese, modulazioni folli, ma soprattutto un paio di quei motivetti altalenanti che inevitabilmente dipingono un sorriso sulle labbra di chi suona e, forse, di chi ascolta. Di sicuro lo hanno dipinto sulle mie, di labbra, tanto che questa Sonata mi pare un concentrato di pura, incontaminata gioia scarlattiana.
Buon ascolto.

Scarlatti D.Sonata - K 445 F major.YT_description:
Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in F major K. 445.
00:10 Introduction
01:23 Sonata 
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
La piccola Sonata in Fa maggiore K. 445 di Domenico Scarlatti che presenteremo oggi è senza dubbio uno di quei pezzi che aiutarono a cementare l'universale  fama di grande virtuoso della tastiera della quale godette Domenico. La Sonata reca una indicazione di tempo piuttosto atipica: “Allegro, o presto”. Vale a dire: “suona veloce, o anche più veloce”! Ad un primo esame della parte capiamo che questa è una toccata che appare piuttosto modesta, un allegro dialogo fra le mani pieno di quei piccoli fuochi d'artificio tipici del tecnicismo di Domenico. Ma quando studiamo la musica più a fondo, ci accorgiamo che se esasperiamo questa musica abbastanza, essa si anima di vita propria e diventa non tanto un pezzo di musica, a proposito del quale possiamo parlare di melodia e di armonia, ma la rappresentazione musicale d'una folata di vento. È molto divertente.
Buon ascolto.

Scarlatti D.Sonatas in C major K501 and.YT_description:
Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in C major K. 501
00:10 Introduction
01:25
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
La Sonata in Do maggiore K. 501 di Domenico Scarlatti è giustamente annoverata fra i lavori più celebri del nostro caro Domenico, anche perché è una di quelle Sonate in cui egli pare guardare nella sua sfera di cristallo e predire il futuro della musica. In questo caso parliamo di forma: qui si trova l'embrione dello sviluppo tematico, ossia quello che diverrà un ingrediente fondamentale della “forma sonata”, in pratica il veicolo preponderante per esprimere la grande musica in epoca classica e romantica con Maestri come Haydn, Mozart, Beethoven e via discorrendo. Non solo. La Sonata si muove nell'ambito dello stile galante, ed è magnificamente scritta. Non mancano gli elementi di contrasto, con una prima parte piuttosto leggera alla quale segue una seconda parecchio più drammatica. Se aggiungiamo a tutto ciò il fatto che la Sonata non è particolarmente difficile da eseguire, e che è un gran bel pezzo di musica, avremo ampi motivi per giustificare la grande popolarità di questo splendido lavoro.
Buon ascolto.

Healy C.Mountain Steps.YT_description:
www.facebook.com/chrishealeymusic

The Mountain Stairs

From the top of a plateau in India, standing more than 2,300 feet tall, is a stone spire. Carved into the stone itself is a staircase known today as the “Climb to Heaven”. It is believed the stairs were made to create a strategic lookout point, but who ordered their construction and from what enemy they sought to be forewarned, no one knows. However, the image struck me when I saw it amongst a collection of photos of abandoned places, and I couldn’t help but be drawn into the atmosphere of the scene. In particular, the imagined susurrus of the wind and breaking of dawn upon the breathtaking panorama seen from atop the spire evoked a musical atmosphere which grew to become The Mountain Stairs.

Pianist: Adam McMillan
Composed by: Christopher Healey (www.facebook.com/chrishealeymusic) 
Recording and Video by: Thomas Green

Tchaikovsky P.Lullaby - op 72 no 2 Ab ma.YT_description:
Five years ago, I performed a recital at midnight on November 6 - the day of Tchaikovsky's passing - in Izhevsk, my hometown, which is a mere 20 miles away from Tchaikovsky's birthplace. It was a significant and heartfelt concert for me, and very unusual - how often one gets to play a midnight recital? The hall was full of young people, and for some of them, it was their very first classical concert. But there also were regular concert-goers and even some kids.
I wore jeans on stage and made an edgy hairdo, many things seemed anew that night, but the main hero of the recital - Tchaikovsky's brilliant cycle of 18 pieces, op.72, - felt even more refreshing, like a discovery. 
This work is a one-piece organism, consisting of different parts-moods. It can be melancholic, striking, soothing, refreshing, mournful, inspiring, colorful, trembling, and at the end of the day, grandiose in its depiction of an enormous human soul. It is Tchaikovsky's last solo piano work.
Today, I am celebrating Tchaikovsky's 180-th Birthday with this performance.

Scarlatti D.Sonata in F minor K 204a.YT_description:
Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in f minor K. 204a.
00:10 Introduction
02:42 Sonata 
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno, 
La grande Sonata in fa minore K. 204a di Domenico Scarlatti che presenteremo oggi è una delle più complesse, articolate e belle dell'intera collezione. Questa Sonata, di fatto, è un'opera in miniatura e come ogni opera comincia con la sua brava Sinfonia: grandi arpeggi di fa minore asseriscono il tono,  poi la musica si tinge di melancolia. Si alza il sipario, e la scena è quella di un paesaggio d'inverno, triste e desolato. Cambia il metro della musica, da “a cappella” a tre ottavi, e si passa ad una danza, magari una piccola seguidilla. La musica, a questo punto, acquista un carattere sarcastico, ed è come se sulla scena fosse entrato Mesfistofele col suo violino: evidentemente vorrebbe sedurre qualcuno, ma ancora non sappiamo chi. Con Mefistofele, ovviamente, arrivano anche le prime complicazioni d'ordine tecnico, come ad esempio degli estesi passi in ottava alla mano sinistra che danno alla musica un senso di urgenza e agitazione. Poi, finalmente, capiamo a chi mira Mefistofele: la musica cambia metro nuovamente, da tre a sei ottavi, Domenico prescrive anche un cambio di tempo, da Allegro ad Allegrissimo, e scrive una bellissima pastorale, davvero virtuosistica e molto gioiosa. Ci dev'essere una bella festa, al villaggio!  All'inizio della seconda parte la musica riverte al tono di fa minore, e pare ammiccare ad una tarantella: evidentemente questa brava gente si sta divertendo un mondo, ed ecco che ritorna Mefistofele col suo balletto pieno di sarcasmo ma, fatalmente, questa volta viene avvistato. I paesani, allora, si uniscono a coorte e, sulla musica della pastorale che abbiamo sentito nella prima parte, lo cacciano a gran voce per poi  continuare i loro festeggiamenti. Nel frattempo, la tessitura del pezzo è andata crescendo, e quando la Sonata arriva al fine par proprio di assistere al “gran finale” della nostra opera in miniatura. Questo, secondo me, è un gran capolavoro.
Buon ascolto.
Scarlatti D.Sonata in F minor K 204a.YT_title: SCARLATTI / ALL SONATAS #461: Sonata in f minor K. 204a

Scarlatti D.Sonata in g minor K 31.YT_description:
Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in g minor K. 31.
00:10 Intorduction
01:18 Sonata
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
Oggi andremo a fare una gita a Venezia, che è particolarmente bella in questa stagione, con la Sonata in sol minore K. 31 di Domenico Scarlatti che presenteremo fra poco. Questa è probabilmente, e giustamente, la più celebre delle Sonate scritte da Domenico in stile veneziano; ha infatti tutti i crismi di un bel “concerto grosso”: vi sono effetti di eco, di contrasto fra “tutti” e “soli”, e vi sono perfino una manciata di battute in tempo “Andante”, stratagemma che i maestri veneziani usavano in un ambito veloce per generare contrasto. Ora, con tutti questi attributi serenissimi, non sarebbe punto difficile attribuire questa musica a Vivaldi, a Corelli, a Marcello... Ma la virtuosità al calor bianco che questa Sonata mette in campo è indubbiamente scarlattiana; secondo me non vi è alcun dubbio a proposito di chi abbia scritto questa bella Sonata.
Buon ascolto.

Three Fantastic Dances, Op. 5, is the earliest piano composition by Dmitri Shostakovich, written in 1922 when he was 16 years old.

Three Fantastic Dances:
March – Allegretto
Waltz – Andantino
Polka – Allegretto

Dmitri Dmitriyevich Shostakovich was a Russian composer and pianist. He is regarded as one of the major composers of the 20th century, with a unique harmonic language and a historic importance. 

A polystylist, Shostakovich developed a hybrid voice, combining a variety of different musical techniques into his works. His music is characterized by sharp contrasts, elements of the grotesque, and ambivalent tonality; he was also heavily influenced by the neoclassical style pioneered by Igor Stravinsky, and (especially in his symphonies) by the late Romanticism of Gustav Mahler.

Shostakovich's orchestral works include 15 symphonies and six concerti. His chamber output includes 15 string quartets, a piano quintet, two piano trios, and two pieces for string octet. His solo piano works include two sonatas, an early set of preludes, and a later set of 24 preludes and fugues. Other works include three operas, several song cycles, ballets, and a substantial quantity of film music; especially well known is The Second Waltz, Op. 99, music to the film The First Echelon (1955–1956), as well as the suites of music composed for The Gadfly.

Franz Joseph Haydn (/ˈdʒoʊzəf ˈhaɪdən/; German: [ˈjoːzɛf ˈhaɪdən]; 31 March[1] 1732 -- 31 May 1809), known as Joseph Haydn, was an Austrian composer, one of the most prolific and prominent of the Classical period. He is often called the "Father of the Symphony" and "Father of the String Quartet" because of his important contributions to these forms. He was also instrumental in the development of the piano trio and in the evolution of sonata form. A lifelong resident of Austria, Haydn spent much of his career as a court musician for the wealthy Esterházy family on their remote estate. Isolated from other composers and trends in music until the later part of his long life, he was, as he put it, "forced to become original". At the time of his death, he was one of the most celebrated composers in Europe.

A central characteristic of Haydn's music is the development of larger structures out of very short, simple musical motifs, often derived from standard accompanying figures. The music is often quite formally concentrated, and the important musical events of a movement can unfold rather quickly.

Haydn's work was central to the development of what came to be called sonata form. His practice, however, differed in some ways from that of Mozart and Beethoven, his younger contemporaries who likewise excelled in this form of composition. Haydn was particularly fond of the so-called "monothematic exposition", in which the music that establishes the dominant key is similar or identical to the opening theme. Haydn also differs from Mozart and Beethoven in his recapitulation sections, where he often rearranges the order of themes compared to the exposition and uses extensive thematic development. (from Wikipedia)

The second of Gershwin's Preludes is one of my all-time favorites. It's bluesy, it's ambiguous as if he can't make up his mind whether to write in minor or major and its beautiful, simplistic melody just sticks in your head for days.
