Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
La Sonata in Si bemolle maggiore K. 529 di Domenico Scarlatti che presenteremo oggi è un pezzo molto famoso. O forse dovrei dire notorio, perché è una Sonata piena di inisidie, di rischi, e di slancio. Si tratta di una piccola tarantella dal fondamentale buonumore, ma dopo l'introduzione del tema principale Domenico si ricorda d'essere un super virtuoso, e allora scrive passi a mani incrociate con salti di distanze immense: quattro ottave, ad ogni mano, la destra sopra la sinistra, la sinistra sopra la destra. La difficoltà esecutiva è a dir poco feroce, ma conta poco perché questo breve pezzo è tremendamente eccitante.
Buon ascolto.

Tchaikovsky P.Impromptu - op 72 no 1 F m.YT_description:
Five years ago, I performed a recital at midnight on November 6 - the day of Tchaikovsky's passing - in Izhevsk, my hometown, which is a mere 20 miles away from Tchaikovsky's birthplace. It was a significant and heartfelt concert for me, and very unusual - how often one gets to play a midnight recital? The hall was full of young people, and for some of them, it was their very first classical concert. But there also were regular concert-goers and even some kids.
I wore jeans on stage and made an edgy hairdo, many things seemed anew that night, but the main hero of the recital - Tchaikovsky's brilliant cycle of 18 pieces, op.72, - felt even more refreshing, like a discovery. 
This work is a one-piece organism, consisting of different parts-moods. It can be melancholic, striking, soothing, refreshing, mournful, inspiring, colorful, trembling, and at the end of the day, grandiose in its depiction of an enormous human soul. It is Tchaikovsky's last solo piano work.
Today, I am celebrating Tchaikovsky's 180-th Birthday with this performance.

Three Fantastic Dances, Op. 5, is the earliest piano composition by Dmitri Shostakovich, written in 1922 when he was 16 years old.

Three Fantastic Dances:
March – Allegretto
Waltz – Andantino
Polka – Allegretto

Dmitri Dmitriyevich Shostakovich was a Russian composer and pianist. He is regarded as one of the major composers of the 20th century, with a unique harmonic language and a historic importance. 

A polystylist, Shostakovich developed a hybrid voice, combining a variety of different musical techniques into his works. His music is characterized by sharp contrasts, elements of the grotesque, and ambivalent tonality; he was also heavily influenced by the neoclassical style pioneered by Igor Stravinsky, and (especially in his symphonies) by the late Romanticism of Gustav Mahler.

Shostakovich's orchestral works include 15 symphonies and six concerti. His chamber output includes 15 string quartets, a piano quintet, two piano trios, and two pieces for string octet. His solo piano works include two sonatas, an early set of preludes, and a later set of 24 preludes and fugues. Other works include three operas, several song cycles, ballets, and a substantial quantity of film music; especially well known is The Second Waltz, Op. 99, music to the film The First Echelon (1955–1956), as well as the suites of music composed for The Gadfly.

Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in d minor K. 191.
00:10 Introduction
01:26 Sonata
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
La grande Sonata in re minore K. 191 di Domenico Scarlatti che presenteremo fra poco è una brillante toccata scritta, principalmente, nello stile veneziano ma con un pizzico di spezie spagnole mescolate al tutto, come vedremo. Questa gli è una delle Sonate meno stravaganti o, se preferite, più lineari dell'intera collezione e, di conseguenza, gode di una certa popolarità, soprattutto come pezzo da studio. Francamente, credo che questo pezzo sia ben più che un mero “essercizio”. La Sonata è molto drammatica, è piena di passi brillanti, ha diversi passi in imitazione canonica e non è punto difficle immaginare questa musica suonata da un'orchestra d'archi nella Cattedrale di San Marco! La cosa interessante è che sul finire di ogni parte della Sonata Domenico scrive un passaggio che mi pare riproduca perfettamente gli sforzi d'un chiterrista che tenti di dare il tempo a dei furiosi ballerini. Tutto molto drammatico, ed assai eccitante.
Buon ascolto.

Bax A.Country-Tune.YT_description:
Arnold Bax (1883-1953) was one of Britain's foremost composers of the early 20th century.  He was a piano pupil of Tobias Matthay, and apparently a very good sight-reader.  His piano music is not that widely played in live recital these days.  I think this may be because the grittiness of some of it leads players to approach it as if it were Prokofiev, whereas I think it needs a more romanticized approach.  Bax wrote this piece around 1920.  In his notes to Ashley Wass's  Naxos recording, Lewis Foreman suggests that the piece might have been commissioned by a publisher for a wide market.  However, although no pedal indications are given, there is a passage about 1/3 of the way through the piece that requires the use of a sostenuto pedal to hold a sustained pedal C# under a staccato melody, and very few domestic pianos of the period would have been equipped with this device.  Note the cuckoo calls in the accompaniment towards the end of the piece.

Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
Una delle poche cose che sappiano di Domenico Scarlatti, oltre al fatto che fosse un genio musicale, è che a quanto pare era un inveterato giocatore d'azzardo. Allora, immaginiamoci d'essere a Madrid, in una sordida taverna, intorno all'anno 1750. Domenico ha giocato a carte tutta la sera, ed è lieto: ha vinto! Chi non è lieto sono i suoi compagni di gioco, che hanno perso tutti i loro denari; allora, per rinfrancarsi lo spirito, portano in sala un clavicembalo e chiedono a Domenico di suonare un ballo. Lui accetta, ed improvvisa un bel Fandango, pieno di tutta la gioia che prova Domenico nell'essere un vincitore... Ecco, se una tale scena fosse avvenuta davvero, probabilmente Domenico avrebbe suonato qualcosa di simile alla sua Sonata in Do maggiore K. 502 che presenteremo oggi. Questa Sonata è un fandango vorticoso, fantastico e pieno di trucchetti; Domenico, qui, ne combina di tutti i colori: cambia metro, salta da una parte all'altra della tastiera, ma soprattutto ci regala un pezzo così pieno di gioiosa energia da esser capace di trasformare un brutto giorno in uno bello!
Buon ascolto.

Busoni F.Die Nachtlichen no 5.YT_description:
The Elegies (published 1908) are extremely significant as they represent a self-conscious shift in Busoni's own compositional and aesthetic approach. They are the flagship examples of a new aesthetic described famously by Busoni in his essay Entwurf einer neuen Aesthetik der Tonkunst [Sketch of a New Aesthetic of Music], published in 1911 but composed in 1907. A link to this highly-engaging text:

http://archive.org/details/sketchofanewesth000125mbp

In the introduction to this work, Busoni claims that "The spirit of an art-work, the measure of emotion, of humanity, that is in it, these remain unchanged in value through changing years; the form which these three assumed, the manner of their expression, and the flavour of the epoch which gave them birth, are transient, and age rapidly." Busoni later states: "...we find cases in which the reformer marched abreast of the times, while the rest fell behind. And then they have to be forced and lashed to take the leap across the passage they have missed. I believe that the major-and-minor key with its transpositional relations, our "twelve-semitone" system, exhibits such a case of failing behind."

Grovlez G.Les anes No 5 in Ab major from.YT_description:
I have always loved this endearing suite by Gabriel Grovlez, a composer about whom I could find little information and only some very sketchy photos. It seems clear that Grovlez was under the spell of Debussy, and I'm pretty sure he must have known that composer's Children's Corner, on which some of these items seem to be modeled. Nonetheless I do not find this derivative music. These pieces, often used in grade exams, are charming, heartfelt, and well-wrought. 

Grovlez wrote a dozen or so other piano works but this is the only one you ever hear. I am intrigued by his Two Etudes of Transcendental Difficulty, but they look so absolutely fiendish that I won't even think of trying them.

I recorded L'Almanach aux Images on Jun 18, 2011. They're not perfect but I hope I have caught(some of) their charm.

Bartok B.Sorrow (No 7 from For Children.PS_title: Sorrow (No 7 from For Children Vol 2 BB 53 Sz 42)
Bartok B.Sorrow (No 7 from For Children.YT_description:
Here is my new recording, made last weekend, of  Bartók's educational set For Children. The colorful Hungarian title "A Gyermekeknek" somehow always amuses me. The pieces were penned down in 1908/09, but Bartók revised the set in 1945, towards the end of his life, leaving out 6 pieces and slightly altering others. It is this final version that I play here.

The two books are quite different in character. I marginally prefer 
Book I, based on Hungarian Folk Tunes. These are more ebullient, the colors brighter, than those in Book II, based on Slovak Folk Tunes, which are generally darker and more introspective, at times 
reminiscent of Janacek (as they ought to be, being Slovak). 

Both books contain a wealth of great music, and certainly not all of the pieces seen suitable for children - unless they have advanced technique and musicality. I hope my cycle can be enjoyed despite a couple of small read errors (which, obviously and  irritatingly, I only noticed during video preparation).

Mikrokosmos was originally designed as a collection of pieces for the beginning pianist, but over time it took on grander proportions, comprising 153 individual pieces that spanned the range of technical difficulty. Dividing into six volumes, it begins with pieces for beginners and progresses to those that challenge even the most accomplished pianist. That Mikrokosmos has become a viable progressive method is demonstrated by its ubiquity in the repertories of modern piano students, but its reputation rests on more than its technical and pedagogical applications; Bartók's work represents a varied and finely crafted catalog of twentieth century musical idioms. In Bartók's own words, it "appears as a synthesis of all the musical and technical problems which were treated and in some case only partially solved in the previous piano works." Perhaps chief among these musical problems was Bartók's attempted synthesis of Eastern and Western European musical traditions, particularly Eastern folk music with the Germanic tradition (as represented by Bach and Beethoven) and with the progressive harmonies of Claude Debussy. 

The first 66 pieces in Mikrokosmos (Vols. 1 and 2) are dedicated to Bartók's son, Peter, for whose use they were originally intended. Many of these pieces are technical exercises, useful for developing finger and hand independence, as well as hand span; however, they are also of interest for their musical language. Hungarian folk tunes, pentatonic, whole-tone and modal harmonies, as well as more adventurous octatonic chromatic scales all form the basis for these short pieces. 

Volumes 3 and 4 make up numbers 67 through 121. These pieces display increased harmonic complexity and technical demands. Bartók employs more polymodes (the use of different modes, or keys, simultaneously), along with octatonic and diatonic scale fragments to construct these pieces. The compositions in the third and fourth volumes are also important because they betray the influence of Franz Liszt, particularly in terms of tone color; Bartók wrote of his desire, in these pieces, to "poetically color the piano tone." 

The final volumes (5 and 6) of the Mikrokosmos were intended as concert pieces for professional pianists. They differ from the preceding pieces in many respects: their contrapuntal texture is more dense (four parts), the melodic and harmonic material is more characteristic of Bartók's non-pedagogical works, and rhythmic structures are much more complicated and include vigorous syncopations and Bulgarian dance rhythms. 

While Bartók's intention to synthesize Bach, Beethoven, and Debussy was perhaps not fully realized, Mikrokosmos nonetheless compares well with some of Bach and Debussy's ostensibly pedagogical keyboard works. Like Bach's Inventions or Debussy's Études, for example, Mikrokosmos is not merely a work of practical value, but also a work of art with much purely musical substance. [Allmusic.com]

Lack T.Sicilienne.YT_description:
Théodore Lack (1846-1921) studied and later taught at the Paris Conservatoire. It was his pedagogical "Methode de piano" of 1909 that introduced Debussy's "Le petit negre" to the world. His many salon pieces are all well-crafted and full of interesting details and unusual harmonic sequences. This early piece lacks the surprise harmonic shifts of Lack's later work, but is nevertheless gently attractive.  It is dedicated to one Jeanne Lyon, who also seems to be the dedicatee of a 1907 part-song by Reynaldo Hahn.  My thumbnail contains a colorized illustration from 1840 by Victor Dollet from the sheet music cover of a song by Meyerbeer with the same title.

Grieg E.Resignation - op 73 no 1 E minor.YT_description:
This collection of piano pieces called Stimmungen ("Moods") was written in 1905 and is among the last things Grieg wrote towards the end of his career. His creative powers dwindling, he harked back to some older sketches and completely reworked them into a set that was meant to be like a new book of Lyric Pieces but a bit more ambitious. The difference in scope turned out to be not all that big.

I would not claim this is one of Grieg's best piano works but as always, there is much to enjoy. My recording was made on august 3, 2010. A couple of tiny imperfections are hopefully not distracting.

Bartok B.Village Joke No 130 from Mikrok.YT_description:
Mikrokosmos, progressive pieces for piano in 6 volumes, Sz. 107, BB 105 (1926-1939)

Claude Helffer, piano

122. Chords Together and in Opposition

127. New Hungarian Folk Song (5:07)

Mikrokosmos was originally designed as a collection of pieces for the beginning pianist, but over time it took on grander proportions, comprising 153 individual pieces that spanned the range of technical difficulty. Dividing into six volumes, it begins with pieces for beginners and progresses to those that challenge even the most accomplished pianist. That Mikrokosmos has become a viable progressive method is demonstrated by its ubiquity in the repertories of modern piano students, but its reputation rests on more than its technical and pedagogical applications; Bartók's work represents a varied and finely crafted catalog of twentieth century musical idioms. In Bartók's own words, it "appears as a synthesis of all the musical and technical problems which were treated and in some case only partially solved in the previous piano works." Perhaps chief among these musical problems was Bartók's attempted synthesis of Eastern and Western European musical traditions, particularly Eastern folk music with the Germanic tradition (as represented by Bach and Beethoven) and with the progressive harmonies of Claude Debussy. 

The first 66 pieces in Mikrokosmos (Vols. 1 and 2) are dedicated to Bartók's son, Peter, for whose use they were originally intended. Many of these pieces are technical exercises, useful for developing finger and hand independence, as well as hand span; however, they are also of interest for their musical language. Hungarian folk tunes, pentatonic, whole-tone and modal harmonies, as well as more adventurous octatonic chromatic scales all form the basis for these short pieces. 

Volumes 3 and 4 make up numbers 67 through 121. These pieces display increased harmonic complexity and technical demands. Bartók employs more polymodes (the use of different modes, or keys, simultaneously), along with octatonic and diatonic scale fragments to construct these pieces. The compositions in the third and fourth volumes are also important because they betray the influence of Franz Liszt, particularly in terms of tone color; Bartók wrote of his desire, in these pieces, to "poetically color the piano tone." 

The final volumes (5 and 6) of the Mikrokosmos were intended as concert pieces for professional pianists. They differ from the preceding pieces in many respects: their contrapuntal texture is more dense (four parts), the melodic and harmonic material is more characteristic of Bartók's non-pedagogical works, and rhythmic structures are much more complicated and include vigorous syncopations and Bulgarian dance rhythms. 

While Bartók's intention to synthesize Bach, Beethoven, and Debussy was perhaps not fully realized, Mikrokosmos nonetheless compares well with some of Bach and Debussy's ostensibly pedagogical keyboard works. Like Bach's Inventions or Debussy's Études, for example, Mikrokosmos is not merely a work of practical value, but also a work of art with much purely musical substance. [Allmusic.com]

Bartok B.Unison No 137 from Mikrokosmos.YT_description:
Mikrokosmos, progressive pieces for piano in 6 volumes, Sz. 107, BB 105 (1926-1939)

Claude Helffer, piano
Haakon Austbö, second piano

132. Major Seconds Broken and Together
133. Syncopation (1:47)
134. Studies in Double Notes (2:48)
135. Perpetuum Mobile (3:41)
136. Whole-tone Scale (5:14)
137. Unison (6:57)
138. Bagpipe (8:40)
139. Marry Andrew (9:57)

Mikrokosmos was originally designed as a collection of pieces for the beginning pianist, but over time it took on grander proportions, comprising 153 individual pieces that spanned the range of technical difficulty. Dividing into six volumes, it begins with pieces for beginners and progresses to those that challenge even the most accomplished pianist. That Mikrokosmos has become a viable progressive method is demonstrated by its ubiquity in the repertories of modern piano students, but its reputation rests on more than its technical and pedagogical applications; Bartók's work represents a varied and finely crafted catalog of twentieth century musical idioms. In Bartók's own words, it "appears as a synthesis of all the musical and technical problems which were treated and in some case only partially solved in the previous piano works." Perhaps chief among these musical problems was Bartók's attempted synthesis of Eastern and Western European musical traditions, particularly Eastern folk music with the Germanic tradition (as represented by Bach and Beethoven) and with the progressive harmonies of Claude Debussy. 

The first 66 pieces in Mikrokosmos (Vols. 1 and 2) are dedicated to Bartók's son, Peter, for whose use they were originally intended. Many of these pieces are technical exercises, useful for developing finger and hand independence, as well as hand span; however, they are also of interest for their musical language. Hungarian folk tunes, pentatonic, whole-tone and modal harmonies, as well as more adventurous octatonic chromatic scales all form the basis for these short pieces. 

Volumes 3 and 4 make up numbers 67 through 121. These pieces display increased harmonic complexity and technical demands. Bartók employs more polymodes (the use of different modes, or keys, simultaneously), along with octatonic and diatonic scale fragments to construct these pieces. The compositions in the third and fourth volumes are also important because they betray the influence of Franz Liszt, particularly in terms of tone color; Bartók wrote of his desire, in these pieces, to "poetically color the piano tone." 

The final volumes (5 and 6) of the Mikrokosmos were intended as concert pieces for professional pianists. They differ from the preceding pieces in many respects: their contrapuntal texture is more dense (four parts), the melodic and harmonic material is more characteristic of Bartók's non-pedagogical works, and rhythmic structures are much more complicated and include vigorous syncopations and Bulgarian dance rhythms. 

While Bartók's intention to synthesize Bach, Beethoven, and Debussy was perhaps not fully realized, Mikrokosmos nonetheless compares well with some of Bach and Debussy's ostensibly pedagogical keyboard works. Like Bach's Inventions or Debussy's Études, for example, Mikrokosmos is not merely a work of practical value, but also a work of art with much purely musical substance. [Allmusic.com]

Grieg E.The Mountaineers Song - op 73 no.YT_description:
This collection of piano pieces called Stimmungen ("Moods") was written in 1905 and is among the last things Grieg wrote towards the end of his career. His creative powers dwindling, he harked back to some older sketches and completely reworked them into a set that was meant to be like a new book of Lyric Pieces but a bit more ambitious. The difference in scope turned out to be not all that big.

I would not claim this is one of Grieg's best piano works but as always, there is much to enjoy. My recording was made on august 3, 2010. A couple of tiny imperfections are hopefully not distracting.

Burgmuller J.F.18 Characteristic Studies.YT_description:
Friedrich Burgmüller - Berceuse op.109 n. 7
Fausto Bongelli, piano
Friedrich Burgmüller, in Paris known under the French form of his name, Frédéric, was born in Regensburg in 1806, the son of the composer, pianist and music teacher Johann August Franz Burgmüller, and elder brother of the composer, conductor and pianist Norbert Burgmüller. Friedrich Burgmüller was taught by his father. After the latter’s death in 1824 he followed him as director of music in Düsseldorf, teaching music in Mühlhausen and as a cellist in Basel. In 1832 he settled in Paris, where he won a considerable reputation as a piano teacher, and internationally as a composer of salon pieces and studies. He did much to promote the work of his brother Norbert, four years his junior, whose career had been cut short by his sudden death at the spa in Aachen in 1836. Friedrich Burgmüller’s activities brought continued success in Paris. Many of his compositions proved successful among amateurs, for whom his pieces offered limited technical challenges, coupled with the satisfaction of musical interest. His Études (‘Studies’) have continued to provide a basis for piano teaching and the development of technical proficiency.

Phillip Sear plays a short study in B minor - sometimes called 'Danse Triste' (Sad Dance) - from a set of 25 'Etudes Mélodiques' (c. 1845) by Stephen Heller.  NOTE - THIS VIDEO WAS RECORDED IN APRIL 2017 (NOT 2016 AS PER TITLES).
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Since recording some other studies a few years ago, I have rather neglected the music of the Hungarian pianist and composer Stephen Heller (Heller István (1813 -- 88)) - mainly owing the the unfeasibly large hands needed to perform many of his works correctly.  These titles appear in American and British editions with titles - but I am not sure if they are authentic - they do not appear in early editions.  The close crossing of hands required in this piece is a technique also much favoured in the piano works of Carl Reinecke.

Bartok B.Lento No 11 from For Children 2.PS_title: Lento No 11 from For Children 2 BB 53 Sz 42
Bartok B.Lento No 11 from For Children 2.YT_description:
Here is my new recording, made last weekend, of  Bartók's educational set For Children. The colorful Hungarian title "A Gyermekeknek" somehow always amuses me. The pieces were penned down in 1908/09, but Bartók revised the set in 1945, towards the end of his life, leaving out 6 pieces and slightly altering others. It is this final version that I play here.

The two books are quite different in character. I marginally prefer 
Book I, based on Hungarian Folk Tunes. These are more ebullient, the colors brighter, than those in Book II, based on Slovak Folk Tunes, which are generally darker and more introspective, at times 
reminiscent of Janacek (as they ought to be, being Slovak). 

Both books contain a wealth of great music, and certainly not all of the pieces seen suitable for children - unless they have advanced technique and musicality. I hope my cycle can be enjoyed despite a couple of small read errors (which, obviously and  irritatingly, I only noticed during video preparation).

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------Rebikov (1866-1920) conceived the Mélomimique as a new art-form, blending music with pantomime (although not intended to be physically moved to), and he wrote several sets around 1900.  This waltz is the most French-sounding of the pieces in the set, with a little Franckian harmony in the central section. Bartok B.For Children Vol 2 No 22 BB 53.YT_description:
Here is my new recording, made last weekend, of  Bartók's educational set For Children. The colorful Hungarian title "A Gyermekeknek" somehow always amuses me. The pieces were penned down in 1908/09, but Bartók revised the set in 1945, towards the end of his life, leaving out 6 pieces and slightly altering others. It is this final version that I play here.

The two books are quite different in character. I marginally prefer 
Book I, based on Hungarian Folk Tunes. These are more ebullient, the colors brighter, than those in Book II, based on Slovak Folk Tunes, which are generally darker and more introspective, at times 
reminiscent of Janacek (as they ought to be, being Slovak). 

Both books contain a wealth of great music, and certainly not all of the pieces seen suitable for children - unless they have advanced technique and musicality. I hope my cycle can be enjoyed despite a couple of small read errors (which, obviously and  irritatingly, I only noticed during video preparation).

Book I - Based on Hungarian Folk Tunes

0:00:23 / 1   Children at play

Ludwig van Beethoven's Piano Sonata No. 8 in C minor, Op. 13, commonly known as Sonata Pathétique, was written in 1798 when the composer was 27 years old, and was published in 1799. It has remained one of his most celebrated compositions. Beethoven dedicated the work to his friend Prince Karl von Lichnowsky. Although commonly thought to be one of the few works to be named by the composer himself, it was actually named Grande sonate pathétique (to Beethoven's liking) by the publisher, who was impressed by the sonata's tragic sonorities.Prominent musicologists debate whether or not the Pathétique may have been inspired by Mozart's piano sonata K. 457, since both compositions are in C minor and have three very similar movements. The second movement, "Adagio cantabile", especially, makes use of a theme remarkably similar to one in the spacious second movement of Mozart's sonata.

Scarlatti D.Sonata - K 468 F major.YT_description:
Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in F major K. 468.
00:10 Introduction
01:41 Sonata
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
La Sonata in Fa maggiore K. 468 di Domenico Scarlatti che presenteremo oggi è una meravigliosa fantasia, ove però il materiale musicale è quasi incidentale: questo pezzo è un monumento, eretto alla gioia del suonare uno strumento a tastiera! La Sonata è scritta magnificamente ed in modo assai sofisticato dall'inizio alla fine, ma soprattutto questa musica è così idiomatica che non è punto difficile immaginarla come “colonna sonora” d'una scena rurale. Sono nato qui, a Vecchiano, un paesino della Toscana; i miei nonni erano contadini, e appena ho cominciato a studiare questo bel pezzo certe immagini della mia infanzia sono tornate a memoria con prepotenza. Vedete, la Sonata comincia con un motivetto che mi ha fatto venire in mente un puledrino che scorrazzava lieto sull'aia. Il secondo elemento della Sonata è ben più serio, e questi sarebbero i vecchi i quali, seduti in un angolo del cortile, parlano di cose molto serie (forse i beni di famiglia?). Ad un certo punto arrivano i bambini, che fanno un gran baccano e tutto divente più movimentato fin quando i vecchi intimano loro di calmarsi. Nella seconda parte della Sonata questi elementi ritornano, finché alla fine tutti i personaggi intonano un'affermazione di allegrezza e bontà d'animo. Questo è un pezzo di musica stupendo: umile nella forma, ma di grandissima classe nei contenuti.
Buon ascolto.

Scarlatti D.Sonata - K 469 F major.YT_description:
Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in F major K. 469.
00:10 Introduction
01:46 Sonata
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
La Sonata in Fa maggiore K. 469 di Domenico Scarlatti che presenteremo oggi non è fra le meglio conosciute della collezione, ma secondo me dovrebbe esserlo. Il pezzo reca l'indicazione  di tempo “Allegro molto” e quindi abbiamo l'obbligo di eseguirlo a velocità elevata. Di fatto, è una piccola toccata: si comincia con qualche arpeggio e poi Domenico accende il motore, genera un abbrivio ritmico che pare inarrestabile e infarcisce il tutto con diavolerie tecniche più che adeguate. Sin qui, tutto pacifico. In apertura della seconda parte, però, comincia a scrivere figure arabescate alla mano destra, mentre la sinistra cambia l'armonia quasi segretamente, di soppiatto, e l'impressione è quella di un momento di incredibile bellezza. In verità, è un momento straordinario! Trattandosi di una piccola toccata, però, ovviamente il virtuosismo torna a farla da padrone, e chiude la Sonata in modo piuttosto deciso. Da musico, quando mi trovo davanti ad un compositore che ci ha lasciato lavori di questa magnitudine, non mi riesce altro che provare un sentimento di profonda gratitudine. Grazie, Domenico!
Buon ascolto.

Scarlatti D.Sonata in A major K. 321.YT_description:
Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in A major K. 321.
00:10 Introduction
01:15 Sonata
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
La Sonata in La maggiore K. 321 di Domenico Scarlatti che presenteremo oggi è un lavoro bellissimo e piuttosto atipico nella produzione di Scarlatti. In verità si sente l'eco di un passo di danza, forse un fandango, ma l'intera Sonata è fatta da lunghe figurazioni elaborate che coprono tutta la tastiera, come in un arabesco. Alcune di queste richiedono che le mani compiano qualche contorsione, ma non si tratta di virtuosismo fine a se stesso: è solo il modo in cui Domenico attesta la volontà d'un far musica florido ed elegante. Sia nella prima che nella seconda parte del pezzo si trova un episodio più scuro, che fa pensare ad un chitarrista mentre suona qualcosa di passionale, ma il tono della Sonata rimane in un ambito di grazia e grande bellezza musicale. Si tratta, secondo me, di un grande piccolo pezzo di musica.
Buon ascolto.
Scarlatti D.Sonata in A major K. 321.YT_title: SCARLATTI / ALL SONATAS #435: Sonata in A major K. 321

Scarlatti D.Sonata - K 483 F major.YT_description:
Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in F major K. 483.
00:10 Introduction
01:43 Sonata
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
La Sonata in Fa maggiore K. 483 di Domenico Scarlatti che presenteremo oggi è un piccolo fandango che emana un forte carattere spagnoleggiante dall'inizio alla fine. Questa è musica di straordinaria vivacità, ma ha anche un forte elemento coreografico. L'inizio della Sonata è il fandango, una ballo spagnolo, ma il secondo episodio del pezzo imita le piroette che fanno i danzatori. Succede questo: le mani si muovono per moto contrario ed eseguono tre note veloci seguite da un mordente, che però, stilisticamente, saremmo giustificati ad eseguire come un trillo (vedremo dopo come fare). La Sonata reca l'indicazione di “Presto”, e ciò significa che Domenico vuole che suoniamo questo pezzo ad una velocità piuttosto sostenuta. Ora, forse questo è dovuto a qualche lacuna nella mia preparazione tecnica, ma ho trovato questo particolare passo, a questa velocità, ferocemente difficile da imparare ed eseguire. Se però consideriamo che tutta la Sonata dura meno di due minuti, forse abbiamo trovato una delle ragioni per cui questa piccola ma brillantissima Sonata non viene suonata più spesso. Ciò detto, credo che sia un pezzo di musica fantastico, ed è mio grande privilegio potervelo presentare.
Buon ascolto.

Bartok B.Bagpipe music No 138 from Mikro.YT_description:
Mikrokosmos, progressive pieces for piano in 6 volumes, Sz. 107, BB 105 (1926-1939)

Claude Helffer, piano
Haakon Austbö, second piano

132. Major Seconds Broken and Together
133. Syncopation (1:47)
134. Studies in Double Notes (2:48)
135. Perpetuum Mobile (3:41)
136. Whole-tone Scale (5:14)
137. Unison (6:57)
138. Bagpipe (8:40)
139. Marry Andrew (9:57)

Mikrokosmos was originally designed as a collection of pieces for the beginning pianist, but over time it took on grander proportions, comprising 153 individual pieces that spanned the range of technical difficulty. Dividing into six volumes, it begins with pieces for beginners and progresses to those that challenge even the most accomplished pianist. That Mikrokosmos has become a viable progressive method is demonstrated by its ubiquity in the repertories of modern piano students, but its reputation rests on more than its technical and pedagogical applications; Bartók's work represents a varied and finely crafted catalog of twentieth century musical idioms. In Bartók's own words, it "appears as a synthesis of all the musical and technical problems which were treated and in some case only partially solved in the previous piano works." Perhaps chief among these musical problems was Bartók's attempted synthesis of Eastern and Western European musical traditions, particularly Eastern folk music with the Germanic tradition (as represented by Bach and Beethoven) and with the progressive harmonies of Claude Debussy. 

The first 66 pieces in Mikrokosmos (Vols. 1 and 2) are dedicated to Bartók's son, Peter, for whose use they were originally intended. Many of these pieces are technical exercises, useful for developing finger and hand independence, as well as hand span; however, they are also of interest for their musical language. Hungarian folk tunes, pentatonic, whole-tone and modal harmonies, as well as more adventurous octatonic chromatic scales all form the basis for these short pieces. 

Volumes 3 and 4 make up numbers 67 through 121. These pieces display increased harmonic complexity and technical demands. Bartók employs more polymodes (the use of different modes, or keys, simultaneously), along with octatonic and diatonic scale fragments to construct these pieces. The compositions in the third and fourth volumes are also important because they betray the influence of Franz Liszt, particularly in terms of tone color; Bartók wrote of his desire, in these pieces, to "poetically color the piano tone." 

The final volumes (5 and 6) of the Mikrokosmos were intended as concert pieces for professional pianists. They differ from the preceding pieces in many respects: their contrapuntal texture is more dense (four parts), the melodic and harmonic material is more characteristic of Bartók's non-pedagogical works, and rhythmic structures are much more complicated and include vigorous syncopations and Bulgarian dance rhythms. 

While Bartók's intention to synthesize Bach, Beethoven, and Debussy was perhaps not fully realized, Mikrokosmos nonetheless compares well with some of Bach and Debussy's ostensibly pedagogical keyboard works. Like Bach's Inventions or Debussy's Études, for example, Mikrokosmos is not merely a work of practical value, but also a work of art with much purely musical substance. [Allmusic.com]

Art by Jean Dubuffet

Tchaikovsky P.A Bit of Schumann - op 72.YT_description:
Five years ago, I performed a recital at midnight on November 6 - the day of Tchaikovsky's passing - in Izhevsk, my hometown, which is a mere 20 miles away from Tchaikovsky's birthplace. It was a significant and heartfelt concert for me, and very unusual - how often one gets to play a midnight recital? The hall was full of young people, and for some of them, it was their very first classical concert. But there also were regular concert-goers and even some kids.
I wore jeans on stage and made an edgy hairdo, many things seemed anew that night, but the main hero of the recital - Tchaikovsky's brilliant cycle of 18 pieces, op.72, - felt even more refreshing, like a discovery. 
This work is a one-piece organism, consisting of different parts-moods. It can be melancholic, striking, soothing, refreshing, mournful, inspiring, colorful, trembling, and at the end of the day, grandiose in its depiction of an enormous human soul. It is Tchaikovsky's last solo piano work.
Today, I am celebrating Tchaikovsky's 180-th Birthday with this performance.

Scarlatti D.Sonata in C major K72 L401.YT_description:
Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in D major K. 72.
00:10 Introduction
01:33 Sonata
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
La Sonata in Do maggiore K. 72 di Domenico Scarlatti che presenteremo oggi è un pezzo estremamente brillante. All'inizio la Sonata ha il carattere di una fanfara, ma poi Domenico si lancia in una interminabile girandola di note, che è quantomeno assai eccitante. In questo pezzo vi sono alcuni problemi tecnici non indifferenti, principalmente dei repentini cambi di registro in ogni mano (si suona in una regione della tastiera, e poi Domenico ci chiede di saltabeccare  velocissimamente in un'altra, senza preavviso né preparazione). Di conseguenza, vi sono alcuni moderni musicologi i quali, considerando queste stravaganze “errori di trascrizione”, hanno prodotto le loro versioni rivedute e corrette del testo primigenio, semplificandone sia la lettura che l'esecuzione. Sinceramente, non sono c'accordo con loro, e credo che questo sia esattamente quello che ha scritto Domenico, senza errori! Con il debito studio e l'ingegno che la musica di Domenico richiede, è ben possibile eseguire il testo così come lui ce lo ha lasciato, ed è proprio quello che cercherò di fare fra qualche minuto. Credo, inoltre, che questa Sonata sia proprio la rappresentazione di un grandissimo Maestro quale Domenico era, intento a godersi un momento di pura virtuosità, al solo fine di godersela.
Buon ascolto.

Scarlatti D.Sonata - K 478 D major.YT_description:
Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in D major K. 478
00:10 Introduction
01:34 Sonata
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
La Sonata in Re maggiore K. 478 di Domenico Scarlatti che presenteremo oggi è una fra le più belle sonate liriche di Domenico, un lavoro così ricco nell'armonia, nella melodia e nella scrittura sofisticata che saremmo tentati di chiamarlo un “poema” musicale. Questa è musica che ha una qualità narrativa molto speciale. La Sonata reca l'indicazione “Andante e Cantabbile”, ed è piena di meravigliosi episodi diversi. Comincia con un canto aperto, molto pastorale e semplice, il quale piano piano si trascoforma in qualcosa di ben più scuro e riflessivo. La musica è di una tale qualità che perfino le figure d'accompagnamento sono scritte in maniera molto evoluta, segno evidente che Domenico profuse molte attenzioni in questa Sonata. Nella seconda parte le varie sezioni sono ripetute ma scorciate di qualche battuta, procedura che dà l'impressione di un incedere inesorabile, e poi, sul finire del pezzo, gli angeli cominciano a cantare so chiudono la Sonata in un'atmosfera gloriosa. Questo, secondo me, è uno di quei pezzi di musica che rendono il mondo un posto migliore.

Ludwig van Beethoven's Piano Sonata No. 8 in C minor, Op. 13, commonly known as Sonata Pathétique, was written in 1798 when the composer was 27 years old, and was published in 1799. It has remained one of his most celebrated compositions. Beethoven dedicated the work to his friend Prince Karl von Lichnowsky. Although commonly thought to be one of the few works to be named by the composer himself, it was actually named Grande sonate pathétique (to Beethoven's liking) by the publisher, who was impressed by the sonata's tragic sonorities.Prominent musicologists debate whether or not the Pathétique may have been inspired by Mozart's piano sonata K. 457, since both compositions are in C minor and have three very similar movements. The second movement, "Adagio cantabile", especially, makes use of a theme remarkably similar to one in the spacious second movement of Mozart's sonata.

Beethoven L.Sonata No 11 in Bb major Op.PS_title: Sonata No 11 in Bb major Op 22 - mvt 2 Adagio con molta espressione
Beethoven L.Sonata No 11 in Bb major Op.YT_description:
Looking back at the sonatas Nos. 8-11, the Sonata No. 11, Op. 22 is the grandest of the four in its scope, probably the most challenging one technically, but curiously also the most conservative in its spirit and musical language. The elegant minuet and the easy-flowing, good-natured finale are even reminiscent of the sonatas Opp. 2 and 7, written 4-5 years earlier.

The opening movement is in textbook-perfect sonata form, putting on hold Beethoven’s previous experiments with structure and dramaturgy. I politely disagree with those who call this movement foursquare or perfunctory (those words could hardly apply to any of Beethoven’s mature works!). However, it is definitely a piece characterised by its sparkle, light-fingered drive and ebullient energy, rather than inventiveness or depth of emotion. Only towards the end of the development (05:05) does Beethoven’s customary ease of surprising us come to the fore, as he brings the left hand to the very bottom of the keyboard in a long, very atmospheric pianissimo passage.

The standout movement, for me, is the second one (7:46). Here, spirituality is abundant, and Beethoven’s sense of colour, texture and register is exquisite. ‘A long aria’, one could say of the big opening phrase – but it’s written in pianissimo, and as such, appears to us as if in a dream, or through a softening mist, an inspired effect. The middle section (11:30), rising from the murky depths of the keyboard, is a delight, rich with unusual, unexpected harmonies. It is also perhaps the most deeply-felt part of the sonata, questingly exploring numerous keys in a long modulating passage.

Having written the above, I wonder if it is unfair to reproach the sonata for mostly playing it safe. It is undoubtedly the work of a master, one in complete control of his craft and his instrument. Beethoven himself thought very highly of the work, and perhaps it is only in hindsight and through the lens of our own sensibilities that we find the sonata falling somewhat short of Beethoven’s greatest works. In a way, we could see it as a closing, summarising chapter of the first third of Beethoven’s sonatas cycle. The next one to follow, No. 12 Op. 26, will present us with very different musical worlds.

This collection of piano pieces called Stimmungen ("Moods") was written in 1905 and is among the last things Grieg wrote towards the end of his career. His creative powers dwindling, he harked back to some older sketches and completely reworked them into a set that was meant to be like a new book of Lyric Pieces but a bit more ambitious. The difference in scope turned out to be not all that big.

I would not claim this is one of Grieg's best piano works but as always, there is much to enjoy. My recording was made on august 3, 2010. A couple of tiny imperfections are hopefully not distracting.

Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
La Sonata in Mi maggiore K. 136 di Domenico Scarlatti che presenteremo oggi è un pezzo a dir poco carino. Di fatto, a me pare la rappresentazione musicale d'una scena di seduzione. Siamo in Spagna, e quindi si presenta un hidalgo armato di chitarra il quale, siccome vuol conquistare qualcuno, si lancia in una danza ammiccante. L'oggetto del suo desiderio, però, gli è un osso duro: lo lascia avvicinare, ma all'ultimo momento sentenzia un “no” secco! Allora l'hidalgo arpeggia qualche accordo desolato sulla sua chitarra, e ci riprova, ma il risultato non cambia. All'inizio della seconda parte, l'astuto hidalgo cambia tattica: invece di ballare racconta una storia ma, ahimé, siamo al punto di partenza; arriva vicino, ma poi viene rifiutato. A questo punto gli accordi sulla sua chitarra diventano drammatici, disperati, ma lui è un uomo di carattere: si ricompone, e prova di nuovo con un'altra storia, poi accenna qualche passo di danza più moderato, ed alla fine ottiene il suo sospirato “si”! Gli amanti riuniti, allora, scompaiono nella notte...
Buon ascolto.

Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in G major K. 454.
00:10 Introduction
01:40 Sonata
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
La Sonata in Sol maggiore K. 454 di Domenico Scarlatti che presenteremo oggi è un bel pezzo che reca l'inusuale indicazione di tempo “Andante spiritoso”. Di fatto questa è così atipica che quando, nel 1906, il Maestro Alessandro Longo pubblicò la prima edizione integrale a stampa delle Sonate di Scarlatti, la credette un errore, e cambiò l'indicazione in “Allegro spiritoso”. Nell'epoca barocca in generale, e con un compositore così fantasioso come Domenico in particolare, certe linee non sono mai nitide, ma sempre un po' sfocate. Spesso, si arriva alla scelta del tempo “ideale” dopo aver svolto un certo lavoro di investigazione musicale. Ad esempio, questo è un pezzo molto operistico ed episodico. Comincia con un tema che pare una marcia, e che ben di presta ad una esecuzione “andante”. Ma poi, Domenico scrive una serie di passaggi brillanti i quali necessitano di un andamento più veloce per manifestare il loro senso musicale. Similmente, in apertura della seconda parte vi è un episodio che a me pare un recitativo d'opera: se lo suonassimo troppo velocemente, la musica non avrebbe il tempo di respirare (come un cantante) ed il risultato sarebbe rovinoso. Ciò detto, la Sonata è un gran bel lavoro!
Buon ascolto.

Composer: Johann Ladislaus Dussek
Artists: Tuija Hakkila (fortepiano)

Jan Ladislav Dussek (1760-1812) was a composer-virtuoso esteemed by Haydn, from the same generation as Beethoven but far more travelled, feted in salons and palaces from London to St Petersburg. 

The four sonatas on this disc all come from different periods: The earliest (Op.5 No.3 in A flat) dates back to 1788, the threshold of the French Revolution, while the last (Op.61 in F sharp minor) was composed in 1807, in the midst of the turmoil of the Napoleonic Wars. The B flat major Sonata Op.24 reflects Dussek's time in London, and Op.43 in A major the period of his hasty departure from London, abandoning his young wife in London and fleeing to Hamburg to avoid his creditors, notably including Lorenzo da Ponte. 

In the sonatas from Op.24 onwards Dussek richly exploits the colourful sonorities of then-new-five-and-a-half-octav Broadwood grand, mingling flamboyant virtuosity and explosive rhetoric with a rhapsodic expansiveness and harmonic side-slips that foreshadow Schubert. The music is tautly structured and passionately argued, with richly imaginative textures and a subtle use of chromaticism for poignant effect.

Liszt F.Chanson bohmienne S250 No2.YT_description:
Franz Liszt (1811 - 1886), Deux Mélodies russes 'Arabesques', S250 (1842)

Performed by Alexandre Dossin

00:00 - No 1: Solovei 'Le rossignol' (second version) 
04:40 - No 2: Chanson bohémienne 

The two transcriptions which Liszt eventually issued together under the title Arabesques were conceived separately, and Solovei appeared in an earlier, rather boisterous version with a title page which attempted to make Cyrillic letters from Roman ones—with laughable results. The revised version used to be a staple encore piece, refashioning a charming song by a rather neglected minor Russian master with attractive emphasis on the imitation of the nightingale’s song. The printed editions of the Chanson bohemienne make no mention of the melody’s origins, but it seems to be the work of one Pyotr Petrovich Bulakhov (not to be confused in any way with Konstantin Bulhakov—see below), about whom the present writer is sadly uninformed. As with many of Liszt’s song transcriptions, the piece is tantamount to a set of variations.

Scarlatti D.Sonata in C minor K 22.YT_description:
Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in c minor K. 22.
00:10 Introduction
01:49 Sonata
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
Nalle famosa introduzione ai 30 “Essercizi per Gravicembalo”, Domenico Scarlatti apostrofa il “Lettore” dicendogli di non aspettarsi “in questi componimenti il profondo intendimento, bensì lo scherzo ingegnoso dell'Arte, per addestrarti alla Franchezza sul Gravicembalo”. Un serio proposito, eccome! La Sonata in do minore K. 22 di Domenico Scarlatti che presenteremo oggi, che è anche il numero 22 degli “Essercizi”, ci offre un esempio calzante di quel che voleva dire Domenico. Il pezzo è una toccata brillante, che comincia con tra grandi arpeggi di do minore in moto discendente: non vi è alcun dubbio in che tonalità ci troviamo, e a questo punto la Sonata dispiega una serie di passi brillanti e coinvolgenti. Domenico, però, mantiene la parola: vi sono tanti “scherzi ingegnosi dell'Arte” in queste pagine. Ad esempio, ci chiede di suonare un passo normalmente, e poi di ripeterlo – nota per nota- con le mani incrociate. Questo espediente trasforma un pezzo di musica carino ma tutto sommato innocuo in un paio di minuti di feroci difficoltà. Nella mia opinione, conviene cercare di obbedire il comando di Domenico, non foss'altro perché è immensamente divertente suonare la sua musica seguendo il suo ingegnoso dettato. Grandiosamente, Domenico chiuse il suo “Aviso” al lettore con un memorabile “Vivi felice”. Gli è lo stesso augurio che porgo a tutti voi, e di cuore.
Buon ascolto.

Scarlatti D.Sonatas in C major K 270 and.YT_description:
Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in C major K. 270
00:10 Introduction
01:50 Sonata
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
La Sonata in Do maggiore K. 270 di Domenico Scarlatti che presenteremo oggi è un lavoro assai impressionante. La Sonata s'ispira ad un ritmo di marcia, ed è suggestiva di un corteo regale o, comunque, qualcosa di solenne. La usa caratteristica più intrigante, però, è di gran lunga la combinazione creata dalla monumentale tecnica di Domenico, che qui si apparenta con uno spiccato senso della forma. La Sonata si apre con una lunga introduzione durante la quale vengono presentati quasi tutti gli elementi che costruiranno il pezzo. Alla fine della prima pagina Domenico modula nel lontano tono di Mi bemolle maggiore, ed è qui che comincia l'azione! Il “motivo di marcia” rimane, ma questa volta è accompagnato da note singole alla mano sinistra, distanziate da due ottave: la mano del suonatore, quindi, deve compiere questi grandi balzi più o meno di continuo, creando delle armonie davvero belle! Alla fine di ciascuna parte, Domenico introduce un elemento totalmente nuovo, che non ha nulla a che vedere con la marcia bensì par suggerire una ninna nanna! Presa nel suo insieme, questa Sonata è una celebrazione della gioia che si prova a suonare uno strumento a tastiera; ho tutta l'intenzione di divertirmi a presentarvela, nella sincera speranza che anche voi vi divertiate ad ascoltarla.
Buon ascolto.

In 1953 Bacewicz started working on the Second Piano Sonata and Poland enters The Khrushchev Thaw phase - a period after Stalin's death when censorship and repression of the Soviet Union (also towards music) relented, giving more freedom to the citizens of the Eastern Bloc. It is perhaps forgotten that Bacewicz, as well as being a violinist, was also a talented pianist and premiered most of her piano works herself, as was the case with the Second Sonata. It is worth mentioning that this is the only piano sonata she agreed to release; the First Piano Sonata was not published and several others have never seen the light of day. The piece is one of the finest of its kind in 20th centuray piano literature  – great formal planning goes along with surprising and powerful changes of action. The first movement calls to mind Prokofiev's 'War Sonatas'; with a heavy, thick approach to the texture, fiery chords and lightning passages in the development section. In contrast, the following Largo introduces a peaceful choral section, which builds and finds its release in the polyphonic imitation of the voices. The final Toccata is based on a Polish folk dance, Oberek. A virtuosic and condensed movement reveals Bacewicz's mischievous character by giving several technical challenges to the pianist.

After Chopin’s death many composers tried to master the artistic form of mazurka. His beloved miniature found a true continuator only almost a century later as Karol Szymanowski. This great Polish composer of the XXth century wrote altogether 22 mazurkas in years 1924-26 (20 Mazurkas op.50) and 1933-34 (2 Mazurkas op.62). Szymanowski very often expressed how difficult he felt it was to undertake the historical dialogue with Chopin’s tradition of the mazurka genre. Although he kept the rhythmical structure and the ABA construction of the piece, he changed the function of the melody making the rich, varied and colourful harmony the core of his compositions. Unlike the later Mazurkas op.62, the 20 Mazurkas op.50 represent a strong connection to the folklore of southern Poland - very characteristic of Szymanowski’s compositions written at the end of his life. The whole cycle consists of contrasting pieces with slower and faster dances following each other alternately. Different miniatures were written for composer’s family and fellows - the first four mazurkas being dedicated to Arthur Rubinstein, Szymanowski’s closest friends and one of the greatest interpreters of his works.

Frank Martin (15 September 1890 – 21 November 1974) was a Swiss composer, who lived a large part of his life in the Netherlands.

8 Préludes pour le piano (1948)

1. Grave (0:00)
2. Allegretto tranquillo (3:36)
3. Tranquillo, ma con moto (5:25)
4. Allegro (8:00)
5. Vivace (9:14)
6. Andantino grazioso (11:15)
7. Lento (13:21)
8. Vivace (20:01)

Lucia Negro, piano

I used my own sheet music. These preludes were part of my final exam at the Royal Conservatory of Music, The Hague,  in 1981 and I still play them often. 

The Petite Symphonie Concertante of 1944–45 made Martin's international reputation, and is the best known of his orchestral works, as the early Mass is the best known of his choral compositions, and the Jedermann monologues for baritone and piano or orchestra the best known of his works for solo voice. Other Martin pieces include a full-scale symphony (1936–37), two piano concertos, a harpsichord concerto, a violin concerto, a cello concerto, a concerto for seven wind instruments, and a series of six one-movement works he called "ballades" for various solo instruments with piano or orchestra.

Among a dozen major scores for the theater are operatic settings of Shakespeare (Der Sturm [ The Tempest ], in August Wilhelm Schlegel's German version [1952–1955]) and Molière (Monsieur de Pourceaugnac [1960–1962]), and the satirical fairy tale La Nique à Satan (Thumbing Your Nose at Satan [1928–1931]). His works on sacred texts and subjects, which include another large-scale theater piece, Le Mystère de la Nativité (The Mystery of the Nativity) 1957/1959, are widely considered to rank among the finest religious compositions of the 20th century. Fellow Swiss musician Ernest Ansermet, a champion of his music from 1918 on, conducted recordings of many of Martin's works, such as the oratorio for soloists, double chorus & orchestra In Terra Pax (1944), with the Orchestre de la Suisse Romande.

Martin developed his mature style based on his personal variant of Arnold Schoenberg's twelve tone technique, starting using it around 1932, although he didn't abandon tonality. His preference for lean textures and his habitual rhythmic vehemence make his style different from the one of Schoenberg. Some of Martin's most inspired music comes from his last decade. He worked on his last cantata, Et la vie l'emporta, until ten days before his death. He died in Naarden, the Netherlands, and was buried in Geneva at the Cimetière des Rois.

Leighton K.Conflicts (Fantasy on Two The.YT_description:
Kenneth Leighton - Conflicts - Fantasy on Two Themes op51 (1971)

Thomas Ang, piano

-------------------------------------------

Kenneth Leighton is remembered mainly for his choral music, especially his setting of the Coventry Carol. Influenced by Vaughn Williams, Walton, and Britten, his harmonic language ranges from the securely tonal to the acerbicity heard in his later oeuvre, after he came into contact with the music of the Second Viennese School.

Recordings of his piano works are only beginning to bubble to the commercial surface, so to speak; they are however difficult to obtain, and this piece has been recorded only once, by Eric Parkin. 

Yet it is one of my favourite modern works, mixing, as it does, an intense lyricism with the harsh permutative techniques of Leighton's more mature compositions. Divided into several clear sections the writing can seem academic at first but will surely grow upon the ear with repeated listening. The driving forces behind this piece are definitely Romantic in nature, but, when couched in dissonant terms, the long stretch of this piece takes on a compelling arch form and eventually dies into nothing. 

(For an easier introduction to Leighton's piano music, the listener can try the first Sonatina or the 5 Studies op22, both more tonally oriented and definitely less heavy an aural meal than this particular work.)

Bartok B.Dance No 8 from For Children 2.YT_description:
Here is my new recording, made last weekend, of  Bartók's educational set For Children. The colorful Hungarian title "A Gyermekeknek" somehow always amuses me. The pieces were penned down in 1908/09, but Bartók revised the set in 1945, towards the end of his life, leaving out 6 pieces and slightly altering others. It is this final version that I play here.

The two books are quite different in character. I marginally prefer 
Book I, based on Hungarian Folk Tunes. These are more ebullient, the colors brighter, than those in Book II, based on Slovak Folk Tunes, which are generally darker and more introspective, at times 
reminiscent of Janacek (as they ought to be, being Slovak). 

Both books contain a wealth of great music, and certainly not all of the pieces seen suitable for children - unless they have advanced technique and musicality. I hope my cycle can be enjoyed despite a couple of small read errors (which, obviously and  irritatingly, I only noticed during video preparation).

Bartok B.Toy Shop Tune Children at Play.YT_description:
Here is my new recording, made last weekend, of  Bartók's educational set For Children. The colorful Hungarian title "A Gyermekeknek" somehow always amuses me. The pieces were penned down in 1908/09, but Bartók revised the set in 1945, towards the end of his life, leaving out 6 pieces and slightly altering others. It is this final version that I play here.

The two books are quite different in character. I marginally prefer 
Book I, based on Hungarian Folk Tunes. These are more ebullient, the colors brighter, than those in Book II, based on Slovak Folk Tunes, which are generally darker and more introspective, at times 
reminiscent of Janacek (as they ought to be, being Slovak). 

Both books contain a wealth of great music, and certainly not all of the pieces seen suitable for children - unless they have advanced technique and musicality. I hope my cycle can be enjoyed despite a couple of small read errors (which, obviously and  irritatingly, I only noticed during video preparation).

Bartok B.Perpetuum Mobile Mikrokosmos Vo.YT_description:
Mikrokosmos, progressive pieces for piano in 6 volumes, Sz. 107, BB 105 (1926-1939)

Claude Helffer, piano
Haakon Austbö, second piano

132. Major Seconds Broken and Together
133. Syncopation (1:47)
134. Studies in Double Notes (2:48)
135. Perpetuum Mobile (3:41)
136. Whole-tone Scale (5:14)
137. Unison (6:57)
138. Bagpipe (8:40)
139. Marry Andrew (9:57)

Mikrokosmos was originally designed as a collection of pieces for the beginning pianist, but over time it took on grander proportions, comprising 153 individual pieces that spanned the range of technical difficulty. Dividing into six volumes, it begins with pieces for beginners and progresses to those that challenge even the most accomplished pianist. That Mikrokosmos has become a viable progressive method is demonstrated by its ubiquity in the repertories of modern piano students, but its reputation rests on more than its technical and pedagogical applications; Bartók's work represents a varied and finely crafted catalog of twentieth century musical idioms. In Bartók's own words, it "appears as a synthesis of all the musical and technical problems which were treated and in some case only partially solved in the previous piano works." Perhaps chief among these musical problems was Bartók's attempted synthesis of Eastern and Western European musical traditions, particularly Eastern folk music with the Germanic tradition (as represented by Bach and Beethoven) and with the progressive harmonies of Claude Debussy. 

The first 66 pieces in Mikrokosmos (Vols. 1 and 2) are dedicated to Bartók's son, Peter, for whose use they were originally intended. Many of these pieces are technical exercises, useful for developing finger and hand independence, as well as hand span; however, they are also of interest for their musical language. Hungarian folk tunes, pentatonic, whole-tone and modal harmonies, as well as more adventurous octatonic chromatic scales all form the basis for these short pieces. 

Volumes 3 and 4 make up numbers 67 through 121. These pieces display increased harmonic complexity and technical demands. Bartók employs more polymodes (the use of different modes, or keys, simultaneously), along with octatonic and diatonic scale fragments to construct these pieces. The compositions in the third and fourth volumes are also important because they betray the influence of Franz Liszt, particularly in terms of tone color; Bartók wrote of his desire, in these pieces, to "poetically color the piano tone." 

The final volumes (5 and 6) of the Mikrokosmos were intended as concert pieces for professional pianists. They differ from the preceding pieces in many respects: their contrapuntal texture is more dense (four parts), the melodic and harmonic material is more characteristic of Bartók's non-pedagogical works, and rhythmic structures are much more complicated and include vigorous syncopations and Bulgarian dance rhythms. 

While Bartók's intention to synthesize Bach, Beethoven, and Debussy was perhaps not fully realized, Mikrokosmos nonetheless compares well with some of Bach and Debussy's ostensibly pedagogical keyboard works. Like Bach's Inventions or Debussy's Études, for example, Mikrokosmos is not merely a work of practical value, but also a work of art with much purely musical substance. [Allmusic.com]

Art by Jean Dubuffet

Scarlatti D.Sonata in c minor K 362.YT_description:
Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in c minor K. 362.
00:10 Introduction
01:51 Sonata
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
La Sonata in do minore K. 362 di Domenico Scarlatti che presenteremo oggi è fra le più brevi dell'intera collezione, ma per nostra fortuna è anche fra le più strabilianti. Se questo pezzo fosse stato scritto in epoca romantica, quasi certamente avrebbe recato il titolo “Improvviso”, ossia quell forma musicale che pretendeva d'emulare il Maestro che immortalava un'idea musicale sul momento, sribacchiandola in fretta e furia, magari per usarla in seguito, e gli “Improvvisi”, o “Impromptus”, di solito erano pezzi brevi e passionali. La mia analogia non è casuale: leggendo questa sonata di Domenico non si trova quasi nulla di “barocco”, pur essendo la Sonata scritta prima del 1754. L'intero pezzo si basa su una cellula musicale molto breve, fatta di due note ascendenti e due discendenti di un tono di mezzo tono, e questa particolare fisionomia linguistica doveva rappresentare un sospiro, l'ansia, l'angoscia, ed in questo piccolo pezzo Domenico riesce bena a riscreare un'atmosfera ansiosa. Ovviamente, Domenico è un grande compositore e quindi non si accontenta di scrivere un pezzo brillante, quasi una toccata, su un motto di quattro note sole: dissemina quindi il pezzo di piccoli controcanti, a volte appena accennati, che però donano alla musica quella qualità particolare, quel “marchio di fabbrica” che è la penna di un maestro monumentale. È un piccolo, grande pezzo di musica.
Buon ascolto.

Scarlatti D.Sonata - K 459 D minor.YT_description:
Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in d minor K. 459.
00:10 Introduction
01:17 Sonata
Sandro dice:
La Sonata in re minore K. 459 di Domenico Scarlatti che presenteremo oggi è una Sonata dalla doppia faccia, un po' come il Dottor Jekyll ed il Signor Hyde, o come diciamo qui in Italia, come il diavolo e l'acqua santa. Comincia in un clima quasi ecclesiastico: questo sarebbe il “Lacrymosae” di una Messa di Requiem, una musica molto triste e dolorosa. Ma poi Domenico cambia idea: modula nel tono maggiore, e scrive una fanfara esplosiva, con le trombe che squillano a perdifiato, i colpi di grancassa, e un sacco di passaggi brillanti. In apertura della seconda parte vi è una reminiscenza del motivo dell'inizio, ma è giusto un momento in cui Domenico ricorda come ha cominciato la Sonata e nulla più. Ben presto, Domenico ha di nuovo voglia di fare un bel baccano, e allora torna prepotente il motivo di fanfara che chiude la Sonata in una esplosione di gioia. Per me è un pezzo davvero divertente.
Buon ascolto.

Friedrich Burgmüller, in Paris known under the French form of his name, Frédéric, was born in Regensburg in 1806, the son of the composer, pianist and music teacher Johann August Franz Burgmüller, and elder brother of the composer, conductor and pianist Norbert Burgmüller. Friedrich Burgmüller was taught by his father. After the latter’s death in 1824 he followed him as director of music in Düsseldorf, teaching music in Mühlhausen and as a cellist in Basel. In 1832 he settled in Paris, where he won a considerable reputation as a piano teacher, and internationally as a composer of salon pieces and studies. He did much to promote the work of his brother Norbert, four years his junior, whose career had been cut short by his sudden death at the spa in Aachen in 1836. Friedrich Burgmüller’s activities brought continued success in Paris. Many of his compositions proved successful among amateurs, for whom his pieces offered limited technical challenges, coupled with the satisfaction of musical interest. His Études (‘Studies’) have continued to provide a basis for piano teaching and the development of technical proficiency.

Mikrokosmos was originally designed as a collection of pieces for the beginning pianist, but over time it took on grander proportions, comprising 153 individual pieces that spanned the range of technical difficulty. Dividing into six volumes, it begins with pieces for beginners and progresses to those that challenge even the most accomplished pianist. That Mikrokosmos has become a viable progressive method is demonstrated by its ubiquity in the repertories of modern piano students, but its reputation rests on more than its technical and pedagogical applications; Bartók's work represents a varied and finely crafted catalog of twentieth century musical idioms. In Bartók's own words, it "appears as a synthesis of all the musical and technical problems which were treated and in some case only partially solved in the previous piano works." Perhaps chief among these musical problems was Bartók's attempted synthesis of Eastern and Western European musical traditions, particularly Eastern folk music with the Germanic tradition (as represented by Bach and Beethoven) and with the progressive harmonies of Claude Debussy. 

The first 66 pieces in Mikrokosmos (Vols. 1 and 2) are dedicated to Bartók's son, Peter, for whose use they were originally intended. Many of these pieces are technical exercises, useful for developing finger and hand independence, as well as hand span; however, they are also of interest for their musical language. Hungarian folk tunes, pentatonic, whole-tone and modal harmonies, as well as more adventurous octatonic chromatic scales all form the basis for these short pieces. 

Volumes 3 and 4 make up numbers 67 through 121. These pieces display increased harmonic complexity and technical demands. Bartók employs more polymodes (the use of different modes, or keys, simultaneously), along with octatonic and diatonic scale fragments to construct these pieces. The compositions in the third and fourth volumes are also important because they betray the influence of Franz Liszt, particularly in terms of tone color; Bartók wrote of his desire, in these pieces, to "poetically color the piano tone." 

The final volumes (5 and 6) of the Mikrokosmos were intended as concert pieces for professional pianists. They differ from the preceding pieces in many respects: their contrapuntal texture is more dense (four parts), the melodic and harmonic material is more characteristic of Bartók's non-pedagogical works, and rhythmic structures are much more complicated and include vigorous syncopations and Bulgarian dance rhythms. 

While Bartók's intention to synthesize Bach, Beethoven, and Debussy was perhaps not fully realized, Mikrokosmos nonetheless compares well with some of Bach and Debussy's ostensibly pedagogical keyboard works. Like Bach's Inventions or Debussy's Études, for example, Mikrokosmos is not merely a work of practical value, but also a work of art with much purely musical substance. [Allmusic.com]

Scarlatti D.Sonata - K 433 G major.YT_description:
Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in G major K. 433.
00:10 Introduction
02:00 Sonata
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
La bella Sonata in Sol maggiore K. 433 di Domenico Scarlatti che presenteremo oggi è una elaborata ed importante tarantella. Il pezzo si compone principalmente di due elementi contrastanti: il primo, in tipico stile di tarantella, è brillante e spensierato, ma il secondo è ben più serio e minaccioso, scritto in modo molto accordale. Nelle mani di un Domenico Scarlatti questi “ingredienti” sarebbero più che sufficienti a confezionare un pezzo di musica rimarchevole, ma qui Domenico va oltre, e la Sonata ha un guizzo finale quasi profetico. Ogni parte del pezzo, infatti, si chiude con una lunga serie di passi molto brillanti i quali sono fatti da una figurazione molto speciale; si tratta di una sequenza di sei note che, secondo me, vanno suonate con tutte le dita della mano: vi è un piccolo mordente in cima, che si suona con il quarto e quinto dito, e poi si scende con le rimanenti. Questa figura si ripete molte volte e, a questa velocità, crea un'impressione bellissima. Pare un ruscello pieno di trote vivaci, ma questo non gli è il punto. Quel che conta, invece, è che questa particolare figura verrà usata di molto nei decenni a venire. Il grande Muzio Clementi, “il padre del pianoforte”, la dispiegò nel suo Studio dal Gradus ad Parnassum intitolato “Bizzarria”; Schumann la usò al punto quasi d'abusarne, e poi Rachmaninov, e Prokof'ev... Questa è di nuovo una di quelle occasioni nelle quali pare che Domenico abbia una sfera di cristallo, con la quale guarda dritto al futuro sella scrittura per tastiera. Impressionante.
Buon ascolto.

Ignaz Moscheles - Etude op. 70 n. 3
Fausto Bongelli, piano
Ignaz Moscheles, (born May 23, 1794, Prague, Bohemia, Austrian Habsburg domain [now in Czech Republic]—died March 10, 1870, Leipzig [Germany]), Czech pianist, one of the outstanding virtuosos of his era.
Moscheles studied at the Prague Conservatory and later at Vienna under Johann Georg Albrechtsberger and Antonio Salieri. In 1814, commissioned by Artaria & Co., publishers, he made the first piano arrangement of Ludwig van Beethoven’s opera Fidelio, under the composer’s supervision. After giving piano recitals in Germany and France, he settled in London in 1821. In 1829 he took part in the first London performance of the Concerto for Two Pianos by Felix Mendelssohn, who had been his pupil. He conducted the first English performance of Beethoven’s Missa Solemnis and later conducted Beethoven’s Ninth Symphony at the Philharmonic Society, of which he was a regular conductor from 1845. From 1846 he was principal professor of piano at the Leipzig Conservatory, and his reputation and skill as a teacher were important factors in the continued success of that institution.
Moscheles belonged to a conservative school of piano playing that did not lend itself to the works of Frédéric Chopin and Franz Liszt; of the younger composers of his day, he leaned more toward Mendelssohn and Robert Schumann. Nevertheless, his explorations of the gradations of tone colour influenced Liszt as well as Schumann. He was also admired for his brilliant extempore performances. His own compositions include eight piano concerti, studies, and chamber works.

Oggi è il mio compleanno. Con questa tremenda pandemia una festa è fuori discussione, sicché celebrerò con la musica, e con grande piacere. Ovviamente, vorrei suonare qualcosa di adatto all'occasione, e con la meravigliosa collezione di Sonate che Domenicoa ci ha lasciato non ho che l'imbarazzo della scelta. All fine, ho selezionato la Sonata in Do maggiore K. 420 di Domenico Scarlatti che presenteremo fra poco. Questa Sonata comincia come una grande fanfara, e poi si butta a capofitto in una serie di passaggi infuocati e pieni di effetti speciali: ci sono effetti di tamburi, suoni di campane, ma soprattutto la Sonata è estremamente gioiosa dal principio sino alla fine. E cosa si può desiderare di più, per il proprio compleanno, di una caterva di gioia?
Buon ascolto.

Scarlatti D.Sonata in Bb major K 189.YT_description:
Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in B flat major K. 189.
00:10 Introduction
02:53 Sonata (no pedals)
05:21 Sonata (pedals)
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
La Sonata in Si bemolle maggiore K. 189 di Domenico Scarlatti che presenteremo oggi è un pezzo che comincia come una fuga, diventa una fanfara (o, se preferite, un “cortège”), poi presenta un assolo di chitarra ed infine si chiude di nuovo come una fanfara, ma questa volta con tanto di rullo di timpani. Qui troviamo Domenico in gran forma, fantasioso e birichino. Non c'è nulla di rimarchevole a proposito dell'inizio, salvo il fatto ch'è bellissima musica scritta divinamente. I problemi arrivano con l'assolo di chitarra: all'inizio Domenico ci lascia suonare come i tastieristi, a due mani, ma poi, pur continuando a scrivere nella stessa maniera, pretende che suoniamo prima con la mano destra sola, e poi con la mano sinistra sola. Spazziamo via ogni dubbio: ciò è difficile, scomodo, e necessita di parecchio studio. Questo mi ha fatto venire un'idea. Tanti di voi mi scrivono chiedendo come io mi avvicini all'esecuzione della musica di Scarlatti sul pianoforte moderno. Ovviamente, la mia risposta è sempre la solita, ossia che siccome sono un pianista, suono da pianista. Non potrei fare altro. Tuttavia, ci sono coloro i quali sono convinti che quando suoniamo al pianoforte qualcosa che supponiamo essere stato scritto per il clavicembalo, non dovremmo usare i pedali. Nella mia opinione, suonare il pianoforte senza il pedale di risonanza è affine ad andare in bicicletta su una ruota sola: si perde metà dello strumento. Vedete, il clavicembalo ha una costruzione molto leggera e vibrante, e quindi produce da subito un'incredibile quantità d'armonici, ma il pianoforte no! Questa, però, gli è una mezza tonnellata di strumento musicale: il pianoforte è robusto come una quercia, ma se non creiamo un minimo di riverbero naturale con il pedale di risonanza tende ad essere povero d'armonici, e risulta secco all'ascolto. Allora ho pensato che oggi avremmo fatto un esperimento assieme. Suonerò questa meravigliosa Sonata una prima volta senza toccare alcuno dei pedali. Poi ripeterò la Sonata, stavolta suonando da pianista e quindi usando il mio strumento per intero. Nel mio pensiero non vi è alcun dubbio su quale dei due approcci sia preferibile, tuttavia è possibile che alcuni di voi siano di opinione diversa. In ogni evenienza, per me è un grande privilegio potervi presentare questa splendida Sonata.
Buon ascolto.

Clutsam G.Berceuse.YT_description:
George Howard Clutsam (1866-1951) was an Australian composer and pianist, who moved to London in 1889. He is still (just about) remembered today for 'Lilac Time' (1922), an adaptation of an existing Viennese operetta—'Das Dreimäderlhaus'—based on the music of Schubert. It is worth reading the extraordinary history of adaptation of this operetta on: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Das_Dreim%C3%A4derlhaus. You can read more about Clutsam himself here:  t.ly/k634 .   Clutsam wrote a lot of light music (for example, his music for use with silent movies) but this piece, written for the august 'Repertoire Series' from Ascherberg, shows a different side of his art.  Certainly the theme is slightly sentimental, but the slithery chromatic underlay puts one in mind of Bax.  The opening is quite striking, and almost makes the piano seem out of tune!

Scarlatti D.Sonata in C minor K 99.YT_description:
Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in c minor K. 99.
00:10 Introduction
01:44 Sonata
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
Non è mia abitudine fare classifiche; specialmente nella musica, esse paiono non rivestire alcuna utilità. Tuttavia, la grande Sonata in do minore K. 99 di Domenico Scarlatti che presenteremo oggi deve per forza annoverarsi fra le più vividamente idiomatiche dell'intera collezione. Questa Sonata è una grande rapsodia spagnola, una musica di straordinaria qualità narrativa che racconta una saga di dame e cavalieri, di gesta memorabili e tempestose storie d'amore. Sotto il profilo tecnico, è un gioiello da ammirare. Comincia con una melodia sinuosa, alla mano destra, la quale divente ben presto assai appassionata. Domenico sottolinea l'incremento di passione con acute dissonanze nell'accompagnamento, e poi comincia a scrivere passi a mani incrociate. Questi divengono via via più complessi, tanto che ad un certo punto Domenico raddopia le note del masso in ottave, e la procedura aggiunge un tocco di eroismo all'intero pezzo. Non lasciamoci fuorviare dal numero di catalogo relativamente basso: questo non è il tentativo di un principiante. Piuttosto, è il prodotto di un grande virtuoso che, seduto al suo strumento come uno stregone o un illusionista, ci fa fare un viaggio musicale epico. Questo è un capolavoro.
Buon ascolto.
