Scarlatti D.Sonata in A major K. 219.YT_description:
Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in A major K. 219.
00:10 Introduction
02:29 Sonata
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
La Sonata in La maggiore K. 219 di Domenico Scarlatti che presenteremo oggi è uno dei grandi lavori cantabili che questo geniale Maestro ci ha lasciato. Di fatto, questa è una di quelle occasioni in cui la già felice mano di Domenico pare guidata da qualcuno lassù, sul Parnaso, per la creazione di quello che è un compendio di straordinaria maestria accoppiata a divina ispirazione. La Sonata comincia con un tema arioso che si muove per grandi intervalli, e questo è già di per sé un segno di grande padronanza tecnica. Poi Domenico dispiega quelle che Joel Sheveloff chiamava “vamps”: piccole cellule melodiche ripetute in continuazione, con l'armonia che cambia velatamente in sottofondo, che creano un sentore ipnotico, quasi vedessimo una grande palla di velluto sospesa a mezz'aria. Una volta preparata la scena, la Sonata propria comincia ed è una scorribanda di melodie e figurazioni una più bella dell'altra. IN apretura di seconda parte Domenico scrive un episodio lirico e drammatico, nel quale apprezziamo a pieno la sua enorme eredità operistica: non dimentichiamo che Alessandro Scarlatti, il suo babbo e maestro, era il più grande operista del tempo. Dopo ulteriori arabeschi, la Sonata giunge al fine in un clima di pacata serenità, e non possiamo non renderci conto d'aver appena frequentato un capolavoro. Siccome questo è un lavoro piuttosto complesso, è possibile che le più recondite bellezze del pezzo non siano evidenti ad un primo ascolto; allora vorrei invitarvi a cercare quante più letture di questo capolavoro possiate, e di ascoltarle tutte. Questa Sonata è uno dei pezzi di musica che rendono il mondo un posto migliore.
Buon ascolto.

Rozsa M.Capricietto No 6 from Bagatellen.YT_description:
Miklós Rózsa (1907–1995) was a Hungarian composer who was trained in Germany, worked in France and England, and eventually settled in the USA where he became one of the foremost film composers. Despite composing nearly 100 film scores (those for Ben Hur and El Cid being the most famous) he kept composing absolute classical music throughout his life, like concertos for piano, cello, and violin,  a Sinfonia Concertante, the Theme, Variations, and Finale, and a handful of piano works.

The "Bagatellen" (Little Pieces for Play & Dance), Op.12 were composed in 1932 (according to the score) and dedicated to his piano tutor Robert Teichmuller.  Rózsa's Hungarian roots are clearly heard in these colorful pieces, which seem to me more related to the sound world of Dohnányi than to that of Bartók.

I recorded this set in November 2013.

Scarlatti D.Sonata - K 494 G major.YT_description:
Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in G major K. 494.
00:10 Introduction
02:03 Sonata
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
La grande Sonata in Sol maggiore K. 494 di Domenico Scarlatti che presenteremo oggi è un pezzo molto coreografico, il quale potrebbe addirittura provenire direttamente da un bel balletto. La prima cosa che salta all'occhio leggendo la partitura è l'estrema densità della musica: note ovunque, molti accordi... Ovviamente, più note significano più suono e questa è una chiara indicazione del fatto che la Sonata dev'esser stata concepita per un'occasione importante, magari addirittura un concerto. Quando studiamo la parte più a fondo, ci accorgiamo che la Sonata è fatta da due elementi contrastanti: il primo robusto a potente, ed il secondo un po'più pacato ed appena incline al lirismo. Quel che rende la Sonata un capolavoro, però, è l'assoluta stravaganza con cui Domenico tratta l'armonia. Per darvi un solo esempio, all'inizio ascoltiamo il primo tema, che dura per otto battute. Poi c'è una piccola fermata, e naturalmente ci aspetteremmo che la musica continuasse con qualcosa di completamente differente. Invece, sentiamo esattamente le stesse note, un'ottava sopra ma nel modo minore! Il contrasto così ottenuto è incredibile. Ecco, questo è il “piano generale” di tutta la Sonata: l'intero pezzo è fatto dal costante alternarsi dei due motivi e dei modi minore e maggiore, e questo modo di far musica apparentemente bislacco e disconnesso, di fatto crea un senso di coesione. Non nutro alcun dubbio sul fatto che questa Sonata sia un esperimento, un tentativo di ricerca espressiva, ma non nutro alcun dubbio anche sul fatto che l'esperimento sia pienamente riuscito!
Buon ascolto.

Tchaikovsky P.A Bit of Chopin - op 72 no.PS_title: A Bit of Chopin - op 72 no 15 C minor
Tchaikovsky P.A Bit of Chopin - op 72 no.YT_description:
Five years ago, I performed a recital at midnight on November 6 - the day of Tchaikovsky's passing - in Izhevsk, my hometown, which is a mere 20 miles away from Tchaikovsky's birthplace. It was a significant and heartfelt concert for me, and very unusual - how often one gets to play a midnight recital? The hall was full of young people, and for some of them, it was their very first classical concert. But there also were regular concert-goers and even some kids.
I wore jeans on stage and made an edgy hairdo, many things seemed anew that night, but the main hero of the recital - Tchaikovsky's brilliant cycle of 18 pieces, op.72, - felt even more refreshing, like a discovery. 
This work is a one-piece organism, consisting of different parts-moods. It can be melancholic, striking, soothing, refreshing, mournful, inspiring, colorful, trembling, and at the end of the day, grandiose in its depiction of an enormous human soul. It is Tchaikovsky's last solo piano work.
Today, I am celebrating Tchaikovsky's 180-th Birthday with this performance.

Bartok B.Childrens Song No 2 from For Ch.PS_title: Childrens Song No 2 from For Children 1 BB 53 Sz 42
Bartok B.Childrens Song No 2 from For Ch.YT_description:
Here is my new recording, made last weekend, of  Bartók's educational set For Children. The colorful Hungarian title "A Gyermekeknek" somehow always amuses me. The pieces were penned down in 1908/09, but Bartók revised the set in 1945, towards the end of his life, leaving out 6 pieces and slightly altering others. It is this final version that I play here.

The two books are quite different in character. I marginally prefer 
Book I, based on Hungarian Folk Tunes. These are more ebullient, the colors brighter, than those in Book II, based on Slovak Folk Tunes, which are generally darker and more introspective, at times 
reminiscent of Janacek (as they ought to be, being Slovak). 

Both books contain a wealth of great music, and certainly not all of the pieces seen suitable for children - unless they have advanced technique and musicality. I hope my cycle can be enjoyed despite a couple of small read errors (which, obviously and  irritatingly, I only noticed during video preparation).

This collection of piano pieces called Stimmungen ("Moods") was written in 1905 and is among the last things Grieg wrote towards the end of his career. His creative powers dwindling, he harked back to some older sketches and completely reworked them into a set that was meant to be like a new book of Lyric Pieces but a bit more ambitious. The difference in scope turned out to be not all that big.

I would not claim this is one of Grieg's best piano works but as always, there is much to enjoy. My recording was made on august 3, 2010. A couple of tiny imperfections are hopefully not distracting.

Bartok B.Round Dance 1 No 6 from For Chi.PS_title: Round Dance 1 No 6 from For Children 2 BB 53 Sz 42
Bartok B.Round Dance 1 No 6 from For Chi.YT_description:
Here is my new recording, made last weekend, of  Bartók's educational set For Children. The colorful Hungarian title "A Gyermekeknek" somehow always amuses me. The pieces were penned down in 1908/09, but Bartók revised the set in 1945, towards the end of his life, leaving out 6 pieces and slightly altering others. It is this final version that I play here.

The two books are quite different in character. I marginally prefer 
Book I, based on Hungarian Folk Tunes. These are more ebullient, the colors brighter, than those in Book II, based on Slovak Folk Tunes, which are generally darker and more introspective, at times 
reminiscent of Janacek (as they ought to be, being Slovak). 

Both books contain a wealth of great music, and certainly not all of the pieces seen suitable for children - unless they have advanced technique and musicality. I hope my cycle can be enjoyed despite a couple of small read errors (which, obviously and  irritatingly, I only noticed during video preparation).

Bartok B.Game of Tag (No 20) from For Ch.PS_title: Game of Tag (No 20) from For Children 2 BB 53 Sz 42
Bartok B.Game of Tag (No 20) from For Ch.YT_description:
Here is my new recording, made last weekend, of  Bartók's educational set For Children. The colorful Hungarian title "A Gyermekeknek" somehow always amuses me. The pieces were penned down in 1908/09, but Bartók revised the set in 1945, towards the end of his life, leaving out 6 pieces and slightly altering others. It is this final version that I play here.

The two books are quite different in character. I marginally prefer 
Book I, based on Hungarian Folk Tunes. These are more ebullient, the colors brighter, than those in Book II, based on Slovak Folk Tunes, which are generally darker and more introspective, at times 
reminiscent of Janacek (as they ought to be, being Slovak). 

Both books contain a wealth of great music, and certainly not all of the pieces seen suitable for children - unless they have advanced technique and musicality. I hope my cycle can be enjoyed despite a couple of small read errors (which, obviously and  irritatingly, I only noticed during video preparation).

Scarlatti D.Sonata - K 464 C major.YT_description:
Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in C major K. 464.
00:10 Introduction
02:08 Sonata
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
La Sonata in Do maggiore K. 464 di Domenico Scarlatti che presenteremo oggi è un bellissimo pezzo di music, pieno di sorprese. Comincia con due notine in cima alla tastiera: un Do ed un Sol, il primo ed il quinto grado della scala; da qui potremmo andare ovunque, e lo faremo! Alla seconda battuta di musica, il pezzo comincia davvero, con un'esplosione di suono di carattere Haendeliano. Forse questa non è Musica per i Reali Fuochi d'Artificio, ma sarebbe ben adatta ad un'occasione solenne ed importante! Poco dopo l'inizio, Domenico introduce un elemento nuovo, un poco più lirico, e siccome lui è un virtuoso della tastiera arricchisce questo motivetto con diverse note ribattute. Ad un certo punto, un tema di fanfara irrompe sulla scena, con trombe squillanti che chiudono la prima parte della Sonata. La seconda parte ha inizio con una variazione del tema lirico, che questa volta Domenico tinge di un acceso patetismo: non dimentichiamoci che lui è anche un grande operista, e nella sua musica per tastiera c'è sempre un forte elemento di teatralità. Dopo una debita espansione del materiale tematico, ritornano le trombe che, con il loro motivo di fanfara, chiudono il pezzo in un clima di gioiosa esuberanza. So che diversi insegnanti di pianoforte seguono questo programma; non sono certo granché come pedagogo, ma sospetto che questa particolare Sonata potrebbe essere un ottimo punto di accesso all'universo di Scarlatti. Qui c'è un po' di tutto, e di sicuro vi si trovano alcuni elementi importanti della poetica scarlattiana: è brillante, ed anche se non è troppo difficile da suonare è molto teatrale. Soprattutto, è un gran bel pezzo di musica!
Buon ascolto.
Scarlatti D.Sonata - K 464 C major.YT_title: SCARLATTI / ALL SONATAS #371: Sonata in C major K. 464

Scarlatti D.Sonata - K 498 B minor.YT_description:
Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in b minor K. 498.
00:10 Introduction
01:42 Sonata
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
Coloro di voi che seguono questo programma con una certa regolarità, sapranno bene che di solito non presento Sonate nella medesima tonalità in giorni consecutivi. In questa occasione, però, sono quasi costretto ad abbandonare la mia pratica usuale: ieri presentammo la Sonata in si minore K. 497, ed oggi, a momenti, presenteremo la Sonata in si minore K. 498 di Domenico Scarlatti perché, secondo me, questi due lavori sono strettamente imparentati. Praticamente partono entrambi dallo stesso punto: entro la seconda battuta di ciascun lavoro, infatti, notiamo che Domenico usa esattamente le stesse note! Se andate al minuto 1:23 del video di ieri (Sonata K. 497) capirete subito di cosa parlo. Questa è ovviamente una dimostrazione di monumentale maestria d a parte di Domenico, come se ci dicesse “guardate che cosa sono capace di fare: parto dalle stesse note, e scrivo due pezzi completamente differenti!”. Mentre la Sonata di ieri mostrava una scrittura densa, quasi corale, la Sonata K. 498 è un meraviglioso arabesco, scritto magnificamente per la tastiera. Suonarlo è una gioia, ed è certamente un grande privilegio, per me, potervelo presentare.
Buon ascolto.

A multiple prizewinner of international competitions and described in the international press as a “poet on the #piano with remarkable maturity”, Georgian born pianist Inga Fiolia has a bright future. Since giving her first performance with an orchestra at the age of seven, she has shown outstanding ability as a soloist, accompanist and interpreter of a wide variety of styles, from baroque to 21st century compositions. She graduated from the Central Music School of the Tchaikovsky Conservatory in Moscow and the Cologne Musikhochschule with Alexey Nasedkin, Rudolf Kehrer and Vassily Lobanov.

As a soloist, she has collaborated with world-renowned orchestras including the Brandenburg State Opera Philharmonic, the Brussels Philharmonic, the Georgian State Chamber Orchestra and National Philharmonic, the Bergische Symphoniker, and the South Westphalia Philharmonic. She has shared stages with Rolando Villazón, Michael Barenboim and Christian Lanza and has also performed for major TV and radio stations including ZDF, ARTE, Classica TV, SWR, Deutschlandradio, WDR and Georgian TV.

Her performance of a selection of Scriabin Preludes and Mendelssohn’s Piano Concerto No. 1 was released on DVD Stars of tomorrow (Unitel Classica, 2015) and her CD with Glinka Piano Variations on Naxos Lable Grand Piano (2017)

Scarlatti D.Sonata - K 552 D minor.YT_description:
Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in d minor K. 552.
00:10 Introduction
01:59 Sonata
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
Mi chiedo spesso come sia stata la relazione fra Domenico e Maria Barbara. Praticamente, hanno passato una vita insieme da maestro e allieva, e non è difficile immaginarli chicchierare di musica, anche in età avanzata. Forse, in una di queste occasioni, l'ormai matura Regina chiese a Domenico di scriverle qualcosa nello stile francese, che era notoriamente ricco di ornamenti. Se ciò fosse davvero successo, Domenico non avrebbe potuto far altro che accontentare il regio capriccio e, probabilmente, avrebbe tirato fuori dal suo cilindro magico qualcosa di molto simile alla grande Sonata in re minore K. 552 che presenteremo oggi. Questa è musica di grande maturità e ispirazione. La Regina desidera qualcosa di francese pieno di fioriture? Nessun problema: Domenico scrive un giungla di abbellimenti! In pratica ce n'è uno ogni due note! La Sonata comincia come un corteo piuttosto serio (siamo in un mero “Allegretto”) e pomposo, ma poi Domenico modula nel modo maggiore e fa miracoli con l'armonia e, ovviamente, con gli ornamenti. Nella seconda parte c'è un passo che pare drammatico, ma non son'altro che nuvole passeggere: presto Domenico torna al modo maggiore, nel quale terminerà la Sonata. Questa mi pare una dichiarazione d'amore e benevolenza assoluta e, detto per inciso, è anche uno dei più sublimi esempi di scrittura tastieristica immaginabili.
Buon ascolto.

Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
La piccola Sonata in La maggiore K. 456 di Domenico Scarlatti che presenteremo oggi è una toccata, un pezzo pieno di buonumore e passaggi brillanti. Fin qui ci sarebbe da riportare ben poco di eccezionale, ma come sappiamo la normalità non va molto a genio a Domenico e quindi, all'inizio della seconda parte, egli scrive un passo sorprendente: modula nel tono minore, e dà alla mano sinistra figurazioni veloci che accompagnano continui sfasamenti di armonia. L'effetto è quello di grandi nubi di tempesta che s'ammassano all'orizzonte! Dopo un po' viene da chiedersi: dove va, Domenico, con queste modulazioni? Si sta mettendo in sei guai con le leggi dell'armonia! Ma... Domenico è un genio, sicché in un batter d'occhio ecco che ritorna all'idea gioviale dell'inizio, quella stessa idea che chiuderà la Sonata fragorosamente.
Buon ascolto.

Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
La Sonata in Re maggiore K. 388 di Domenico Scarlatti che presenteremo oggi è un pezzo estremamente vivace, permeato di tipica bonomia scarlattiana. Curiosamente, la Sonata comincia con un motto dal carattere Haendeliano: due note corte e quattro lunghe che servono a Domenico come ottimo pretesto per scrivere una serie di passi brillanti praticamente per tutta la durata del pezzo. Dopo una introduzione piuttosto importante, però, Domenico modula nel tono minore e tinge la musica di colori moreschi e andalusi in un colpo di teatro non indifferente. Non contento, nella seconda parte scrive l'accenno di un passaggio lirico che crea un grande contrasto drammatico fra quello che abbiamo ascoltato sinora e quello che ascolteremo subito dopo, che ancora una volta sarà uno sfarzo di smalto tecnico brillante e divertente. Questo, cari amici, è proprio un pezzo allegro!
Buon ascolto.

Scarlatti D.Sonata in g minor K 76.YT_description:
Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in g minor K. 76.
00:10 Introduction
02:02 Sonata
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
Johann Sebastian Bach è il maestro incontrastato del contrappunto, forse dell'intera storia della musica, ma quando voleva anche Domenico Scarlatti poteva dire la sua in questa particolare disciplina. Prendiamo ad esempio la sua Sonata in sol minore K. 76 che presenteremo oggi: è una giga all'italiana, in tre ottavi, e parte con un tema piuttosto semplice, ossia un arpeggio di sol minore con una fioritura. Il problema è che questo tema è quasi sempre presente attraverso la Sonata, in ogni dove! Continua a confrontarsi con altre voci che Domenico affastella su questa semplice melodia, e di fatto, eccetto nel finale delle due parti del pezzo, il discorso musicale è portato avanti da non meno di tre voci concorrenti. Ho il sospetto che per Domenico questo stile contrappuntistico sia servito, in questa occasione almeno, come scusa per esperimentare effetti di scrittura anche orchestrali. Ad esempio, specialmente nella seconda parte del pezzo, si trovano passaggi che vengono ripetuti alla lettera, ma mentre la prima volta le voci che accompagnano cantano singolarmente, nella ripetizione sono raddoppiate all'ottava, dando così l'impressione di qualcosa che cresce senza requie, di un inarrestabile crescendo. Va da se che questo tipo di scrittura risulti assai denso e punto agevole da suonare, ma siccome Domenico era Domenico, scelse di chiudere le sue parti che compongono questa piccola Sonata con delle furiose scale discendenti, quasi a strizzarci l'occhiolino per dirci: “vedete? O che ci vuole?”. Mi pare un pezzo di musica davvero bello e interessante.
Buon ascolto.

Scarlatti D.Sonata - K 484 D major.YT_description:
Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in D major K. 484
00:10 Introduction
01:49 Sonata
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
Nel 1676, quando il grande compositore tedesco Johann Caspar Kerll pubblicò le sue otto Toccate, intitolò la quinta “Tutta de' salti”. Era un pezzo avanguardista per quei tempi, ma il Signor Kerll non si spinse oltre l'ottava, con i suoi salti. Purtroppo il Maestro morì nel 1693: sarebbe stato interessante sapere cosa avrebbe pensato della Sonata in Re maggiore K. 484 di Domenico Scarlatti che presenteremo oggi. Questa Sonata è una danza rustica, ma presenta un gran numero di grandi salti specialmente alla mano sinistra che deve impegnarvisi sin dall'inizio. A mano a mano che la musica e il dramma progrediscono, così fanno anche le difficoltà. Ad un certo punto la famosa mano sinistra deve prodursi in passaggi molto infidi, ove i salti aumentano ad ogni nota fino a raggiungere la distanza di tre ottave: una follia. Ma perché Domenico scriveva in questa maniera? Voleva solo sfoggiare la sua bravura, o cercava invece effetti particolari sul suo strumento? Naturalmente, propendo per la seconda ipotesi: l'accostamento di toni distanti può essere molto affascinante. A parte ciò, la Sonata è molto divertente, e spero proprio che vi piaccia.
Buon ascolto.

01:18 Sonata
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
La Sonata in Si bemolle maggiore K. 489 di Domenico Scarlatti che presenteremo oggi è un esempio meraviglioso di bella scrittura per tastiera, un pezzo ove grande maestria e grande fantasia si uniscono a dipingere un ben grazioso paesaggio. La Sonata comincia nello stile galante, con linee pure e riccamente ornamentate, ma poi Domenico scrive un passaggio che richiama vagamente qualche passo di danza spagnolo, pieno di piccoli salti e molto divertente da suonare. A questo punto, il Nostro ha rotto i ponti con lo stile galante, ed allora in aperture di seconda parte scrive un episodio passionale e drammatico, che è il culmine della Sonata. Da qui in avanti, poi, procede all'inverso: rivisita il passo di danza, e poi torna all'idea gioconda dell'inizio per chiudere la Sonata. Un ben grazioso paesaggio.
Buon ascolto.

This little-known but delightful suite, composed in 1936, consists of piano adaptations Bartók made of five items from his 44 Duos for Two Violins. I wish Bartók had reworked more of these for the piano - it is amazing how idiomatic and colorful these folk music inspired pieces sound on either instrument.

Scarlatti D.Sonata in F major K 366.YT_description:
Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in F major K. 366
00:10 Introduction
01:24 Sonata
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
La Sonata in Fa maggiore K. 366 di Domenico Scarlatti che presenteremo oggi è un pezzo molto evocativo, ed è evocativo di un crosello: il balletto per cavalli (e cavalieri). Chissà? Forse Domenico andò alla Plaze de Toros, qualche volta; un tempo si soleva offrire uno spettacolo equestre prima della corrida: squilli di trombe annunciavano l'inizio della rappresentazione, i cavalli entravano nell'arena e inscenavano il loro ballo su musiche assai cadenzate... Naturalmente, Domenico usa la scusa del carosello per scrivere un pezzo brillantemente intricato. La caratteristica principale della Sonata è una figura alla mano destra, la quale punteggia il ritmo con le dita inferiori mentre le superiori cantano la melodia: è molto interessante, ed è una prodezza tecnica la quale, tuttavia, è messa ad esclusivo servizio di un gran bel pezzo di musica.
Buon ascolto.

Glazunov A.Theme et variations Op 72.YT_description:
Recorded today on december 21, 2019, Alexander Glazunov's magnificent Theme and Variations Op.72, written in St.Petersburg in 1900. I decided to do a video with score because, as far as I could find, one was not yet available on YouTube.
 
This is one of my all time favorite sets of variations, which I must have known for at least 40 years. Admittedly I have a soft spot for Glazunov, and really do not understand why he is not considered one of the major Russian composers. He was not primarily a piano composer but nonetheless an excellent pianist, and in his piano works, which are all very rewarding,  he could roar, whisper and glitter with the best of them. 

Despite long exposure and lengthy preparation, I could not get my recording 100% squeaky clean. Some variations are very difficult and my amateur technique occasionally falls short. But I think there is nothing really horrible here :)

Falla M. deAragonesa No 1 from 4 pieces.YT_description:
I have many favorite Spanish composers, but Manuel de Falla is one of my most favorite. And among his piano oeuvre, the Quatre Pieces Espagnoles, dating from 1908, are among my most favorite, second only to the Fantasia Baetica. These works show Falla being under the spell of Albeniz, and they have something of the grandeur and exuberant pianism of Iberia, albeit on a smaller scale. These rather difficult pieces have been taunting me for many years, and I believe I finally got the better of them.

I would like to dedicate these humble amateur recordings to the memory of Alicia de Larrocha, who will forever reign supreme in this repertoire.

Bartok B.Farewell (No 34) from For Child.PS_title: Farewell (No 34) from For Children 2 BBb 53 Sz 42
Bartok B.Farewell (No 34) from For Child.YT_description:
Here is my new recording, made last weekend, of  Bartók's educational set For Children. The colorful Hungarian title "A Gyermekeknek" somehow always amuses me. The pieces were penned down in 1908/09, but Bartók revised the set in 1945, towards the end of his life, leaving out 6 pieces and slightly altering others. It is this final version that I play here.

The two books are quite different in character. I marginally prefer 
Book I, based on Hungarian Folk Tunes. These are more ebullient, the colors brighter, than those in Book II, based on Slovak Folk Tunes, which are generally darker and more introspective, at times 
reminiscent of Janacek (as they ought to be, being Slovak). 

Both books contain a wealth of great music, and certainly not all of the pieces seen suitable for children - unless they have advanced technique and musicality. I hope my cycle can be enjoyed despite a couple of small read errors (which, obviously and  irritatingly, I only noticed during video preparation).

Bartok B.The Highway Robber (No 31) from.YT_description:
Here is my new recording, made last weekend, of  Bartók's educational set For Children. The colorful Hungarian title "A Gyermekeknek" somehow always amuses me. The pieces were penned down in 1908/09, but Bartók revised the set in 1945, towards the end of his life, leaving out 6 pieces and slightly altering others. It is this final version that I play here.

The two books are quite different in character. I marginally prefer 
Book I, based on Hungarian Folk Tunes. These are more ebullient, the colors brighter, than those in Book II, based on Slovak Folk Tunes, which are generally darker and more introspective, at times 
reminiscent of Janacek (as they ought to be, being Slovak). 

Both books contain a wealth of great music, and certainly not all of the pieces seen suitable for children - unless they have advanced technique and musicality. I hope my cycle can be enjoyed despite a couple of small read errors (which, obviously and  irritatingly, I only noticed during video preparation).

Burgmuller J.F.18 Characteristic Studies.YT_description:
Friedrich Burgmüller - La Serenade op.109 n. 11
Fausto Bongelli, piano
Friedrich Burgmüller, in Paris known under the French form of his name, Frédéric, was born in Regensburg in 1806, the son of the composer, pianist and music teacher Johann August Franz Burgmüller, and elder brother of the composer, conductor and pianist Norbert Burgmüller. Friedrich Burgmüller was taught by his father. After the latter’s death in 1824 he followed him as director of music in Düsseldorf, teaching music in Mühlhausen and as a cellist in Basel. In 1832 he settled in Paris, where he won a considerable reputation as a piano teacher, and internationally as a composer of salon pieces and studies. He did much to promote the work of his brother Norbert, four years his junior, whose career had been cut short by his sudden death at the spa in Aachen in 1836. Friedrich Burgmüller’s activities brought continued success in Paris. Many of his compositions proved successful among amateurs, for whom his pieces offered limited technical challenges, coupled with the satisfaction of musical interest. His Études (‘Studies’) have continued to provide a basis for piano teaching and the development of technical proficiency.
Burgmuller J.F.18 Characteristic Studies.YT_title: Friedrich Burgmüller - La Serenade op.109 n. 11

Scarlatti D.Sonata - K 523 G major.YT_description:
Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in G major K. 523.
00:10 Introduction
01:37 Sonata
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
La musica dei grandi virtuosi compositori è spesso assai difficile da eseguire. Siccome questi avevano il totale controllo del loro strumento, e lo dominavano completamente, presi dalla foga creativa e, magari, in cerca di un qualche effetto speciale non badavano minimamente al numero di note che scrivevano, né a quanto difficile fosse eseguirle, perché loro stessi erano capaci di farlo. La difficoltà, quindi, era incidentale. In questo modo ci siamo ritrovati i Concerti di Rachmaninov, i Cparicci di Paganini, gli Studi Trascendentali di Liszt, e molte Sonate di Domenico Scarlatti. In verità, però, gli è vero anche il contrario. Proprio perché questi compositori avevo il completo dominio del loro strumento, a volte sapevano sfruttarne le caratteristiche tecniche in maniera tale da ottenere il massimo effetto dallo strumento, ma chiedendo il minimo sforzo al suonatore. Noialtri interpreti siamo sempre felici quando incontriamo docesti pezzi, ovviamente, ed uno di questi è senza dubbio la piccola Sonata in Sol maggiore K. 523 di Domenico Scarlatti che presenteremo oggi. Non è un caso che essa sia fra le più note dell'intera collezione: è una piccola giga, piena di saltelli, che pare tremendamente difficile da eseguire. In verità, non lo è affatto. Ma è un bel pezzo di musica, dal piglio entusiasmante.
Buon ascolto.

Friedrich Burgmüller  - Vélocité op.109 n.10
Fausto Bongelli, piano
Friedrich Burgmüller, in Paris known under the French form of his name, Frédéric, was born in Regensburg in 1806, the son of the composer, pianist and music teacher Johann August Franz Burgmüller, and elder brother of the composer, conductor and pianist Norbert Burgmüller. Friedrich Burgmüller was taught by his father. After the latter’s death in 1824 he followed him as director of music in Düsseldorf, teaching music in Mühlhausen and as a cellist in Basel. In 1832 he settled in Paris, where he won a considerable reputation as a piano teacher, and internationally as a composer of salon pieces and studies. He did much to promote the work of his brother Norbert, four years his junior, whose career had been cut short by his sudden death at the spa in Aachen in 1836. Friedrich Burgmüller’s activities brought continued success in Paris. Many of his compositions proved successful among amateurs, for whom his pieces offered limited technical challenges, coupled with the satisfaction of musical interest. His Études (‘Studies’) have continued to provide a basis for piano teaching and the development of technical proficiency.

Scarlatti D.Sonata - K 500 A major.YT_description:
Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in A major K. 500.
00:10 Introduction
01:44 Sonata
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
La Sonata in La maggiore K. 500 di Domenico Scarlatti che presenteremo oggi è un lavoro pieno d'immaginazione che si rivela a poco a poco, proprio come le grandi novelle. Comincia la mano sinistra sola, cha canta due voci dal carattere piuttosto pastorale, quasi un canto popolare. Queste due voci son poi riprese dalla mano destra mentre la sinistra accompagna discreta, ed a questo punto di accorgiamo che la scrittura, in questa Sonata, è particolarmente densa. Dopo questa breve introduzione, un chitarrista solitario entra sulla scena e comincia a suonare il suo strumento con una serie di passi brillanti dal carattere d'arabesco. Ora sappiamo dove siamo: siamo di certo in Spagna, forse in un afoso giorno d'estate. Subito dopo Domenico scrive un passo straordinario, ove la mano destra suona note doppie in cima alla tastiera mentre la sinistra discende sino alle note più gravi e la giustapposizione di questi due suoni così differenti è un effetto davvero speciale. Nella seconda parte, la Sonata diventa più appassionata, perfino drammatica, ma il riapparire dell'effetto a suoni distanti segnala l'avvicendarsi della fine, che avverrà di lì a poco con un'affermazione di gioia e buonumore. Un piccolo, grande pezzo.
Buon ascolto.

Hofmann H.By the Mountain Torrent No 2 f.PS_title: By the Mountain Torrent No 2 from Nachklange Op 37
Hofmann H.By the Mountain Torrent No 2 f.YT_description:
Hofmann (1842-1902) was a German composer, born in Berlin, and well-known in his lifetime for orchestral works and operas. He is mainly remembered today for shorter piano works, some of which are still used for educational purposes. These two pieces come from the second set of Nachklänge (Echoes) from 1876.  The first piece 'To the Lute' is quite popular, and I recorded it once before.  I thought I would do it again, with a different camera and better sound, and follow it up with 'Am Giessbach', sometimes known as 'By the Mountain Torrent'.  It is actually a portrayal of the famous Giessbach watercourse in the Bernese Oberland - which, incidentally, was visited by my great-great uncle, William Buckle in 1885 and documented in a detailed account of his journey.

01:40 Sonata
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
Quando vidi per la prima volta la musica della Sonata in Do maggiore K. 340 di Domenico Scarlatti che presenteremo oggi, sapendo che avrei dovuto impararla la mia prima reazione fu piena di sgomento. La pagina era nera d'inchiostro, musica densa, ma quel che saltò al mio occhio erano strane figurazioni alla mano sinistra: si doveva suonare un bicordo, e poi un'ottava spezzata piu in basso. Volta dopo volta, e siccome la Sonata reca l'indicazione di “Allegro” ed è scritta nel tempo di sei ottavi, non c'era né c'è via di scampo: bisogna suonare velocemente. Questo mi spaventava, e sicché mi misi a studiare. Scoprii ben presto che la Sonata è un grazioso Saltarello, ma continuavano a darmi fastidio quei passi astrusi. Mi pareva d'aver trovato il Domenico spaccone, che scriveva a quella maniera solo perché lui poteva. Piano piano, però, mi resi conto che queste acrobazie, queste specie di arpeggi rafforzati con l'ultima nota nelle regioni gravi dello strumento, davano alla musica un aire particolare, una specie d'irresistibile rincorsa verso la fine che, assieme alla solita miriade di folli modulazioni ed anche a qualche accenno di lirismo, fa di questo pezzo una vera perla musicale. Ed è un privilegio potervela presentare.
Buon ascolto.

The form of Suite was very popular in baroque. It brings together dances from diferrent parts of Europe making it one integrated whole. There are four dances that originally form the core of the baroque suite: German Allemande, French Courante, Spanish Sarabande and Enligh Gigue. Additionally the Suite could be (and usually was) extended by other dances: Menuet, Passapied or even Polonaise. Bach wrote his six French Suites in year 1722-25 and they were originally designed to be played on a harpsichord. Bach himself considered the Suites as a bridge between the Inventions and Das Wohltemperierte Klavier. The title ‘French’ was not given by the composer but by the society to differentiate the French Suites from the previously written English Suites. Funny enough, they are, however, written in an Italian manner.
There is no surviving manuscript of these Suites, therefore the execution of the ornaments can be a very exciting and inspiring challenge for the performer. The third Suite in B minor is one of the most frequently played ones. It consists of Allemande, Courante, Sarabande, Anglaise (previously named as Gavotte), Menuet, Trio and Gigue.

Scarlatti D.Sonata in D major K. 137.YT_description:
Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in D major K. 137.
00:10 Introduction
01:19 Sonata
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
Per anni il Regno di Napoli fu sotto il domino spagnolo, ed inevitabilmente le due culture si influenzarono a vicenda. Questo accade anche nella musica. La Sonata in Re maggiore K. 137 di Domenico Scarlatti che presenteremo oggi è senza dubbio una tarantella. Nella seconda parte del pezzo, però, c'è una fermata: per un attimo la musica tace, e quando riprende ha un sapore assai spagnoleggiante, quasi come se qualcuno volesse suonare la tarantella con la chitarra. Lo trovo molto interessante, anche perché la Sonata non è punto conosciuta e questo è un peccato! Si tratta di un meraviglioso pezzo di musica. Tecnicamente siamo di fronte ad un pezzo fiammeggiante, con la mano sinistra che cavalca su e giù per la tastiera continuamente mentre la destra ne combina di tutti i colori... Di fatto, la Sonata rappresenta poco più di due minuti di follia alla tastiera, ma è un pezzo molto eccitante.
Buon ascolto

Scarlatti D.Sonata in C major K. 243.YT_description:
Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in C major K. 243.
00:10 Introduction
01:47 Sonata
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
La Sonata in Do maggiore K. 243 di Domenico Scarlatti è senza dubbio un passo di danza, ed io credo che sia un “minuetto” il quale però ha perso la via di casa. Comincia in modo molto bello in uno stile assai galante, ma ben presto la tessitura s'ispessisce e diventa quasi sinfonica: ovviamente Domenico vuole che facciamo un po' di baccano! Il diavolo, dicono, è nei dettagli. Nel mezzo del cammin della Sonata Domenico comincia a scrivere degli intricati abbellimenti: curiosamente, le mani suonano in posizione molto ravvicinata e creano parecchie dissonanze anche astruse. Siccome suoniamo nel tono di Do maggiore e spesso ci troviamo su delle quarte, parecchie di esse sono tritoni, ciò che gli antichi chiamavano “Diabulus in Musica”. Sarà un caso? Chissà... Debbo dirvi la verità: non sembrerebbe, ma questo pezzo mi ha fatto davvero sudare freddo, in quanto ho trovato diversi degli abbellimenti scritti da Domenico estremamente difficili da realizzare. Una volta superato l'ostacolo tecnico, però, non ho potuto fare a meno di rimanere estasiato di fronte al genio di Domenico: tirare fuori qualcosa di così apparentemente semplice, ma allo stesso tempo estremamente complesso. Questa Sonata è senza dubbio uno sfoggio di virtuosismo. In incognito.
Buon ascolto.

Scarlatti D.Sonata - K 493 G major.YT_description:
Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in G major K. 493.
00:10 Introduction
01:40 Sonata
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
La Sonata in Sol maggiore K. 493 di Domenico Scarlatti che presenteremo oggi è un bellissimo pezzo di musica, un'offerta piuttosto inusuale dal catalogo di Domenico: esso infatti non mostra la solita grande varietà di episodi né la pletora di fantastiche modulazioni alle quali Domenico ci ha abituato. Di fatto, ci sono solo due idee musicali che, assieme, costituiscono l'intero pezzo, e mi rendo conto che, presentandolo così, corro il rischio di farvi sospettare qualcosa di molto noioso e poco interessante. Non è così. La Sonata comincia in modo contrappuntistico, come un'invenzione a due voci, e sin dall'inizio la musica è riccamente ornamentata. Quando Domenico introduce il secondo elemento, troviamo il genio: una piccola melodia, con un ritmo puntato molto distintivo, che pare perfino mozartiana nel carattere. Questo è uno di quei motivetti orecchiabili che, se li ascolti una volta, non ti lasciano più. A seguire Domenico varia questo materiale, mettendo in campo anche dei grandi salti alla mano sinistra che aggiungono un tocco di carattere orchestrale alla musica, fino a che la Sonata giunge al fine in modo un po' trionfale. Questo, secondo me, è un magnifico pezzo di musica!
Buon ascolto.

Scarlatti D.Sonata in c minor K 116.YT_description:
Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in c minor K. 116.
00:10 Introduction
01:54 Sonata
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
La Sonata in do minore K. 116 di Domenico Scarlatti che presenteremo oggi è fra quelle che godono di maggior popolarità, e fra i pianisti almeno è assai notoria a causa di un passaggio molto scomodo nella prima parte del pezzo, ove la mano destra deve sostenere un trillo lungo su di un Si bemolle (che necessita d'essere suonato con il secondo e primo dito) mentre le dita più deboli intonano la melodia. Davvero ingegnoso, e anche avveniristico: questo diverrà uno dei trucchetti più cari a Ludwig van Beethoven, che lo userà largamente nelle sue Sonate per pianoforte; nel caso di Beethoven, i pianisti posso usare il pedale e semplificare un po' la faccenda ma qui, con Domenico, bisogna stare attenti ed eseguire tutte le note precisamente o, quantomeno, il più correttamente possibile. In verità questa non è l'unica volta in cui Domenico usa questo stratagemma, ma mentre le altre Sonate che lo presentano sono di natura piuttosto intellettuale e sperimentale, qui si trova nel mezzo ad un gran bel pezzo di musica. Parliamo di un focoso e sensuale fandango, lustro di smalto tecnico con passi brillanti, incroci di mano, e bellissime melodie. Un grande, piccolo pezzo di musica!
Buon ascolto.

This specific prélude should be performed "entre quatre-z-yeux" (literally "between four eyes") meaning intimately, as if privately. Des pas sur la neige sonically creates a sense of isolation. There is something particularly impactful about this composition in 2020 as so much music making is happening at home with so many unable to safely collaborate in real time together. Although one of the least technically challenging of Debussy's 24 préludes, I personally find less to be more in this instance.

The dates of composition of the 13 Pieces, Op. 76, vary, the earliest, the first two or perhaps three, written in 1911 and some others as late as 1916. Published by Westerlund in Finland and later by Hansen, they respond to the same financial needs and commercial realities. Esquisse and Etude are similar infiguration, and bells are aptly suggested in Carillon.

The capricious Humoresque leads to a characteristic Consolation and the graceful figuration of Romanzetta. The seventh piece, Affettuoso, is marked Agitato and followed by a most uncharacteristic Pièce enfantine and a rapid Arabesque. The C sharp minor Elegiaco marked Poco agitato is succeeded by the inventive Linnaea (Twinflower of the North), marked Andantino con moto, the arpeggios of Capriccietto and the whimsical Harlequinade

Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
La Sonata in Si bemolle maggiore K. 57 di Domenico Scarlatti che presenteremo oggi è quasi certamente un lavoro giovanile. La capacità di dire cose molto importanti con poche parole è la prerogativa dei grandi artisti, ma anche i grandi artisti hanno conosciuto un tempo in cui erano giovani, pieni d'entusiasmo, ma sprovvisti d'esperienza. Questa Sonata principia come una danza dignitosa, quasi un minuetto glorificato, ma in questa particolare forma il giovane Domenico è come un leone in gabbia: gli pare che non ci sia abbastanza movimento nella musica, e allora la infarcisce di folli incroci di mano, di vasti salti, di floride figurazioni, ed ovviamente, anche se è giovane, è un genio che pur con tutti questi elementi riesce a mettere assieme un pezzo di musica fra i più godibili ed entusiasmanti.
Buon ascolto.

Mikrokosmos, progressive pieces for piano in 6 volumes, Sz. 107, BB 105 (1926-1939)

140. 00:00

Claude Helffer, piano

Mikrokosmos was originally designed as a collection of pieces for the beginning pianist, but over time it took on grander proportions, comprising 153 individual pieces that spanned the range of technical difficulty. Dividing into six volumes, it begins with pieces for beginners and progresses to those that challenge even the most accomplished pianist. That Mikrokosmos has become a viable progressive method is demonstrated by its ubiquity in the repertories of modern piano students, but its reputation rests on more than its technical and pedagogical applications; Bartók's work represents a varied and finely crafted catalog of twentieth century musical idioms. In Bartók's own words, it "appears as a synthesis of all the musical and technical problems which were treated and in some case only partially solved in the previous piano works." Perhaps chief among these musical problems was Bartók's attempted synthesis of Eastern and Western European musical traditions, particularly Eastern folk music with the Germanic tradition (as represented by Bach and Beethoven) and with the progressive harmonies of Claude Debussy. 

The first 66 pieces in Mikrokosmos (Vols. 1 and 2) are dedicated to Bartók's son, Peter, for whose use they were originally intended. Many of these pieces are technical exercises, useful for developing finger and hand independence, as well as hand span; however, they are also of interest for their musical language. Hungarian folk tunes, pentatonic, whole-tone and modal harmonies, as well as more adventurous octatonic chromatic scales all form the basis for these short pieces. 

Volumes 3 and 4 make up numbers 67 through 121. These pieces display increased harmonic complexity and technical demands. Bartók employs more polymodes (the use of different modes, or keys, simultaneously), along with octatonic and diatonic scale fragments to construct these pieces. The compositions in the third and fourth volumes are also important because they betray the influence of Franz Liszt, particularly in terms of tone color; Bartók wrote of his desire, in these pieces, to "poetically color the piano tone." 

The final volumes (5 and 6) of the Mikrokosmos were intended as concert pieces for professional pianists. They differ from the preceding pieces in many respects: their contrapuntal texture is more dense (four parts), the melodic and harmonic material is more characteristic of Bartók's non-pedagogical works, and rhythmic structures are much more complicated and include vigorous syncopations and Bulgarian dance rhythms. 

While Bartók's intention to synthesize Bach, Beethoven, and Debussy was perhaps not fully realized, Mikrokosmos nonetheless compares well with some of Bach and Debussy's ostensibly pedagogical keyboard works. Like Bach's Inventions or Debussy's Études, for example, Mikrokosmos is not merely a work of practical value, but also a work of art with much purely musical substance. [Allmusic.com]

Mikrokosmos was originally designed as a collection of pieces for the beginning pianist, but over time it took on grander proportions, comprising 153 individual pieces that spanned the range of technical difficulty. Dividing into six volumes, it begins with pieces for beginners and progresses to those that challenge even the most accomplished pianist. That Mikrokosmos has become a viable progressive method is demonstrated by its ubiquity in the repertories of modern piano students, but its reputation rests on more than its technical and pedagogical applications; Bartók's work represents a varied and finely crafted catalog of twentieth century musical idioms. In Bartók's own words, it "appears as a synthesis of all the musical and technical problems which were treated and in some case only partially solved in the previous piano works." Perhaps chief among these musical problems was Bartók's attempted synthesis of Eastern and Western European musical traditions, particularly Eastern folk music with the Germanic tradition (as represented by Bach and Beethoven) and with the progressive harmonies of Claude Debussy. 

The first 66 pieces in Mikrokosmos (Vols. 1 and 2) are dedicated to Bartók's son, Peter, for whose use they were originally intended. Many of these pieces are technical exercises, useful for developing finger and hand independence, as well as hand span; however, they are also of interest for their musical language. Hungarian folk tunes, pentatonic, whole-tone and modal harmonies, as well as more adventurous octatonic chromatic scales all form the basis for these short pieces. 

Volumes 3 and 4 make up numbers 67 through 121. These pieces display increased harmonic complexity and technical demands. Bartók employs more polymodes (the use of different modes, or keys, simultaneously), along with octatonic and diatonic scale fragments to construct these pieces. The compositions in the third and fourth volumes are also important because they betray the influence of Franz Liszt, particularly in terms of tone color; Bartók wrote of his desire, in these pieces, to "poetically color the piano tone." 

The final volumes (5 and 6) of the Mikrokosmos were intended as concert pieces for professional pianists. They differ from the preceding pieces in many respects: their contrapuntal texture is more dense (four parts), the melodic and harmonic material is more characteristic of Bartók's non-pedagogical works, and rhythmic structures are much more complicated and include vigorous syncopations and Bulgarian dance rhythms. 

While Bartók's intention to synthesize Bach, Beethoven, and Debussy was perhaps not fully realized, Mikrokosmos nonetheless compares well with some of Bach and Debussy's ostensibly pedagogical keyboard works. Like Bach's Inventions or Debussy's Études, for example, Mikrokosmos is not merely a work of practical value, but also a work of art with much purely musical substance. [Allmusic.com]

Valente A.Lo ballo dellIntorcia.YT_description:
The Horniman has a weekly music performances on Thursday afternoons called Hear it Live! which usually takes place in the Music Gallery. These are free, live sessions.

The musicians have been working with Horniman staff to create informal musical recordings, playing a piece of their own choosing and using one of four expertly restored and maintained early keyboard instruments. The instruments are: the Neapolitan virginals by Onofrio Guarracino, 1668; the square piano by Adam Beyer, London, 1777; the English chamber organ, attributed to Joseph Beloudy, London, c.1800; and the double-manual harpsichord by Jacob Kirckman, London, 1772.

We hope that, with the hum of visitors in the background, you will feel that you are experiencing the Music Gallery first-hand, with your friends and family. And, what’s more, that you are being welcomed by live music! 

Videos: Beatrice Brooker, Programming and Admin Assistant – Musical Events

The Hear It Live! programme and recordings are made possible through the generosity of the National Lottery Heritage Fund.

(Please note, these performances took place prior to the Horniman closure, following the lockdown).


------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
https://www.horniman.ac.uk

The Horniman Museum and Gardens is an inspiring, surprising, family-friendly, free attraction in South London’s Forest Hill. We’ve been open since Victorian times, when Frederick John Horniman first opened his house and extraordinary collection of objects to visitors. Since then, our collection has grown tenfold and includes internationally important collections of anthropology and musical instruments, as well as an acclaimed aquarium, Butterfly House and natural history collection. 

Unusually for such an important museum, you can see our collection up-close and face-to-face. You can even pick up, try on and play with some of our objects.

Bartok B.Ballad (No 35) from For Childre.YT_description:
Here is my new recording, made last weekend, of  Bartók's educational set For Children. The colorful Hungarian title "A Gyermekeknek" somehow always amuses me. The pieces were penned down in 1908/09, but Bartók revised the set in 1945, towards the end of his life, leaving out 6 pieces and slightly altering others. It is this final version that I play here.

The two books are quite different in character. I marginally prefer 
Book I, based on Hungarian Folk Tunes. These are more ebullient, the colors brighter, than those in Book II, based on Slovak Folk Tunes, which are generally darker and more introspective, at times 
reminiscent of Janacek (as they ought to be, being Slovak). 

Both books contain a wealth of great music, and certainly not all of the pieces seen suitable for children - unless they have advanced technique and musicality. I hope my cycle can be enjoyed despite a couple of small read errors (which, obviously and  irritatingly, I only noticed during video preparation).

Mel (Mélanie) Bonis (1858-1937)
France

* Born into a lower middle class family, she taught herself piano
* At the age of 12 her parents were encouraged to get her formal training 
* She began her studies at the Conservatoire when she was 16 and attended school at the same time that Claude Debussy did
* Studied with César Franck
* Her parents arranged a marriage for her to a businessman who did not like music so she retreated from music while she raised her children
* She ended up having an affair and having a child with a man she had previously fallen in love with who encouraged her to return to composing which she did
* Became a member of the Société des compositeurs de musique and also became a published composer
* Wrote over 300 pieces for piano, organ, orchestra, and various chamber music groupings

Bartok B.Teasing Song (No 18) from For C.YT_description:
Here is my new recording, made last weekend, of  Bartók's educational set For Children. The colorful Hungarian title "A Gyermekeknek" somehow always amuses me. The pieces were penned down in 1908/09, but Bartók revised the set in 1945, towards the end of his life, leaving out 6 pieces and slightly altering others. It is this final version that I play here.

The two books are quite different in character. I marginally prefer 
Book I, based on Hungarian Folk Tunes. These are more ebullient, the colors brighter, than those in Book II, based on Slovak Folk Tunes, which are generally darker and more introspective, at times 
reminiscent of Janacek (as they ought to be, being Slovak). 

Both books contain a wealth of great music, and certainly not all of the pieces seen suitable for children - unless they have advanced technique and musicality. I hope my cycle can be enjoyed despite a couple of small read errors (which, obviously and  irritatingly, I only noticed during video preparation).

Mel (Mélanie) Bonis (1858-1937)
France

* Born into a lower middle class family, she taught herself piano
* At the age of 12 her parents were encouraged to get her formal training 
* She began her studies at the Conservatoire when she was 16 and attended school at the same time that Claude Debussy did
* Studied with César Franck
* Her parents arranged a marriage for her to a businessman who did not like music so she retreated from music while she raised her children
* She ended up having an affair and having a child with a man she had previously fallen in love with who encouraged her to return to composing which she did
* Became a member of the Société des compositeurs de musique and also became a published composer
* Wrote over 300 pieces for piano, organ, orchestra, and various chamber music groupings

Bailey K.Triplet Falls.YT_description:
https://kerinbailey.com.au/music-shop/triplet-falls-piano-solo/#.YnRjqOhByUk
Triplet Falls is a jazz waltz in A minor - intermediate standard - grade 4.
Listings in Australia in AMEB, ANZCA, St. Cecilia, School Syllabi etc.

Form: Intro, AABA. The intro phrase re-occurs after each A section. Key is A minor.
A1: 5-15. A2: 16-26. B: 27-35; 27-30 is C major (relative), 31-32 is Bb major. A3: 36-46. Coda: 47-end.

Triplet Falls begins with the classic jazz waltz vamp, and this recurs in the LH throughout.
The main A theme is a descending run which fits nicely under the hand - the suggested fingering makes it easier!
The B section starts in C major with the descending triplet phrase, which is repeated in Bb major at measure 31. The LH here is the classic II-V-I progression - Dm9 G13 | Cmaj9; Cm9 F13 | Bbmaj7.
A3 is the same melody and the LH expands to the leap from root to chord.
The intro vamp returns for the coda from 47.
The pedal is marked in detail in the online download and most recent print edition.

Ignaz Moscheles - Etude op. 70 n. 11
Fausto Bongelli, piano
Ignaz Moscheles, (born May 23, 1794, Prague, Bohemia, Austrian Habsburg domain [now in Czech Republic]—died March 10, 1870, Leipzig [Germany]), Czech pianist, one of the outstanding virtuosos of his era.
Moscheles studied at the Prague Conservatory and later at Vienna under Johann Georg Albrechtsberger and Antonio Salieri. In 1814, commissioned by Artaria & Co., publishers, he made the first piano arrangement of Ludwig van Beethoven’s opera Fidelio, under the composer’s supervision. After giving piano recitals in Germany and France, he settled in London in 1821. In 1829 he took part in the first London performance of the Concerto for Two Pianos by Felix Mendelssohn, who had been his pupil. He conducted the first English performance of Beethoven’s Missa Solemnis and later conducted Beethoven’s Ninth Symphony at the Philharmonic Society, of which he was a regular conductor from 1845. From 1846 he was principal professor of piano at the Leipzig Conservatory, and his reputation and skill as a teacher were important factors in the continued success of that institution.
Moscheles belonged to a conservative school of piano playing that did not lend itself to the works of Frédéric Chopin and Franz Liszt; of the younger composers of his day, he leaned more toward Mendelssohn and Robert Schumann. Nevertheless, his explorations of the gradations of tone colour influenced Liszt as well as Schumann. He was also admired for his brilliant extempore performances. His own compositions include eight piano concerti, studies, and chamber works.

Scarlatti D.Sonata in Bb major K 392.YT_description:
Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in B flat major K. 392.
00:10 Introduction
02:27 Sonata
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
Agli albori di questo progetto stavo leggendo alcune Sonate di Domenico Scarlatti quando il mio occhio fu colpito da un passaggio molto strano: una nota, un Re, era ripetuto non meno di trentadue volte! Ora, nella musica moderna queste cose accadono assai spesso, ma nell'epoca barocca un passo del genere dev'essere stato rivoluzionario (a meno che, ovviamente, non si parli d'un suonatore d'orchestra il cui strumento rimpolpi l'armonia; da solisti, cose del genere non si vedeono spesso). Incuriosito, incominciai ad indagare. La prima cosa che scoprii fu che il passo in questione appartiene alla Sonata in Si bemolle maggiore di Domenico Scarlatti che presenteremo oggi. La seconda, e qui devo scoprire un altarino, è che il mio riferimento all'orchestra non è punto casuale: questa Sonata è molto “orchestrale”, sia per scopo e scrittura. Ad esempio, vi sono passi (specialmente alla mano sinistra), in cui dopo un salto d'ottava si ripete il basso due volte, e questa era una figura molto usata dai musicisti veneziani del Settecento. Ciò detto, però, questa Sonata non appartiene a nessuna “scuola nazionale”. Piuttosto, si tratta di un pezzo quasi operistico, molto brillante e pieno di indizi e ammiccamenti i quali, secondo me, indicano che qui Domenico desidera una lettura fantastica ed estrosa. Ad esempio, vi è un piccolo passaggio che si ripete tre volte: la prima con molta ornamentazione, la seconda con meno ornamenti, e la terza senza abbrallimenti di sorta; sono convinto che questo significhi un aumento d'intensità, forse anche di velocità, o di intento. Qua e là vi sono momenti di intenso lirismo, bellissimi, interpolati da passi focosi. Nell'insieme, questa Sonata è un meraviglioso pezzo di musica, ed è un grande privilegio, per me, potervelo presentare.
Buon ascolto.

Rebikov V.Morceau Lyrique Op 13 No 9.YT_description:
As you might know, I already played pieces by Rebikov, and there are not many left which I haven't played. This set is one of them. Apparently (or I overlooked it....) it is even not listed in the work list on Imslp, so I was very surprised to find it. I found the score on pianophilia
http://www.pianophilia.com/phpBB3/viewtopic.php?f=11&t=570&p=32625&hilit=rebikov#p32625

Rebikov (1866-1920) russian composer, music teacher (in Moscow), composed operas, pantomimes, orchestral suites, sacral works. In Op.48 he is the first composer in the history of music to use diatonic clusters for piano as a repeated pattern (I'm not counting Biber here). Yes, even before Cowell, because they were composed in 1913. Rebikov composed a lot of very sensitive and beautiful late-romantic style piano pieces, often with a unique touch to them, for example here one can note the repeated use of movements of fourths in a particular way (like early Prokofiev also experimented with...). Also, he is a pretty obscure composer. While his early works (let's say pre 20th century) are mostly romantic and easy to grasp, he later developed a very characteristic style which uses a lot of repetition of small musical cells and a diminished/augmented harmonic language, also with typical russian chromatic elements. one could say it is rather experimental, but not in an "ugly" completely atonal way. It's highly interesting. In La Danse Gaie for example one can see the quirkiness of his pieces sometimes, literally it feels like he sat down one evening and just wanted to write the most unpianistic piano piece every composed. And indeed, it is extremely nasty to play if you don't have gigantic hands. My left hand really hurt a lot, just after playing through it one time. Also the melody within(!) those big chords played by the left hand is just attacking the piano player. But things like that make composers very interesting I think. That's why many people love Alkan for example. In his ouvre there are many of those little quirks and strange details, and it's just a joy to explore and understand them if you study it long enough.

Scarlatti D.Sonata - K 550 Bb major.YT_description:
Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in B flat major K. 550.
00:10 Introduction
01:34 Sonata
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
La primavera è alle porte, ma per fortuna Domenico ha una Sonata per ogni stagione! La Sonata in Si bemolle maggiore K. 550 di Domenico Scarlatti che presenteremo oggi potrebbe benissimo esser chiamata la sua “Primavera”. Un lavoro della maturità scritto magnificamente dall'inizio alla fine, esordisce con un tema arioso, la personificazione musicale di un idillio arcadico. Significativamente, anche l'armonia segue questa inclinazione bucolica della musica, e tinge la melodia con piccoli tocchi di luce nello stesso modo in cui farebbe un grande Maestro d'Arte con il suo dipinto. Un grande pezzo di musica, per essere tale, abbisogna di contrasti; allora Domenico scrive un passaggio in cui la mano sinistra esegue continui cambi di armonia in una modulazione costante che dà l'impressione di un qualcosa che pulsa lentamente, e l'effetto è ipnotico, forse addirittura scioccante. Subito dopo, per chiudere la Sonata, Domnico scrive delle terzine veloci e sbarazzine, quasi a dirci: “vedete? E che ci vuole? È facile..”. Suppongo che anche questa sia una manifestazione del suo genio.
Buon ascolto.

Palmgren S.Kevatyo Op 27 No 4.YT_description:
Selim Palmgren (1878–1951) was a Finnish composer, pianist, and conductor.  One of Finland's finest pianist-composers, he trained with Conrad Ansorge and Ferrucio Busoni in Berlin. 

This lovely piece May Night (Kevätyö) is part of a set of seven pieces Op.27 called "Spring", written in 1906/07. In its day it was very popular, and remains one of Palmgren's best known piano pieces.

I recoirded it today on february 23, 2020 because the continually dismal weather, with high winds driving sheets of rain, made me yearn for a balmy spring night.

The painting is "After the storm" (1885) by Eero Järnefelt.

Mussorgsky M.Scherzo in C minor.YT_description:
Modest Petrovich Mussorgsky - Модест Петрович Мусоргский (1839-1881)
Scherzo in C# Minor - Скерцо cis-moll (1858) (version 2)

The Могучая кучка ('Mighty Handful') were at least initially a group of individuals to whom music was a secondary career. Mussorgsky became a military cadet at age 13 and eventually received a commission with the Preobrazhensky Guards Regiment.  In 1856 Mussorgsky met Alexander Borodin, who later recollected:

'His little uniform was spic and span, close-fitting, his feet turned outwards, his hair smoothed down and greased, his nails perfectly cut, his hands well groomed like a lord's. His manners were elegant, aristocratic: his speech likewise, delivered through somewhat clenched teeth, interspersed with French phrases, rather precious. There was a touch—though very moderate—of foppishness. His politeness and good manners were exceptional. The ladies made a fuss of him. He sat at the piano and, throwing up his hands coquettishly, played with extreme sweetness and grace (etc) extracts from Trovatore, Traviata, and so on, and around him buzzed in chorus: "Charmant, délicieux!" and suchlike. I met Modest Petrovich three or four times at Popov's in this way, both on duty and at the hospital.'

Acquaintance with Borodin led to introductions to Dargomyzhsky, Cui, the hugely influential critic Stasov, and Balakirev. The latter two would later become mentors to the young composer. The Scherzo in C# minor was composed in the same year that Mussorgsky began to study with Mily Balakirev.

Perle G.Six New Etudes.YT_description:
George Perle (1915-2009): Six New Etudes, per pianoforte (1984).

1.Praeludium
2. Gigue
3. Romance
4. Papillons
5. Variations
6. Perpetuum mobile

Michael Boriskin, pianoforte

Cover image: painting by Alma Thomas.

The dazzling Six New Etudes (1984) is the companion set to Perle's immensely successful Six Etudes of 1976. Like the earlier collection, the new studies explore both the "usual" mechanical problems and more subtle pianistic concerns involving articulation, nuance, pedaling, and rhythm. The short "Praeludium" is a dashing curtain-raiser, full of daredevil stretches and double notes. The whirling "Gigue," in rondo form, is filled with treacherous leaps and quick hand-crossings. The "Butterflies" in the title of the third etude are probably the only bi-rhythmic ones in music; they flutter along quietly in fours in the right hand against threes in the left, and disappear in just a minute. "Romance" is a sensitive study in subtle dynamic inflection and controlled rubato, with a yearning, rising phrase at the outset which becomes progressively more insistent with each appearance. "Variations" is a tour-de-force of rapid, wide-ranging chordal passages and sudden changes of dynamics and articulation; any of the eleven uninterrupted sections could conceivably be considered the main material, while the remaining ten sections offer various perspectives, somewhat like a prism revealing its many facets when observed from different positions. "Perpetuum mobile," the solo version of the identically-titled movement of Serenade No. 3, is an exhilarating study of ethereal scales, prickly cross-rhythms, and nimble, intricate pedaling.
(Michael Boriskin).

For his second solo album on Decca, Benjamin Grosvenor has assembled a typically imaginative and appealing programme of piano music inspired by the dance form. Dances is a dazzling display of solo works for piano from Bach to Boogie Woogie; via Chopin, Granados, Albeniz, Scriabin and the Blue Danube. Shining the spotlight on the music of movement, this album was inspired by a letter from the great pianist-composer Ferruccio Busoni to his pupil Egon Petri proposing a “dance programme” as a theme for Petri’s recitals, a concept Grosvenor expanded on for his Queen Elizabeth Hall debut recital in 2012.

A former Gramophone Young Artist of the Year, Grosvenor will appearing at two BBC Proms in 2014 with a performance of Chopin’s First Piano Concerto with the BBC Philharmonic Orchestra (8th August), followed by a solo recital at Cadogan Hall (1st Sep). In 2011, he was awarded the honour of opening the BBC Proms Concerts season and the youngest-ever soloist to perform on the ‘First Night’.

Scarlatti D.Sonata - K 509 D major.YT_description:
Sandro Ivo Bartoli plays Domenico Scarlatti's Sonata in D major K. 509.
00:10 Introduction
02:46 Sonata
Sandro dice:
Cari amici buongiorno,
A meno che non siate devoti appassionati della produzione tastieristica di Domenico Scarlatti, è assai probabile che non conosciate la sua Sonata in Re maggior K. 509 che presenteremo oggi. Di fatto, confesso nadidamente che nemmeno io la conoscevo, prima d'imbarcarmi in questo progetto. E mi dispiece, perché è un gran bel pezzo di musica! Senza alcun dubbio, si tratta di una composizione matura, che appartiene agli ultimi anni del Maestro, ove la purezza della linea melodica è quasi mozartiana (in un'evidente anacronismo: Mozart nacque nel 1756, e Domenico morì l'anno successivo: non c'è verso che Domenico abbia imparato qualcosa da Wolfgang). Si comincia alla militaresca, con un tema baldanzoso, ma ben presto Domenico introduce una figura che sarà il fulcro dell'intera Sonata: entrambe le mani si producono in un motivo ritmico nel bel mezzo della tastiera, ma poi svolazzano verso le estremità della stessa. Tutto ciò è molto carino, ma siccome questa Sonata la ha scritta Domenico Scarlatti, quando le mani si producono in queste mosse estreme non vanno mai verso la medesima nota. Per esempio, la sinistra va a prendere un La grave, ma la destra prende un Do diesis acuto. Oppure, la sinistra prende un Fa diesis grave, e la destra vola verso un Re acuto! Tutto ciò rende il lavoro del suonatore un po' più complicato del solito, ma la stessa tecnica sarà usata alla perfezione da Frédérik Chopin, nello Scherzo della Sonata in si bemolle minore Op. 35, la celeberrima “marcia funebre”. Ora, spendiamo un momento per raccogliere le nostre idee: questa è una Sonata della maturità del Maestro; lui non ha nulla da dimostrare a chicchessia, ma scrive questa figura ove le mani si lanciano verso le estremità della tastiera, quasi come volessero abbracciarla. Almeno nella mia opinione, questa Sonata è un eloquente testimone alla gioia di suonare uno strumento a tastiera. Ed è con la medesima gioia che ve la presento.
Buon ascolto.

Reger M.Moment musical in C minor Op 44.YT_description:
The collection this piece is taken from is called 'Zehn kleine Vortragsstücke' (ten little pieces for performance) and they were composed in 1899. Reger himself had mixed feelings about composing for educational purposes and said as much in a letter to a magazine editor he sent these pieces to shortly after their publication. But I think these misgivings are groundless. The collection as a whole is certainly easier than any of his four books of pieces entitled  'Aus meinem Tagebuch' (from my diary) Op.82 and individually the pieces are shorter. However, the level of inspiration remains high, while the essentials of Reger's style fully present. 

The piece is in ABA form: the B section is quite short, in A major, the outer sections in C sharp minor. It is marked 'Anmutig, etwas lebhaft, doch nicht zu sehr' (gracefully, somewhat lively, but not too much so) and there is no metronome marking. The two-step rhythm, occasionally reminiscent of a polka, neutralises any feeling of sadness you might expect from the minor mode.

This piece has often been anthologised and has appeared on exam syllabuses too (Trinity had it on their grade 8 list for 2018-20). Reger's writing for the piano tends to be quite full-bodied and the double note passage in bars 6-8 in the right hand is characteristic. So although the music is easy to make sense of, the player occasionally faces awkward technical challenges (which are not usually apparent to the listener). Don't let me put you off, though: it's really worth the effort!

Moscheles I.24 Studies Op. 70 no. 1.YT_description:
Ignaz Moscheles Etude op.70 n.1
Fausto Bongelli, piano
Ignaz Moscheles, (born May 23, 1794, Prague, Bohemia, Austrian Habsburg domain [now in Czech Republic]—died March 10, 1870, Leipzig [Germany]), Czech pianist, one of the outstanding virtuosos of his era.
Moscheles studied at the Prague Conservatory and later at Vienna under Johann Georg Albrechtsberger and Antonio Salieri. In 1814, commissioned by Artaria & Co., publishers, he made the first piano arrangement of Ludwig van Beethoven’s opera Fidelio, under the composer’s supervision. After giving piano recitals in Germany and France, he settled in London in 1821. In 1829 he took part in the first London performance of the Concerto for Two Pianos by Felix Mendelssohn, who had been his pupil. He conducted the first English performance of Beethoven’s Missa Solemnis and later conducted Beethoven’s Ninth Symphony at the Philharmonic Society, of which he was a regular conductor from 1845. From 1846 he was principal professor of piano at the Leipzig Conservatory, and his reputation and skill as a teacher were important factors in the continued success of that institution.
Moscheles belonged to a conservative school of piano playing that did not lend itself to the works of Frédéric Chopin and Franz Liszt; of the younger composers of his day, he leaned more toward Mendelssohn and Robert Schumann. Nevertheless, his explorations of the gradations of tone colour influenced Liszt as well as Schumann. He was also admired for his brilliant extempore performances. His own compositions include eight piano concerti, studies, and chamber works.

Moscheles I.Studie in E major No 4 from.YT_description:
I. Moscheles Etude  op.70 n.4
Fausto Bongelli, piano
Ignaz Moscheles, (born May 23, 1794, Prague, Bohemia, Austrian Habsburg domain [now in Czech Republic]—died March 10, 1870, Leipzig [Germany]), Czech pianist, one of the outstanding virtuosos of his era.
Moscheles studied at the Prague Conservatory and later at Vienna under Johann Georg Albrechtsberger and Antonio Salieri. In 1814, commissioned by Artaria & Co., publishers, he made the first piano arrangement of Ludwig van Beethoven’s opera Fidelio, under the composer’s supervision. After giving piano recitals in Germany and France, he settled in London in 1821. In 1829 he took part in the first London performance of the Concerto for Two Pianos by Felix Mendelssohn, who had been his pupil. He conducted the first English performance of Beethoven’s Missa Solemnis and later conducted Beethoven’s Ninth Symphony at the Philharmonic Society, of which he was a regular conductor from 1845. From 1846 he was principal professor of piano at the Leipzig Conservatory, and his reputation and skill as a teacher were important factors in the continued success of that institution.
Moscheles belonged to a conservative school of piano playing that did not lend itself to the works of Frédéric Chopin and Franz Liszt; of the younger composers of his day, he leaned more toward Mendelssohn and Robert Schumann. Nevertheless, his explorations of the gradations of tone colour influenced Liszt as well as Schumann. He was also admired for his brilliant extempore performances. His own compositions include eight piano concerti, studies, and chamber works.

Max Bruch is much better known as a composer for the violin. - http://www.allmusic.com/artist/q7108/biography - http://www.classiccat.net/bruch_m/biography.php

From the CD booklet: "Although Bruch was known as an excellent piano player and often appeared publicly as a pianist, he chose the violin as the instrument of his creative expression. When asked why, he once replied, 'Because the violin can sing a melody better than the piano can, and melody is the soul of music.' One may disagree with Bruch, but his statement is reason enough to comprehend his lack of interest in composing for the piano."

The booklet goes on to say that these 6 "disarmingly simple and lyrical" pieces date from Bruch's youth and are evidence of "his firm grasp of compositional form and technique, of his emerging creativity," and of his "idiomatic sense of melody and warmth."

🎼How much can you say in just one minute?

Mozart W.Ein Madchen oder Weibchen arr..YT_description:
Ein Mädchen oder Weibchen
For a Girl or a Woman
from Die Zauberflote, K. 620
by W.A. Mozart (1756-91)
Arr. by Christopher Norton

In Mozart's 1791 opera Die Zauberflote (The Magic Flute), this tune is sung by a comic character called Papageno, the queen's bird-catcher.  He accompanies the hero Tamino in his quest to rescue the queen's daughter Pamina, who has been abducted.  To protect them, Tamino is given a magic flute, and Papageno magic bells.  In the aria arranged here for piano, Papageno longs to meet the girl of his dreams, who later turns out to be Papagena.  He accompanies the song on his magic bells, which in the opera are played on the glockenspiel.

Moscheles I.Studie No 19 from Studien Op.YT_description:
Ignaz Moscheles - Etude op. 70 n. 19
Fausto Bongelli, piano
Ignaz Moscheles, (born May 23, 1794, Prague, Bohemia, Austrian Habsburg domain [now in Czech Republic]—died March 10, 1870, Leipzig [Germany]), Czech pianist, one of the outstanding virtuosos of his era.
Moscheles studied at the Prague Conservatory and later at Vienna under Johann Georg Albrechtsberger and Antonio Salieri. In 1814, commissioned by Artaria & Co., publishers, he made the first piano arrangement of Ludwig van Beethoven’s opera Fidelio, under the composer’s supervision. After giving piano recitals in Germany and France, he settled in London in 1821. In 1829 he took part in the first London performance of the Concerto for Two Pianos by Felix Mendelssohn, who had been his pupil. He conducted the first English performance of Beethoven’s Missa Solemnis and later conducted Beethoven’s Ninth Symphony at the Philharmonic Society, of which he was a regular conductor from 1845. From 1846 he was principal professor of piano at the Leipzig Conservatory, and his reputation and skill as a teacher were important factors in the continued success of that institution.
Moscheles belonged to a conservative school of piano playing that did not lend itself to the works of Frédéric Chopin and Franz Liszt; of the younger composers of his day, he leaned more toward Mendelssohn and Robert Schumann. Nevertheless, his explorations of the gradations of tone colour influenced Liszt as well as Schumann. He was also admired for his brilliant extempore performances. His own compositions include eight piano concerti, studies, and chamber works.

Phillip Sear plays a beautiful cradle song from 1950 by the Italian pianist and composer Ettore Pozzoli (1873-1957).
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Ettore Pozzoli (1873-1957) studied at the Milan conservatory, where he later taught.  He is best-known for piano studies and theoretical textbooks, which are still used in Italy today.  There is a piano competition named after him that takes place every two years in Seregno, where he was born and died.  The winner of the first competition (1959) was the great Maurizio Pollini.  This piece has a charming dedication to the composer's granddaughter, Maria Teresa Fossati, in memory of the day when he first heard her sing a note: "Alla mia cara nipotana Maria Teresa Fossati a ricordo del giorno in cui fiori sulle sue labbra il primo "Do"".  My thumbnail shows 'Two children singing' by the Swedish artist Jenny Nyström (1854-1946).
